Reconstructive surgeries for congenital malformations of the pinna (auricle) are usually performed after 5 or 6 years of age. The ideal timing for these surgeries is between 6-10 years.

At around 3 years of age, 85% of the auricular growth is complete, and the cartilaginous growth is almost complete by 5 years. Surgery performed on the auricle after 5 or 6 years of age doesn't hinder further growth. Also, autologous cartilages from ribs are harvested for these reconstructive surgeries, which attain full development only after 6 years of age, which is another reason for the timing of these surgeries.

Korner’s septum separates superficial squamosal air cells from the deep petrosal air cells. It can lead to difficulty in locating the mastoid antrum and the deeper cells. The development of the inner ear begins in the 3rd week of fetal life and is completed by the 20th week. The surface ectoderm on each side of the rhombencephalon thickens to form otic/auditory placodes, which then invaginate to form the otic vesicle (otocysts).

The cells of the otic vesicle differentiate to form ganglion cells, which later develop into the vestibulocochlear ganglia. Later, each otic vesicle divides into a dorsal component called pars superior and a ventral component called pars inferior.

Pars superior gives rise to the utricle, semicircular canals, and endolymphatic ducts. Pars inferior gives rise to the saccule and the cochlear duct. The saccule is connected to the cochlea through a narrow duct called the ductus reuniens.

question: A patient with otitis externa develops parotitis. You suspect that the infection has spread through the fissures of Santorini. Which of the following best describes this fissure?

explanationHtml:

Skin is also very tightly adherent to the cartilage, and hence, furuncles are extremely painful.

Option D: Isthmus, which is the narrowest part of the EAC, is not present at the junction of cartilaginous and bony parts. It is situated 5-6 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane, in the bony part of the EAC. Foreign bodies that go beyond the isthmus are difficult to remove and are called impacted and need surgical instrumentation for removal.

Ceruminous glands are modified apocrine sweat glands. They open into hair follicles & participate in wax production.

Apocrine glands release their products by decapitation. It is a process by which membrane-bound cytoplasm from the apical surface of the cells buds off into the lumen of the duct and is secreted. Some apocrine glands have specific names. Those on the eyelids are referred to as Moll’s glands, and those on the external auditory meatus are termed ceruminous glands.

There are 2 main types of secretory glands: exocrine and endocrine. Exocrine glands are subclassified as merocrine (or eccrine), apocrine, and holocrine.

The structure given in the image is the incus, one of the three ear ossicles.

Incus is shaped like an anvil (a large metal striking surface for shaping metals). It has a body, a short process, and a long process. It has a saddle-shaped articular facet on its anterior surface that articulates with the malleus. The long process descends vertically and ends as a rounded lenticular process, which articulates with the head of the stapes. Incus has a single nutrient vessel within the long process and no collateral circulation. Thus, it is more susceptible to aseptic necrosis following a middle ear infection.

Option C: The stapes is the smallest bone in the body. It has a head, neck, footplate, and anterior and posterior crura. It is also called a stirrup as it looks like the stirrup/footrest for jockeys while riding a horse.

question: Which of the following nerves supply the tensor tympani?

explanationHtml:
The sensory supply to the middle ear cavity is provided by the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, which is known as Jacobson's nerve.

Jacobson's nerve forms the tympanic plexus along with the caroticotympanic nerves from the internal carotid plexus of the sympathetic fibers. The tympanic plexus innervates the entire middle ear cavity.

Other options:

Options A, B & D: Facial, vagus, and trigeminal nerves do not have any contribution to the tympanic plexus; therefore, they do not provide sensory supply to the middle ear cavity. These nerves supply other parts of the ear.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following cranial nerves provide sensory supply to middle ear cavity?

correctAnswer: D. Tympanic branch of Facial nerve
explanationHtml:
The tympanic branch of the facial nerve does not contribute to the tympanic plexus.

The tympanic plexus is formed by 3 nerves :

  • The glossopharyngeal nerve forms the tympanic branch (Jacobson's nerve)
  • The sympathetic fibers from internal carotid sympathetic plexus forms the superior and inferior caroticotympanic nerve.

The tympanic plexus innervates the tympanic membrane's medial surface, the tympanic cavity, mastoid air cells, and the bony eustachian tube. It also carries secretory fibres for the parotid gland.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: Which of the following nerves does not contribute to the tympanic plexus?

correctAnswer: A. Horizontal in the medial wall, vertical in the posterior wall
explanationHtml:
The facial nerve runs horizontally in the medial wall and vertically in the posterior wall of the middle ear cavity.

The facial nerve consists of intracranial, intratemporal, and extratemporal portions. The intratemporal portion is further divided into meatal, labyrinthine, tympanic (horizontal), and mastoid (vertical) segments.

  • The medial wall is related to the 3rd part of the intratemporal portion, which runs from 1st genu (processus cochleariformis) to 2nd genu (pyramid). It is called the tympanic or horizontal part.
  • The posterior wall is related to the 4th part of the intratemporal portion, which runs from the 2nd genu (pyramid) to the stylomastoid foramen where it exits the temporal bone. It is called the mastoid or the vertical part.

correctAnswer: C. Runs in between the malleus and incus
explanationHtml:
In the middle ear, the chorda tympani runs in between the malleus and incus.

Other options:

Option A: It runs from posterior (posterior canaliculus) to anterior (canal of Huguier) in the middle ear.

explanationHtml:
The fibers of the lesser petrosal nerve synapse in the otic ganglion and not pterygopalatine ganglion.

The lesser petrosal nerve is the parasympathetic or secretomotor nerve for the parotid glands. It arises over the promontory of the middle ear from the tympanic plexus (glossopharyngeal nerve).

The flat non-ciliated epithelium is found in the mastoid air cells and the epitympanum.

The mucosal lining of the middle ear is continuous with that of the nasopharynx but shows variations:

  • Bony eustachian tube- ciliated columnar
  • Cartilaginous eustachian tube- ciliated pseudostratified columnar
  • Protympanum and hypotympanum- ciliated columnar
  • Most of the middle ear space (mesotympanum)- cuboidal
  • Epitympanum & mastoid air cells- flat non-ciliated (pavement-like)

Note: The middle ear is not lined by keratinizing squamous epithelium, and hence its presence anywhere within the middle ear cleft is considered cholesteatoma.

explanationHtml:
The mastoid antrum is the largest mastoid air cell.

The mastoid air cell system is a complex network of air-filled cavities within the mastoid process of the temporal bone. Mastoid antrum is the largest and most constant mastoid air cell because it is present even in a sclerotic mastoid.

Other options:

Option B: Aditus ad antrum is the pathway or the connection between the mastoid antrum and the attic.

Option C: The attic or the epitympanum is the part of the middle ear adjacent to its roof.

Option D: The lower part of the middle ear cavity is sometimes called atrium.
question: Which is the largest mastoid air cell?

explanationHtml:
MacEwen’s (suprameatal) triangle is used as a surgical landmark to locate the mastoid antrum.

MacEwen's triangle directly overlies the mastoid antrum and guides the surgeon, allowing for drainage or removal of diseased tissue during mastoidectomy. By precisely locating the mastoid antrum through this landmark, surgeons can minimize the risk of damaging vital structures nearby, such as the facial nerve, the temporal lobe of brain, and sigmoid sinus. In an adult, the antrum lies 12–15 mm from the surface. This triangle is also the site of tenderness in acute mastoiditis.

The image below shows the boundaries and location of MacEwen's triangle:

[[figure-1]]
question: A patient with acute coalescent mastoiditis undergoes cortical mastoidectomy. Which of the following is used as a surgical landmark to locate the mastoid antrum?

explanationHtml:
Mastoid process does not form the boundary of the suprameatal triangle.

Boundaries of MacEwen’s (suprameatal) triangle:

  • Superior- temporal line, also called the supramastoid crest
  • Anterior- posterosuperior segment of the bony external auditory canal
  • Posterior- the line drawn as a tangent to the external canal.

It is an important landmark to locate the mastoid antrum in mastoid surgery.

The image below shows the boundaries and location of MacEwen's triangle:

Tangent drawn to external auditory canal

explanationHtml:
The mandible is not a pneumatic bone.

In some bones of the skull, notably the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the paranasal sinuses of the frontal, maxilla, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones, many of the internal cavities are filled with air, i.e. they are variably pneumatized. The maxillae are the largest of the pneumatized bones of the midface. They contain the maxillary air sinuses and bear the upper teeth. The mastoid consists of a bone cortex with a 'honeycomb' of air cells underneath.

Note: Types of mastoid pneumatization:

  • Well-pneumatized or cellular: contains multiple air spaces
  • Diploetic: contains marrow spaces and a few air cells.
  • Acellular or sclerotic: No cells or marrow spaces. It can occur due to eustachian or middle ear disease in childhood preventing mastoid development.
question: Which of the following is not a pneumatic bone?

explanationHtml:
The pterygoid is not a part of the temporal bone, it is a part of the sphenoid bone.

The temporal bone consists of the following parts:

  • Squamous part- anterosuperiorly

It articulates with the parietal bone. The persistence of petrosquamous suture is called Korner's septum.

  • Mastoid part- posteroinferiorly.

Its outer surface forms a conical projection called the mastoid process. Sternocleidomastoid, splenius capitis and longissimus capitis attach here.

  • Petrous part- medially
  • The arcuate eminence is related to the superior semicircular canal below
  • The posterior surface contains the internal auditory meatus (IAM). The vestibular aqueduct is present behind the IAM.
  • The inferior surface contains the carotid canal and the jugular fossa (jugular notch).
  • Tympanic part- centrally
  • It contains the external auditory meatus (EAM), and the bony EAM is 16 mm long.
  • The suprameatal triangle is present above the EAM
  • Styloid process- anteroinferior

It gives attachment to:

  • 3 muscles - stylohyoid, styloglossus, stylopharyngeus
  • 2 ligaments - stylohyoid ligament, stylomandibular ligament
  • Zygomatic process

The temporal bone gives the zygomatic process, which articulates with the temporal process of the zygomatic bone to form the zygomatic arch.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

explanationHtml:
Citelli’s angle or sinodural angle is the angle between the sigmoid sinus plate and the tegmen or dural plate.

Citelli's angle, also known as the sinodural angle, is a landmark in cortical mastoidectomy. During mastoidectomy, the surgeon carefully drills up to this angle to identify and protect vital structures while removing the mastoid air cells.

The boundaries of cortical mastoidectomy are:

  • Tegmen plate superiorly
  • Sigmoid sinus plate posteriorly
  • Posterior bony external auditory canal wall anteriorly

This is also called the triangle of attack.

[[figure-1]]
question: While performing cortical mastoidectomy, the head and neck surgeon drills the bone up to the Citelli's angle. This angle is seen between which of the following structures?

explanationHtml:
Donaldson’s line is the surgical landmark to locate the endolymphatic sac.

It is an imaginary line drawn from the horizontal semicircular canal, which bisects the posterior semicircular canal. The endolymphatic sac lies just inferior to it.

question: Endolymphatic sac surgery is performed on a patient who has Ménière disease with intractable vertigo. Which of the following is the surgical landmark to identify the sac?

explanationHtml:
Trautmann’s triangle is a landmark to approach the posterior cranial fossa.

  • It is a triangular area on the medial wall of the mastoid antrum.
  • It is bounded superiorly by the dura or superior petrosal sinus, posteriorly by the sigmoid sinus, and anteriorly by the bony labyrinth.
  • Since here the bone is thin, it can lead to the spreading of infections from the mastoid to the cerebellum.

explanationHtml: The bony cochlea is a coiled tube making 2.5 to 2.75 turns around a central pyramid of bone called the modiolus.
question: The bony cochlea is a coiled tube making _____ turns around a bony pyramid called ____

correctAnswer: C. Scala vestibuli and scala tympani
explanationHtml:
The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate with each other at the apex of the cochlea through an opening called the helicotrema.

Option D: Scala tympani and subarachnoid space are connected by the aqueduct of the cochlea.
question: Which two structures does the helicotrema connect?

explanationHtml:
The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani. It allows for the electrodes to be in close proximity to the ganglion cells and their dendrites which are located in the modiolus and bony spiral lamina of the cochlea.

A cochlear implant is an electronic device used for patients with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), who cannot benefit from a hearing aid. It converts sound to an electrical signal (transduction) and delivers this to the auditory nerve. Prerequisites include an intact cochlear nerve and an intact higher auditory pathway. The electrodes of the cochlear implant are placed in the scala tympani through the round window.

Note: In the auditory brainstem implant, the site of the implant is the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle. It is used when the cochlear nerve is not intact.

[[figure-1]]
question: Where is the electrode placed in cochlear implant procedures?

explanationHtml:
The organ of Corti, present in the scala media, is a part of the membranous labyrinth. It cannot be visualized on a CT scan.

Bony labyrinth consists of:

  • Cochlea (Option A)
  • Vestibule (Option B)
  • Semicircular canals (Option C)

These structures, present in the bony labyrinth, can be seen on a CT scan of the temporal bone. The inner ear lies in the petrous part of the temporal bone.

Membranous labyrinth consists of:

  • Saccule and utricle
  • Cochlear duct/ scala media
  • Semicircular ducts
  • Endolymphatic duct and sac

These structures, present in the membranous labyrinth, cannot be seen on a CT scan of the temporal bone.
question: Which of the following structures can not be visualized on the CT scan of the temporal bone?

explanationHtml:
Scala media or the cochlear duct, is part of the membranous cochlea. It is a separate membranous structure contained within the bony labyrinth of cochlea, but not a part of the bony wall itself.

[[figure-1]]

The main components of the bony cochlea are:

  • Modiolus: bony pillar around which the cochlear canal spirals.
  • Osseous spiral lamina: partially divides the bony cochlear canal.
  • Scala vestibuli: upper perilymph-filled chamber, separated from the scala media (cochlear duct) by Reissner's membrane.
  • Scala tympani: lower perilymph-filled chamber, separated from the scala media (cochlear duct) by the basilar membrane.

Scala media is part of the membranous cochlea and contains the sensory organ of Corti with hair cells. It is filled with endolymph.
question: Which of the following is not a part of the bony labyrinth of the cochlea?

correctAnswer: C. Contains spherical recess for saccule
explanationHtml:
The vestibule contains the spherical recess for the saccule.

It is part of the bony labyrinth and not a part of the auditory pathway. The inside of the medial wall presents with recesses & openings:

  • A spherical recess, which lodges the saccule
  • An elliptical recess, which lodges the utricle
  • An opening for the aqueduct of vestibule
  • An opening for the semicircular canals

[[figure-1]]

options.text: It is a part of the membranous labyrinth
It is a part of the auditory pathway

question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the vestibule?

explanationHtml:
Crus commune is a part of the semicircular canals.

Each semicircular canal has 2 ends, ampullated & non-ampullated which open into the vestibule. The non-ampullated ends of posterior and superior canals unite to form a common channel called crus commune. Therefore, 3 semicircular canals open into vestibule through 5 openings.
question: Which of the following structures is the crus commune a part of?

explanationHtml:
The organ of Corti is the sensory organ of hearing and is present in the inner ear.

Noise-induced hearing loss is a sensorineural hearing loss and is seen in chronic exposure to loud sounds in an occupation. It is caused by irreversible damage to the outer hair cells in the organ of Corti.
question: A 45-year old construction worker presents to you with hearing loss. His audiogram reveals a diagnosis of noise-induced hearing loss. Which organ is most likely to be affected?

correctAnswer: D. Reissner's membrane overlies the organ of Corti
explanationHtml:
The tectorial membrane overlies the organ of Corti, not Reissner's membrane, which separates scala media from scala vestibuli.

The membranes of the cochlea are shown in the image below:

Other options:

Option A: The ampullated end of semicircular canals contains a thickened neuroepithelium ridge called crista ampullaris.

Option B: The sensory epithelium of the utricle and saccule is called macula and is concerned with linear acceleration and deceleration.

Option C: The basilar membrane separates scala media from scala tympani and supports the organ of Corti.

question: Which of the following sentence is false?

explanationHtml:
Endolymph resembles intracellular fluid and is hence high in potassium and low in sodium content.

Endolymph fills the entire membranous labyrinth, i.e., scala media, saccule, utricle, semicircular ducts, and endolymphatic duct and sac. It is secreted by the stria vascularis, which contains the vascular endothelium.

Perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are both extracellular fluids (ECF) that are high in sodium. Perilymph fills the space between the bony and the membranous labyrinth.

The differences between the endolymph and the perilymph are discussed in the pearl below:
question: Which of the following fluids has high potassium and low sodium content?

explanationHtml:
Infections can spread from the CNS (meningitis) to the inner ear (labyrinthitis) or vice versa through the aqueduct of cochlea.

Scala tympani, which is filled with perilymph, is connected with the subarachnoid space, which is filled with CSF, through the aqueduct of cochlea.

Other options:

Vestibular aqueduct (Option D) gives a passage to the endolymphatic duct. The terminal part of the endolymphatic duct forms the endolymphatic sac (Option A). The endolymphatic duct and sac are filled with endolymph and are not connected to CSF, as opposed to perilymph. Similarly, scala media (Option C) is filled with endolymph. Since endolymph is not connected to CSF via any path, this is not a route of spread of infection between CNS and inner ear.

Note: The internal acoustic meatus provides another path of spread of infection between CNS and inner ear.
question: A 20-year-old man diagnosed with meningitis later develops sensorineural hearing loss. Which structure is responsible for the spread of his infection to the cochlea?

correctAnswer: A. Higher frequencies are heard at the base
explanationHtml:
Higher frequencies of sound are heard at the basal coil, while lower frequencies are heard at the apical coil of the membranous cochlea.

This is because the length of basilar membrane increases as we proceed from the basal coil to the apical coil.

options.text: Higher frequencies are heard at the base
Lower frequencies are heard at the base
All frequencies are heard at the base
All frequencies are heard at the apex

question: Which of the following statements is true about membranous cochlea?

explanationHtml:
Semicircular canals respond to angular acceleration and deceleration. The receptors are the cristae, located in the ampullated ends of the three semicircular ducts.

Other options:

Options A & B: The utricle and saccule, which contain the macula, are stimulated by linear acceleration and deceleration or gravitational pull during the head tilts.

Option D: The cochlea contains the organ of Corti, which is responsible for hearing.
question: Angular movements are sensed by

correctAnswer: D. Utriculosaccular duct and endolymphatic sac
explanationHtml:
The endolymphatic duct is formed as a continuation of the utriculo-saccular duct, the union of two ducts, one each from the saccule and the utricle. Its terminal part is dilated to form an endolymphatic sac. Therefore endolymphatic duct connects the utriculosaccular duct and the endolymphatic sac.

Other options:

Option A: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani are filled with perilymph and communicate with each other at the apex of cochlea through an opening called the helicotrema.

Option B: Ductus reunions connect the cochlear duct to the saccule.

Option C: Aqueduct of cochlea connects scala tympani with the subarachnoid space.

Note: Endolymphatic sac lies between the two layers of dura. It is surgically important and is exposed for drainage or shunt operation in Meniere’s disease.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which two structures does the endolymphatic duct connect?

explanationHtml:
Blood supply to the inner ear is by labyrinthine artery. The labyrinthine artery has a variable origin. It usually arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, but may arise from basilar artery, the superior cerebellar artery or, occasionally, the posterior inferior cerebellar artery.

The labyrinthine artery enters the inner ear via the internal acoustic meatus. It divides into cochlear and vestibular branches to supply various parts of the inner ear.
question: Blood supply to the labyrinth is most commonly from which of the following arteries?

explanationHtml:
The external ear anomaly seen here is a pre-auricular tag/appendage.

Pre-auricular tags/appendages are congenital external ear anomalies. They are seen as skin-covered pieces of cartilage anywhere between the tragus and the angle of the mouth. The majority of pre-auricular tags are isolated findings; in some cases, they may be a part of a genetic syndrome like Goldenhar syndrome.
question: Which of the following external ear anomalies can be seen in the image below?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the image are suggestive of a preauricular sinus seen between the tragus and crus of the helix. It arises due to a developmental defect during formation of pinna.

Preauricular sinus is the most common congenital anomaly of the 1st branchial arch. It arises due to the incomplete fusion of the hillocks of His/tubercles that develop to form the pinna. It can get repeatedly infected and form an abscess, which would then require surgical excision.

The development of pinna is from the fusion of 6 tubercles known as hillocks of His as shown in the illustration below:

[[figure-1]]

question: A patient presents to the OPD with the following finding and history of pus discharge from the same area. What is the likely etiology of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given image showing a malformed/underdeveloped pinna appearing like tubercles is suggestive of microtia. It is frequently accompanied by hearing loss.

Microtia is frequently associated with anomalies of the external auditory canal, middle and internal ear. The condition may be unilateral or bilateral. It may be associated with congenital canal atresia or canal stenosis.

question: An 8-month-old child was brought to your OPD with the following finding.  What is your diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Traverses close to the facial nerve
explanationHtml:
Collaural fistula traverses close to the facial nerve within the substance of the parotid. It is a congenital anomaly of 1st branchial cleft.

The fistula has two openings:

  • One situated in the neck just below and behind the angle of the mandible
  • The other one is in the external auditory canal or the middle ear.

The fistula can get infected. In case of recurrent infections, the fistula tract needs to be excised.

question: A 5-year-old girl was brought to you with complaints of serous discharge from a cutaneous opening on the right side of her neck. A fistulogram confirms your diagnosis of collaural fistula. Which of the following is a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The image shows a cauliflower ear deformity, which is likely due to untreated auricular hematoma.

Auricular hematoma is a collection of blood between the auricular cartilage and its perichondrium. If left untreated, the extravasated blood may clot and then organize, resulting in a typical deformity called cauliflower ear. It is also called pugilistic or boxer’s ear.

Auricular hematoma is often seen in boxers, wrestlers, and rugby players due to blunt trauma. Treatment comprises of aspiration of the hematoma under strict aseptic precautions and a pressure dressing, to prevent reaccumulation. Aspiration may need to be repeated. If aspiration fails, incision and drainage should be done. All cases should receive prophylactic antibiotics.
question: A professional wrestler presents to your OPD with the deformity of the ear shown below. What is the most likely cause of the same?

correctAnswer: C. By peeling its skin and inserting cartilage into postauricular area
explanationHtml:
The avulsed pinna is preserved by peeling its skin and inserting the cartilage into the postauricular area, which can then be used for delayed reconstruction.

However, immediate reimplantation using microvascular techniques would be ideal.

If the pinna is still attached to the head by a small pedicle of skin, primary reattachment should be considered.

By suturing it to buccal mucosa after careful cleaning

question: A young man is rushed to the ER following a road traffic accident with severe injuries and a completely avulsed pinna. How would you preserve the avulsed pinna until the patient is stable enough for reconstructive surgery?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of painful, erythematous ear swelling is suggestive of perichondritis.

The most common cause is trauma, either iatrogenic (surgical incision) or non-iatrogenic (laceration, hematoma, piercing). It can also be due to the extension of infection from diffuse otitis externa or furuncle of the meatus. The most common organism responsible is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Perichondritis spreads to involve the entire auricular cartilage. The lobule is characteristically spared as it is not composed of cartilage.

Other options:

Option A: The image given below shows a patient with a cauliflower ear deformity. It is usually caused by repeated episodes of trauma causing auricular hematoma, which organize.

[[figure-1]]

Option C: Chondrodermatitis nodularis chronica helicis is a small, nodular, tender, chronic inflammatory lesion occurring on the helix of the ear. The patient will have difficulty sleeping on the affected side. Treatment includes excision of the lesion. It needs to be differentiated from carcinoma. It is shown in the image below.

[[figure-2]]

Option D: Otitis externa, also called swimmer's ear, is the inflammation of the ear canal. It has the following appearance:

[[figure-3]]
question: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who presents with a painful ear swelling as shown below?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a keloid of the pinna, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy does not reduce its recurrence post-excision.

Keloids occur due to abnormal proliferation of fibroblasts following wound healing. Keloids extend beyond the margins of the original wound. Keloid commonly occurs following trauma or piercing. The common sites are the lobule and helix.

There is a high chance of recurrence after surgical excision, which can be prevented by:

  • Intralesional steroids
  • Pre and post-operative radiotherapy
question: A patient is planned for excision of the following lesion. Which of the following measures will not prevent its recurrence post-excision?

correctAnswer: A. Patients with repeated attacks should be investigated for diabetes mellitus
explanationHtml:
Patients with repeated attacks of furunculosis should be investigated for diabetes mellitus.

A furuncle is a staphylococcal infection of the hair follicle. A furuncle in the EAC (also known as localised otitis externa) presents with severe pain and tenderness. There is pain in the ear on movement of the jaw. Treatment is antibiotics and analgesics. 10% ichthammol glycerine ear packs are used to splint and relieve pain. Incision and drainage are done if an abscess forms.

Other options:

Option B: The most common cause of a furuncle is staphylococcal infection and not streptococcal.

Option C: As the hairs are confined only to the cartilaginous part, a furuncle is seen only in the outer one-third of EAC and not anywhere in EAC.

Option D: The tragal sign is positive. A negative tragal sign in a patient with ear pain suggests referred pain.

Most common cause is streptococcal infection of hair follicle
