question: Which of the following is true about furunculosis of ear?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of diffuse otitis externa following trauma. Aural toilet remains the most important factor in the treatment for this condition.

Trauma to the ear canal in the form of scratching can break the continuity of skin in the EAC, predisposing to infection. Excessive sweating and prolonged swimming also change the pH of the skin in EAC to alkaline, predisposing to infection; therefore, otitis externa is also known as swimmer's ear.

Aural toilet includes removal of all exudate and debris carefully, with special emphasis on the anteroinferior meatal recess, which forms a blind pocket and acts as a reservoir of infective secretion. The aural toilet can be done by dry mopping, suction clearance, or irrigating the canal with warm, sterile normal saline.

Further treatment modalities:

  • After the aural toilet is done, wicks medicated with antibiotic-steroid preparation can be used. These wicks have to be changed daily for 2 to 3 days, which thereafter can be substituted by ear drops.
  • Broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics are used when there is cellulitis and acute tender lymphadenitis.
  • Analgesics are usually a part of management, as otitis externa is associated with severe pain.
  • Gauze wick soaked in 10% ichthammol glycerine is used to reduce swelling.
  • Astringents such as aluminum acetate (8%) or silver nitrate (3%) are used to dry up an oozing meatus.
question: A 40-year-old male presents with right-sided ear discharge, itching and pain for the past 4 days. He gives a history of insect entry into the external auditory canal which he removed himself. On examination, there is purulent discharge in a narrow canal and the tympanic membrane is normal. Which of the following is the most important factor in the treatment of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the otoscopic image showing black-headed filamentous growth is suggestive of otomycosis by Aspergillus niger.

Otomycosis is a fungal infection of the external auditory canal. The condition can occur as a primary infection in hot and humid climates or secondary to antibiotic treatment of the external ear. It occurs due to Aspergillus niger (most common), Aspergillus fumigatus, or Candida albicans.

Irritation, itching, and discharge are the predominant symptoms. Pain is not as common as in bacterial otitis externa.

The appearances of otomycosis on otoscopy suggest causative organisms as:

  • Black-headed filamentous growth, wet newspaper appearance - Aspergillus niger infection
  • Green or brown - Aspergillus fumigatus infection
  • White and creamy deposit, cotton ball appearance - Candida infection

Management includes an aural toilet and topical antifungal drops.

Rhizopus oryzae (Option B) is one of the causative agents of mucormycosis. The common clinical form of this opportunistic infection is rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis (ROCM). It is rarely implicated in otomycosis.
question: A young man presented with irritation and itching in the ear, associated with watery discharge and a musty odor. Otoscopic imaging is shown below. What is the causative organism?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of facial paralysis along with vesicular eruptions in the external auditory canal and tympanic membrane is suggestive of Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus).

Ramsay Hunt Syndrome is caused by the reactivation of herpes zoster in the geniculate ganglion. In most patients, there is an involvement of the trunk of the facial nerve, which results in severe facial palsy.

Often, the 8th cranial nerve is also involved, which causes hearing loss and vertigo. There may also be anesthesia of the face due to the involvement of the 5th cranial nerve.

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic, peripheral facial paralysis or paresis of acute onset due to a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve.

[[figure-2]]

Option C: Moebius syndrome is a congenital unilateral/bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve paralysis with abducens palsy causing limited ocular abduction.

Option D: Melkersson syndrome is an idiopathic disorder consisting of a triad of:

  1. Facial paralysis
  2. Swelling of lips
  3. Fissured tongue.

[[figure-3]]
question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the OPD with right-sided facial weakness. On examination, she has vesicles in the external auditory canal and over the tympanic membrane. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario of an elderly diabetic with severe otalgia, otorrhoea, granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, and lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy indicates malignant otitis externa.

It is termed malignant, even though it is an infection, due to the high mortality rate and poor response to treatment.
question: A 60-year-old diabetic presents to the ER with fever, excruciating left ear pain, and otorrhoea. On examination, she has a deviation of the angle of the mouth to the right side, and granulation tissue is seen in the left external auditory canal. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Statements 3 and 4 are incorrect:

Statement 3-The treatment of malignant otitis externa includes diabetes control, aural toilet, and prolonged (6-8 weeks) systemic antibiotics against Pseudomonas. Topical antibiotic ear drops are ineffective.

Statement 4-Technetium 99 bone scan remains positive for a year or so and cannot be used to follow up the response to treatment. It is particularly useful when the clinical suspicion for malignant otitis externa is high but the CT scan is negative.

Features of malignant otitis externa:

  • Pseudomonas infection of the external auditory canal (Statement 1), seen in elderly diabetics and those on immunosuppressive drugs. (Statement 2)
  • Excruciating pain, profuse discharge & granulations on the floor of the external auditory canal.
  • Necrosis of bone aids in the spread of infection.
  • Infection may spread to the skull base and jugular foramen, causing multiple cranial nerve palsies.
  • Facial paralysis is the most common nerve palsy seen. (Statement 5)
  • It can mimic malignancy, but on biopsy, mitotic figures will be normal since it is an infectious and not a malignant condition.
  • Gallium-67 is more useful in the follow-up of the patient.
question:
Which of the following statements is/are false about malignant otitis externa?

  1. It is due to a Pseudomonas infection
  2. It mainly affects immunocompromised individuals
  3. It is responsive to topical antibiotic ear drops
  4. Technetium 99 bone scan is used for follow-up
  5. The facial nerve is the most commonly affected nerve

explanationHtml:
During syringing, the pinna is pulled upwards and backward, and the water jet is directed along the posterosuperior wall of the meatus. This is preferred because of two anatomical reasons:

  1. On maneuvering the pinna to bring the EAC into a straight configuration, the posterior wall is straighter and easily accessible than the anterior wall.
  2. The posteroinferior wall of EAC is supplied by the vagus. Direct stimulation of this can lead to sudden cardiac arrest.

Complications of syringing:

  • Vertigo– caloric stimulation of lateral semicircular canal if water is too hot or too cold
  • Perforation of the tympanic membrane
  • Reactivation of quiescent otitis media, if there is a pre-existing perforation

Contraindications for syringing:

  • Presence of ear infection, tympanic membrane perforation
  • Presence of a grommet or history of ear surgery
question: While performing syringing for a patient with impacted wax, along which wall of the meatus would you direct the jet of water?

correctAnswer: D. Narrowing of meatus causing facial nerve palsy
explanationHtml:
Keratosis obturans, by pressure effect, causes absorption of bone, which causes widening (not narrowing) of the meatus leading to facial nerve palsy.

Normally, epithelium from the surface of the tympanic membrane migrates onto the posterior meatal wall. Failure of this migration, or obstruction to migration caused by wax, may lead to keratosis obturans which is the accumulation of a large plug of desquamated epithelial cells and keratin plug in the external auditory meatus, arranged in a lamellar fashion (onion-skin pattern).

Features of keratosis obturans:

  • Severe otalgia
  • Conductive hearing loss
  • Keratin plug/pearly white mass occluding the canal
  • Widened ear canal- may lead to facial nerve paralysis
  • Hyperemia of canal skin, sometimes with ulcerations and granulomas
  • May be associated with systemic conditions like bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis
  • Removed by syringing or instrumentation

options.text: Narrowing of meatus causing facial nerve palsy

question: Which of the following is not seen in a patient with keratosis obturans?

explanationHtml:
The surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal is meatoplasty.

Meatoplasty is a surgical procedure that involves the removal of a crescent-shaped portion of conchal cartilage to widen the external auditory meatus. It is performed in combination with all canal wall-down procedures like modified radical and radical mastoidectomies, for easy access to the mastoid cavity for periodic inspection and cleaning.

It is also done as an isolated procedure in elderly people with sagging auricles. A sagging auricle causes obstruction to the meatus leading to the retention of wax and difficulty in hearing.

Other options:

Option B: Tympanoplasty is the surgical reconstruction to correct damage in the middle ear and restore the integrity of the tympanic membrane for improved hearing. It is ossicular reconstruction only or ossicular reconstruction with myringoplasty.

Option C: Myringoplasty refers to the reconstruction of the tympanic membrane only.

Option D: Otoplasty is the correction of external ear/deformities of the pinna.
question: What is the surgery done to widen the cartilaginous part of the external auditory canal called?

explanationHtml:
Meatoplasty is not a part of canal wall-up (CWU) procedures as the meatus is preserved in these procedures.

However, meatoplasty is performed in combination with all canal wall down procedures like modified radical and radical mastoidectomies, and for the treatment of middle ear disease such as cholesteatoma. The widened meatus helps to easily visualize and access the mastoid cavity for periodic inspection and cleaning.

It is also done in atresia/stenosis of the EAC to recanalize the ear and in tortuous canals post-tympanoplasty to improve hearing.
question: In which of the following is meatoplasty not performed?

correctAnswer: A. Shiny, pearly grey tympanic membrane
explanationHtml:
A retracted TM is dull and lustreless, not shiny and pearly grey.

A retracted tympanic membrane is the result of negative intratympanic pressure when the eustachian tube is blocked. Features of retracted TM are:

  • The cone of light is absent or distorted
  • Malleus - the handle appears shorter, and the lateral process is more clearly visible
  • Anterior and posterior malleal folds become sickle-shaped

The image below shows a retracted TM with the above-mentioned findings:

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Sickling of anterior and posterior malleal folds

question: Which of the following is false regarding retracted tympanic membrane?

explanationHtml:
Draping of pars tensa over the incudostapedial joint is classified as Sade's grade II retraction.

Sade classification of retraction of Pars tensa:

Grade Description
Grade 1 Mild retraction not touching the long process of the incus
Grade 2 Retracted drum touching the long process of the incus
Grade 3 Touching promontory but mobile on seigalization - atelectasis of the middle ear
Grade 4 Plastered to promontory and immobile - adhesive middle ear

Tos classification of retraction of Pars flaccida:

Grade Description
Grade 1 Mild attic retraction not touching the neck of the malleus.
Grade 2 Touching the neck of the malleus
Grade 3 Limited outer attic wall erosion
Grade 4 Severe outer attic wall erosion
question: While performing routine otoscopy, a patient is found to have tympanic membrane retraction with the pars tensa draping over the incudostapedial joint. What is the grade of retraction?

explanationHtml:
The eustachian tube is the most common route of infection in acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM).

The eustachian tube connects the nasopharynx with the tympanic cavity. The interference with the normal functioning of the eustachian tube predisposes the middle ear to infections. The infection travels via the lumen of the tube or along subepithelial peritubal lymphatics.

The infection to the middle ear can also spread from the external ear through a traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane or via the blood, but these routes are less common.
question: What is the most common route of infection in acute suppurative otitis media?

explanationHtml:
Choanal atresia does not predispose to eustachian tube obstruction.

Eustachian tube obstruction is caused by:

  • Extrinsic causes:
    • Adenoid hypertrophy
    • Nasopharyngeal tumors
    • Nasal pack
  • Intrinsic causes:
    • Allergic rhinitis
    • Rhinosinusitis
    • Upper respiratory tract infection
  • Defective functioning of the tube:
    • Cleft palate: The muscles that help open the eustachian tube are often malformed in individuals with cleft palate. Because of this, the tube remains closed.
    • Down syndrome
    • Submucous cleft palate

Eustachian tube obstruction can lead to complications such as:

  • Acute suppurative otitis media
  • Otitis media with effusion
  • Chronic suppurative otitis media
  • Atelectasis and ossicular necrosis
question: Which of the following conditions does not predispose to eustachian tube obstruction?

explanationHtml:
The most likely organism implicated in acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM) is Streptococcus pneumoniae.

Organisms causing ASOM in infants and young children:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common)
  • nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae
  • Moraxella catarrhalis
  • Streptococcus pyogenes
  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
question: Which of the following is the most likely organism implicated in acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM)?

explanationHtml:
The otologic image shows the cartwheel appearance of the tympanic membrane, which is seen in the pre-suppuration stage of acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM).

During this stage, due to prolonged tubal occlusion, pyogenic organisms invade the tympanic cavity. An inflammatory exudate appears in the middle ear and there is congestion of pars tensa. A leash of blood vessels appears along the handle of malleus and at the periphery of the tympanic membrane imparting it a cart-wheel appearance. Later, the whole of the tympanic membrane including pars flaccida becomes uniformly red.

Symptoms of this stage include marked earache, fever, hearing loss, and tinnitus (seen only in adults). Tuning fork tests show a conductive type of hearing loss.

Suppuration stage of ASOM (Option D) is characterised by formation of pus in the middle ear cavity leading to bulging of tympanic membrane as seen in the otoscopic image below:

[[figure-1]]
question: Otologic examination of a febrile child with otalgia is shown below. What is the stage of acute suppurative otitis media seen here?

explanationHtml:
The ear pain is most severe in stage of suppuration in acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM).

The severity of ear pain gives an idea of the stage at which ASOM has progressed. The ear pain is mild in the tubal occlusion stage and becomes marked in the stage of pre-suppuration. In the stage of suppuration, the ear pain is the most severe, which is due to the pressure of pus inside the middle ear on the tympanic membrane. In the following stage of resolution, the tympanic membrane ruptures and the pus drains, which leads to a relief in pain as the pressure on the tympanic membrane decreases due to pus drainage.

The various stages of ASOM are discussed in the pearl below:
question: The ear pain is most severe in which stage of acute suppurative otitis media?

correctAnswer: C. Posterior half of pars tensa
explanationHtml:
The most common site of perforation of the tympanic membrane in ASOM is the posterior half of pars tensa where usually, a small perforation is seen.

Note: As per Dhingra Diseases of Ear Nose and Throat 8th edition, the perforation most commonly occurs in the anteroinferior quadrant. However, as Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery; 8th Edition mentions the most common site as the posterior half of pars tensa, we have picked it as the best option in this question.
question: What is the most common site of perforation of the tympanic membrane in acute suppurative otitis media?

explanationHtml:
Management of ASOM in the pre-suppuration stage involves the usage of antibiotics and decongestants.

Myringotomy is indicated when the tympanic membrane bulges with an impending rupture, which occurs in the suppuration stage of ASOM.
question: How will you manage a patient who is diagnosed to have acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM) in the pre-suppuration stage?

explanationHtml:
The scenario points towards a diagnosis of acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM), in the stage of suppuration. Antibiotics form the mainstay of treatment in ASOM, and if the tympanic membrane is bulging, myringotomy should be done.

Myringotomy is the procedure involving incising the tympanic membrane to evacuate pus. It is indicated in ASOM when:

  • The tympanic membrane is bulging, and there is acute pain.
  • There is an incomplete resolution despite antibiotics, and the drum remains full with persistent conductive deafness.
  • Complications of ASOM develop, like facial nerve palsy, labyrinthitis.
  • There is persistent effusion beyond 12 weeks, i.e., serous otitis media develops.
  • Recurrent ASOM.

Grommet insertion (Option A) is required in serous otitis media for the drainage and ventilation of the middle ear. It is not required in ASOM.

options.text: Antibiotics and myringotomy with grommet insertion

question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with fever and severe earache. On examination, the tympanic membrane appears congested and bulging with a loss of landmarks. What is the next line of management?

explanationHtml:
In serous otitis media, a radial incision is made in the anteroinferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane.

This is in contrast to curvilinear incision used in acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM) in the posteroinferior quadrant (smiling incision). The myringotomy performed in the ASOM and the serous otitis media are compared in the table below:

ASOM Serous otitis media/otitis media with effusion/secretory otitis media/glue ear
Incision site Posteroinferior Anteroinferior
Shape of incision Curvilinear (to allow complete drainage of pus) Radial (to hold grommet in place tightly)
Is the grommet inserted? No Yes

[[figure-1]]

Note: In serous otitis media, although an anteroinferior incision is the first step, we can also make a second incision in anterosuperior quadrant in the case of thick secretions that are difficult to aspirate. The 'beer-can' principle supports the said mechanism.

An incision is never made in posterosuperior quadrant due to risk of damage to incus and stapes.
question: You are an ENT resident assisting on a myringotomy in a patient with serous otitis media. In which quadrant would you make the incision?

explanationHtml:
Otitis media with effusion, also known as glue ear, is the most common cause of acquired hearing loss in children.

Clinical features of glue ear include:

  • Bilateral, painless, and fluctuating hearing loss. Conductive hearing loss not more than 40 dB is observed.
  • Defective and delayed development of speech.
  • Occasional mild earaches are present.
question: What is the most common cause of acquired hearing loss in children?

correctAnswer: D. The effusion is thick, viscid and septic in most cases
explanationHtml:
The effusion is thick, viscid and sterile (and not septic) in most cases of serous otitis media.

Etiology of serous otitis media:

  • Malfunctioning of eustachian tube:
    • Adenoid hyperplasia in children - causes bilateral serous otitis media
    • Benign and malignant tumors of the nasopharynx - should always be excluded in unilateral serous otitis media in an adult
    • Cleft lip, cleft palate and chronic tonsillitis - interference with ET opening
  • Otitic barotrauma
  • Allergy - increased middle ear secretions
  • Unresolved ASOM - due to inadequate treatment dosage or duration
  • Viral infections - increased secretory activity due to stimulation of middle ear mucosa

options.text: Function of the eustachian tube is abnormal in most cases
Adenoid hypertrophy is the most common cause in children causing bilateral serous otitis media
Tumors of nasopharynx is the most common cause in adults causing unilateral serous otitis media
The effusion is thick, viscid and septic in most cases

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding serous otitis media?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and image suggest a diagnosis of serous otitis media. The image shows bubbles in middle ear and a dull , retracted tympanic membrane.

Patients having serous otitis media will have hearing loss that rarely exceeds 40 dB. This deafness can pass unnoticed, and maybe accidentally discovered during audiometric screening tests. Because of hearing loss, the development of speech is delayed or defective.

Otoscopic findings in serous otitis media:

  • The tympanic membrane is often dull and opaque with a loss of light reflex. Fluid level and air bubbles are seen when fluid is thin and the tympanic membrane is transparent.
  • In chronic cases, the fluid becomes very sticky. Hence, the name glue ear.
  • The mobility of the tympanic membrane is restricted.
  • Tympanic membrane may show retraction. It may also show bulging due to effusion.
question: You see a child with delayed development of speech as part of a health visit in a local school. The otoscopic appearance of the ear is shown below. Hearing loss of 20 dB is detected in audiometric tests. What is your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
B-type tympanogram is expected in a case of serous otitis media.

Here, compliance decreases i.e., mobility of tympanic membrane is restricted due to the effusion, usually secondary to negative middle ear pressure (eustachian tube obstruction). This results in a B-type tympanogram.

Hearing tests suggestive of conductive hearing loss as seen in serous otitis media:

  • Rinne negative (BC>AC).
  • Weber - lateralized towards the worse ear
  • Audiogram - AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present
  • Impedance audiometry - flat curve (reduced compliance, shift to the negative side)

Note: Tympanograph is Flat when there is Fluid in the middle ear.
question: What type of tympanogram would you expect to see in a patient with serous otitis media?

explanationHtml:
Serous otitis media or glue ear can be managed by cortical mastoidectomy. It is sometimes required for removing loculated thick fluid or other associated pathologies, such as cholesterol granuloma.

Management of glue ear:

  • Medical:
    • Antihistaminics-if the cause is allergy
    • Decongestants to relieve edema of the eustachian tube
    • Antibiotics if underlying URTIs or unresolved ASOM
    • Valsalva maneuver, politzerization
  • Surgical:
    • Myringotomy and aspiration
    • Grommet insertion
    • Tympanotomy or cortical mastoidectomy to remove thick loculated fluid
    • Adenoidectomy or tonsillectomy for the underlying cause.

A grommet is placed in the middle ear to aerate and drain the middle ear. It acts as a substitute for the blocked eustachian tube. It is placed through radial myringotomy in the anteroinferior quadrant. The device is shown in the image below:

[[figure-1]]

Note: Atrophic tympanic membrane, tympanosclerosis, cholesteatoma, middle ear atelectasis, and ossicular necrosis are some of the sequelae of long-standing glue ear.
question: Which of the following procedures is not used to treat a patient with glue ear?

explanationHtml:
Earache is not a feature of tubercular otitis media. It is a painless condition.

Tuberculosis of the ear is usually secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis. It occasionally spreads hematogenously, from a tubercular focus in the lungs, tonsils, and cervical or mesenteric lymph nodes

It presents as a painless condition with foul-smelling discharge from the ear, that does not respond to standard antibiotic treatment. Patients have severe hearing loss that is out of proportion to symptoms. Although predominantly conductive, sensorineural hearing loss may also occur if the labyrinth is involved.

A thickened tympanic membrane with multiple perforations in pars tensa of the tympanic membrane and pale granulations in the middle ear cleft is seen.

The image below shows the tympanic membrane in tuberculous otitis media:

[[figure-1]]

Histopathology shows submucosal tubercles with Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis. Smears and culture of ear discharge may be positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Evidence of primary pulmonary tuberculosis may also be seen on chest radiography.

Facial nerve palsy is a common complication. Mastoiditis, postauricular fistula, and osteomyelitis are also seen.

Treatment includes aural toilet, treatment of secondary bacterial infections, and a full course of antitubercular therapy followed by reconstructive surgery.
question: Which of the following is not a feature of tubercular otitis media?

correctAnswer: C. It is also known as epidermosis
explanationHtml:
The image shows the presence of a large mass of white keratin debris in the left upper quadrant of the left tympanic membrane. This, along with clinical scenario, is suggestive of cholesteatoma which is also known as epidermosis or keratoma.

A central white mass, consisting of keratin debris is produced by the outer matrix. For this reason, it has also been named epidermosis or keratoma.

Other options:

Options A & B: The term cholesteatoma is a misnomer because it neither contains cholesterol crystals nor is it a tumor to merit the suffix “oma.”

Option D: Cholesteatoma is the presence of keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium in middle ear where it is not usually present, i.e., skin in wrong place.

options.text: It is also known as epidermosis
It is made up of columnar epithelium

question: Otoscopic image of a patient with a history of repeated middle ear infections is shown below. Which one of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of secondary acquired cholesteatoma. The history of middle ear infection and hearing loss after surgery of the tympanic membrane makes the diagnosis likely.

Classification of cholesteatoma:

1. Congenital cholesteatoma is that which has its nidus of trapped squamous epithelium present at birth.

2. Primary acquired cholesteatoma presents with no history of previous otitis media or tympanic membrane perforation. It is associated with a retraction pocket in pars flaccida, as a result of persistent negative pressure.

3. Secondary acquired cholesteatoma presents with a history of tympanic membrane perforation, which might have occured due to infection, trauma, or surgery. It is associated with a defect in pars tensa.

Malignant cholesteatomas (Option B) do not occur. Cholesteatomas are by definition benign.
question: You see a patient with a history of painless foul-smelling ear discharge and loss of hearing for the past year. He had undergone tympanoplasty on the same ear 3 years back. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. von Bekesy's theory of mucosal metaplasia
explanationHtml:
von Békésy proposed the traveling wave theory, whereas Sade’s metaplasia theory explains the origin of cholesteatoma.

The theories which explain the origin of different types of cholesteatomas can be found in the pearl attached:

options.text: Ruedi’s theory of basal cell hyperplasia
von Bekesy's theory of mucosal metaplasia

question: Which of the following theories does not explain the origin of cholesteatoma?

explanationHtml:
The most accepted theory for secondary acquired cholesteatoma is Habermann's theory of migration of squamous epithelium.

It proposes that the squamous epithelium of the external auditory meatus or outer surface of the tympanic membrane grows or migrates into the middle ear through the posterosuperior marginal perforation or attic perforation, forming cholesteatoma.
question: Which of the following is the most accepted theory for secondary acquired cholesteatoma?

explanationHtml:
Prussak’s space is the most common site of primary acquired cholesteatoma.

Eustachian tube dysfunction, which leads to negative pressure in the middle ear leads to retraction of the weakest part of the tympanic membrane, the pars flaccida, inward. This retraction pocket extends directly into Prussak's space, a space in the epitympanum lying in between pars flaccida laterally and the neck of the malleus medially. The retraction pocket accumulates the keratin debris, leading to formation of keratin debris.

The second most common site for the formation of retraction pocket is postero-superior quadrant of pars tensa.
question: What is the most common site for primary acquired cholesteatoma?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with the otoendoscopy showing a white pearly mass behind the intact eardrum in the anterosuperior quadrant is suggestive of congenital cholesteatoma. Levenson's criteria should be satisfied in order to diagnose this condition.

Levenson's criteria:

  1. A white mass behind the normal tympanic membrane
  2. Normal pars tensa and pars flaccida
  3. No prior history of otorrhoea or perforation
  4. No prior history of otological surgeries
  5. Exclusion of canal atresia, intramembranous, or giant cholesteatoma
  6. Episodes of otitis media should not be considered as exclusion criteria.

Another criterion, which is not used now, is Derlaki and Clemis.
question: An 8-year-old boy was referred to an otolaryngologist for subjective left-sided hearing loss. A hearing test revealed mild conductive hearing loss at low and middle frequencies. Otoendoscopy showed a mass with the appearance as shown below. Which of the following criteria is used to diagnose this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Destruction of bone mediated by pressure necrosis
explanationHtml:
Cholesteatoma does not cause bone destruction by pressure necrosis. Pressure necrosis theory was believed earlier but has been abandoned now.

Other options:

Options A & C: Bone destruction by cholesteatoma has been attributed to enzymes liberated by osteoclasts and mononuclear inflammatory cells such as collagenase, acid phosphatase and proteolytic enzymes.

Option D: Pediatric cholesteatoma (PC) has more inflammation and greater chances of ossicular erosion compared to adults. However, PC has lesser chances of petrous labyrinth invasion and lateral semicircular canal fistula formation.

options.text: Release of enzymes like collagenase and acid phosphatase at the site of destruction
Destruction of bone mediated by pressure necrosis
Osteoclasts and mononuclear cells play a role in bone destruction
Erosion of ossicles is more common in children compared to adults

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the expansion of cholesteatoma and destruction of bone?

explanationHtml:
The sinus tympani is the most common site for residual cholesteatoma. It is the hidden area of middle ear.

The involvement of sinus tympani, along with posterior mesotympanum, is a recognized risk factor for residual cholesteatoma. This is because it is particularly difficult to remove the disease from these areas. Canal wall-up procedures have a higher risk of leaving residual disease behind than the canal wall-down procedures.

Sinus tympani or infra pyramidal recess is the medial of the two posterior spaces in the middle ear.

It is bounded by:

  • Pyramid and vertical segment of facial nerve laterally
  • The stapes & oval window medially
  • Ponticulus superiorly
  • Subiculum inferiorly

Image showing sinus tympani:

[[figure-1]]

Prussak’s space (Option D) is the most common site of primary acquired cholesteatoma. It is not the most common site for residual cholesteatoma.
question: A patient presented to your OPD for a second look surgery following a canal wall-up procedure for cholesteatoma removal. Where is the residual disease most likely to be seen?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario of intermittent mucoid discharge and central perforation of the tympanic membrane points to a diagnosis of tubotympanic type of CSOM, which is not associated with cholesteatoma.

Atticoantral type is associated with cholesteatoma and it leads to dangerous complications due to its bone-eroding properties. This is the reason it is known as unsafe type of CSOM.

Etiology of tubotympanic (benign or safe) type of CSOM:

  • As a sequela of acute otitis media
  • Ascending infection via the eustachian tube
  • Allergic conditions

Other options:

Option A: There is no evidence of bone destruction on CT scans of temporal bone. Presence of bone destruction is a feature of atticoantral type.

Option B: Culture reveals mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection.

Option C: Aural polyp, if present, should be removed and not avulsed. This is due to the fact that the polyp may be arising from the stapes, facial nerve, or horizontal canal and its avulsion can lead to facial paralysis or labyrinthitis.

options.text: No evidence of bone destruction in CT scans
Mixed aerobic and anaerobic infections are seen
Aural polyp if present, should never be avulsed

question: A young adult presents with intermittent non-foul smelling mucoid discharge from the left ear for the past few years. Otologic examination revealed a central perforation of the tympanic membrane. Which of the following statements is false regarding his condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and visualisation of chalky white deposits between ossicles is suggestive of tympanosclerosis.

Tympanosclerosis is a sequela of long-standing middle ear disease like serous otitis media or CSOM, where there are hyaline deposits within the middle ear, which calcify leading to impaired mobility of these structures, interfering with the conduction of sound. The common sites are the tympanic membrane, promontory, ossicles, joints, tendons, and oval and round windows.

Other options:

Option A: Otosclerosis is a disease of the bony labyrinth, most commonly involving the stapes bone, leading to stapes fixation.

Option C: When hyalinization and calcification involve only the tympanic membrane, it is known as myringosclerosis.

Option D: Candidal infection in ear presents as a thick, creamy white discharge along with redness, itching and swelling. It most commonly involves external ear and not middle ear.

options.text: Candidal infection of the middle ear

question: A known case of tubotympanic disease was taken up for surgery and on examining the middle ear, few chalky white deposits were found between the ossicles. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario describes the round window-shielding effect that is seen in tubotympanic type of CSOM.

The round window-shielding effect is where the ear discharge in the active phase of CSOM shields the round window from sound waves. During the inactive phase of CSOM (no discharge), the sound strikes both the oval window and round window together, and the noise cancels itself out. So, the hearing is worse when the ear is dry.

Cholesteatoma hearer (Option B) is a patient with a discontinuous ossicular chain but the sound is conducted through the cholesteatoma to the footplate. On removing the cholesteatoma by surgery, the patient has worse hearing.
question: A young adult presents with a 3-year history of intermittent ear discharge. He complains of poor hearing, which improves during discharge periods, but is worse when the ear is dry. Which of the following explains this phenomenon?

correctAnswer: A. Central perforation is most commonly seen
explanationHtml:
Central perforation of tympanic membrane is most commonly seen in tubotympanic type, while marginal perforation in the postero-superior quadrant is most commonly seen in atticoantral type of CSOM.

Other options:

Option B: Blood-stained discharge is seen in atticoantral type of CSOM.

Option C: Scanty and foul-smelling ear discharge is seen in the atticoantral type of CSOM. The foul smell is due to the bone destruction.

Option D: Ossicular destruction due to erosion by cholesteatoma is seen in atticoantral type of CSOM and not the tubotympanic type.

options.text: Central perforation is most commonly seen
Blood stained ear discharge is seen
The discharge is scanty and foul smelling
Ossicular destruction due to erosion by cholesteatoma is seen

question: Which of the following is true regarding the tubotympanic type of chronic suppurative otitis media?

correctAnswer: D. Involvement of Shrapnell's membrane is seen
explanationHtml:
Atticoantral type of CSOM, also called unsafe or dangerous type, involves perforation of Shrapnell's membrane or pars flaccida (attic perforation).

The disease is often associated with a bone-eroding process such as cholesteatoma, granulations, or osteitis. The risk of complications is high in this variety.

Other options:

Options A, B & C: Tubotympanic type of CSOM involves the protympanum. It rarely has associated polyps. The ear discharge is profuse.

options.text: Involvement of Shrapnell's membrane is seen

question: Which of the following is true about the atticoantral type of chronic suppurative otitis media?

explanationHtml:
Tympanoplasty is the most common surgery done in the tubotympanic type of CSOM.

The management of tubotympanic type of CSOM begins with medical management in the form of aural toilet and antibiotics. Once the ear is dry for a period of 6 weeks, tympanoplasty is performed to restore hearing and prevent recurrent infections.

Tympanoplasty refers to any operation involving reconstruction of the tympanic membrane and/or the ossicular chain. Myringoplasty is a tympanoplasty without ossicular reconstruction.

In contrast, mastoidectomy is performed in the atticoantral type of CSOM and not usually in the tubotympanic type.
question: Which of the following is the most common surgery done for tubotympanic type of chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)?

correctAnswer: C. CT scan of temporal bone
explanationHtml:
CT scan of the temporal bone is not required in tympanoplasty procedures for tubotympanic type of CSOM. It is required only in cases of mastoidectomy.

For tympanoplasty, routine blood investigations, pure tone audiometry, and an X-ray of the mastoid are sufficient.
question: As a first-year ENT resident, you are preparing a patient for tympanoplasty as a management for tubotympanic type of CSOM. Which of the following would not be in your pre-operative checklist?

explanationHtml: Zollner and Wullstein’s classification is used to classify tympanoplasty.
question: Wullstein’s classification is used for which of the following procedures?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and image showing a medium central perforation of the pars tensa is suggestive of tubo-tympanic type (TTD) of chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM). Canal wall down mastoidectomy is not a part of the management plan.

This is only performed in attico-antral type and in cases of tubo-tympanic type where a reservoir of infection in the middle ear is suspected.

Management of tubo-tympanic type of CSOM:

  • Medical management:
    • Aural toilet
    • Topical antibiotics with steroid drops
    • Systemic antibiotics
    • Treatment of causative factors.
  • Surgical management:
    • It is done once the ear is dry for 6 weeks without antibiotics.
    • Tympanoplasty (ossiculoplasty with or without myringoplasty).
question: A 30-year-old man presents with complaints of painless, odourless and profuse discharge from the right ear. An otoscopic image of the affected ear is given below. Which of the following would not be a part of the management?

explanationHtml:
Temporalis fascia is the most common graft material used for tympanoplasty

Other graft materials used are:

  • The areolar fascia overlying the temporal fascia
  • Perichondrium from the tragus
  • Conchal cartilage
  • Vein
  • Periosteum

Dura mater was used earlier but then discontinued due to the risk of prion diseases like Cruetzfeldt Jacob disease.
question: Which of the following is the most common graft material used for tympanoplasty?

correctAnswer: A. In underlay technique, graft is placed medial to annulus
explanationHtml:
In the underlay technique, the graft is placed medial to the annulus. Whereas, in the overlay technique, the graft is placed lateral to the annulus. The graft is medial to malleus in both techniques.

Myringoplasty techniques are based on the relation of the graft with lamina propria of tympanic membrane remnants and fibrous annulus.

The placement of graft with respect to the annulus and malleus, in the two techniques, can be seen in the illustration below:

[[figure-1]]

options.text: In underlay technique, graft is placed medial to annulus
In underlay technique, graft is placed lateral to malleus
In overlay technique, graft is placed medial to annulus
In overlay technique, graft is placed lateral to malleus

question: A patient having chronic otitis media with perforation of pars tensa is scheduled for myringoplasty to restore hearing. Which of the following is true regarding the techniques used here?

explanationHtml:
Wilde’s (or post-aural) incision is used in myringoplasty.

Wilde's incision is used in the following:

  • Cortical mastoidectomy
  • Modified radical and radical mastoidectomy
  • Tympanoplasty - when perforation extends anterior to handle of malleus
  • Exposure of CN VII in the vertical segment
  • Surgery of endolymphatic sac.

Lempert's (endaural) incision and Rosen's (transcanal) incision can also be used in myringoplasty.

Other options:

Option A: Killian’s incision is used in submucous resection surgery for deviated nasal septum. In cases of a deviated septum, a slightly curvilinear incision is made, 2–3 mm behind the caudal end of septal cartilage at the mucocutaneous junction, always on the left side.

Option B: Freer’s hemitransfixion incision is used in septoplasty done for deviated nasal septum. In case of caudal dislocation, a transfixion or hemitransfixion incision is made. It is a septocolumellar incision between the caudal end of septal cartilage and columella on the concave side.

[[figure-1]]

Option D: Gluck–Sorenson’s incision used for laryngectomy with radical neck dissection.
question: A patient with mucosal disease of the middle ear is set to undergo myringoplasty. Which of the following incisions is used here?

correctAnswer: D. Malleus handle and stapes suprastructure
explanationHtml:
Austin's classification of anatomical defects in the ossicular chain is based on the presence or absence of handle of malleus and stapes suprastructure.

Incus is the most common bone to be eroded and assuming it to be absent in most cases, the remaining 2 ossicles, i.e., malleus and stapes are considered for the classification.

This classification helps surgeons assess the extent of ossicular damage and plan appropriate surgical reconstruction. Kartush added 3 more classes to Austin's classification.
question: Austin’s classification for anatomical defects in the ossicular chain is based on which of the following structures?

explanationHtml:
The otoscopic image shows a cherry-red small mass of granulation tissue arising from the pars flaccida of the left tympanic membrane strongly suggesting that there is an underlying cholesteatoma in the attic area. The given clinical scenario describes a case of atticoantral type of CSOM and modified radical mastoidectomy is the treatment of choice here.

The continuing discharge from the granulation tissue has caused the surface epithelia of the tympanic membrane to become edematous and thickened. This gives the surface of the tympanic membrane a thickened whitish appearance.

The primary aim in surgical treatment is to remove the disease and render the ear safe, and second in priority is to preserve or reconstruct hearing but never at the cost of the primary aim.

Other options:

Option A: Myringotomy is done in cases of acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM) and serous otitis media.

Options C and D: Medical management followed by myringoplasty or tympanoplasty once the ear is dry for 6 weeks without antibiotics is the treatment of choice for tubotympanic type of CSOM.
question: A patient presents to your OPD with hearing difficulty and scanty, foul-smelling discharge from the left ear. Otologic examination reveals the following finding. What is the treatment of choice in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the otoscopic image showing marginal perforation is suggestive of atticoantral type of chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), and the definitive management plan is surgical intervention with tympanomastoid exploration.

Tympanomastoid exploration is the essential surgical treatment for atticoantral CSOM to remove the cholesteatoma and infected bone, thereby preventing complications and creating a safe ear. Mastoidectomy is a component of tympanomastoid exploration.
question: A 7-year-old child presents with scanty, foul-smelling ear discharge. Otologic examination shows the following finding. Which of the following is the definitive management plan?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a white mass located in the anterosuperior quadrant behind the intact eardrum suggestive of cholesteatoma. The primary aim is to clear the disease and render the ear safe.

The first priority of surgery for cholesteatoma is safety. Because a cholesteatoma can cause life-threatening complications like meningitis, brain abscesses, and facial paralysis, the surgeon's primary goal is to remove it and create a "safe" ear. Hearing reconstruction is important but not the primary aim; it is only attempted after the cholesteatoma has been thoroughly cleared.
question: What would be the primary aim of surgery in a patient presenting with the following otoscopic finding?

correctAnswer: C. Post surgery healing is rapid and periodic cleaning is unnecessary in CWU procedure
explanationHtml:
Post-surgery healing is rapid, and periodic cleaning is unnecessary in case of canal wall up procedure (CWU). This procedure has a low predisposition to infection but carries the risk of leaving behind residual disease requiring the need for second-look surgery.

CWU and CWD are the two types of surgical procedures performed to remove cholesteatoma in atticoantral CSOM. In a CWU procedure, the posterior wall of the ear canal is preserved, whereas in CWD procedure it is removed to create a single large cavity. The two procedures are differentiated in a tabular format below:

Canal wall up procedure (CWU) Canal wall down procedure (CWD)
Indication Limited disease
  • Extensive disease
  • Patients with unlikely follow-up
  • Patients with only one functional ear
Meatoplasty Not done

Meatus opening is widened with meatoplasty
Healing Rapid

Slow
Cleaning problems Does not require routine cleaning Cleaning once or twice a year required.
Residual/ recurrent cholesteatoma High rate Low rate
Second-look surgery Required after 6 months Not required
Water entry The patient is allowed to swim. No limitation. Swimming can lead to infection of the mastoid cavity
Hearing rehab Easy to wear a hearing aid if needed Problems in fitting a hearing aid due to large meatus and mastoid cavity

options.text: Incidence of residual disease is very low not requiring second look surgery in CWU procedure
Easy to wear a hearing aid if needed after CWD procedure
Post surgery healing is rapid and periodic cleaning is unnecessary in CWU procedure
The patient is allowed to swim after CWD procedure

question: A 12-year-old child with chronic suppurative otitis media and cholesteatoma is planned for a mastoidectomy. He is part of the school swimming club and wants to pursue the sport. Which of the following would you mention while counselling the parents regarding canal wall up (CWU) and canal wall down (CWD) mastoidectomies?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of the patient with pain in and behind his left ear associated with low-grade fever, decreased hearing, profuse ear discharge is suggestive of acute mastoiditis.

Acute mastoiditis is a complication of otitis media. The important signs of acute mastoiditis are:

  • Mastoid tenderness
  • Conductive hearing loss
  • Swelling over the mastoid leading to a smooth “ironed out” feel over the mastoid. Pinna pushed outwards and downwards.
  • Mucopurulent or purulent ear discharge that is often pulsatile, giving a light-house effect
  • Perforation of the tympanic membrane in pars tensa
  • Sagging of posterosuperior meatal wall

HRCT scan of the temporal bone shows clouding of air cells due to the collection of exudate. Bony partitions between air cells become indistinct.

Other options:

Option A: Lateral sinus thrombophlebitis presents with a hectic picket-fence fever with rigors, headache, Griesinger's sign and papilloedema.

Option B: Petrositis presents with Gradenigo syndrome, which consists of a triad of external rectus palsy (VIth nerve palsy), deep-seated ear or retro-orbital pain (Vth nerve involvement) and persistent ear discharge.

Option D: Otosclerosis presents with paracusis willisii, conductive hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo.
question: A 20-year-old boy complains of pain in and behind his left ear associated with low-grade fever, decreased hearing and profuse ear discharge for the past 25 days. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Battle sign refers to retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from a fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. It is prominent when there is a fracture of the temporal bone. Battle sign is not seen in the case of otitis media.

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.

Option B: Griesinger sign refers to edema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein, seen in sigmoid sinus thrombosis. It is a complication of acute otomastoiditis.

Option D: Delta sign is a contrast-enhanced CT finding seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis, which can occur as a complication of acute mastoiditis or chronic suppurative otitis media. It is a triangular area with rim enhancement and the central low-density area is seen in the posterior cranial fossa on axial cuts. MR venography is useful to assess the progression or resolution of a thrombus.

The image below depicts a filling defect (thrombus) outlined by contrast medium in the sagittal sinus.

[[figure-2]]
question: Which of the following is not seen in a case of otitis media?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario along is most likely suggestive of the diagnosis of Bezold's abscess.

Bezold abscess is defined as a complication of acute coalescent mastoiditis and is formed when pus breaks inferiorly, through the thin medial aspect of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck. This is shown in the illustration below:

[[figure-1]]

Other abscesses in relation to mastoid infection:

  • Post auricular abscess - it is the most common abscess that forms over the mastoid. In infants and children, this presents over MacEwen’s triangle.
  • Zygomatic abscess - it is situated at the posterior root of the zygoma. Presents with swelling in front and above the pinna with associated edema over the upper eyelid.
  • Luc's abscess (meatal abscess) - the pus breaks through the bony wall between the mastoid antrum and external auditory meatus
  • Citelli’s abscess - the abscess is formed posterior to the mastoid, occupying a position more towards the occipital bone. In any case, a diagnosis of Bezold abscess is more appropriate for this patient owing to the location of the abscess.

[[figure-2]]
question: A 12-year-old boy who was treated for acute otitis media 2 weeks back presents with fever,  and pain behind his right ear. On examination, tenderness is present over the mastoid and the pinna is pushed anteriorly suggesting acute mastoiditis. A fluctuant swelling is present between the tip of the mastoid and the angle of the jaw. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Gradenigo’s syndrome, which is the classical presentation of petrous apicitis. Spread of infection from middle ear and mastoid to the petrous part of the temporal bone is called petrositis/ petrous apicitis.

The triad of Gradenigo's syndrome consists of:

  • Ipsilateral abducens nerve palsy (6th nerve palsy) - lateral rectus palsy causing diplopia
  • Deep-seated ear or retro-orbital pain (5th nerve involvement)
  • Persistent ear discharge (otitis media)

The incidence of this syndrome has reduced with the advent of antibiotics.

Other options:

Option A: Following acute coalescent mastoiditis the pus breaks through the bony wall between the mastoid antrum and the external meatus and forms Luc's abscess. The swelling can burst into the meatus causing otorrhea.

Options B and C: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and trigeminal schwannoma can present with cranial nerve palsy, but they do not follow the above clinical course.
question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a history of ear discharge in the left ear for the past 4 weeks, deep-seated ear pain for the past 1 week, and diplopia for the past 2 days. What is the most probable diagnosis in this scenario?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral sinus thrombophlebitis. It is an inflammation of the inner wall of the lateral venous sinus with the formation of an intrasinus thrombus.

Clinical features of lateral sinus thrombophlebitis:

  • Hectic picket fence fever with chills and rigors. This is due to septicemia. The clinical picture resembles malaria but lacks regularity.
  • Headache - In the early stage, it may be due to peri-sinus abscess and is mild. Later, it may be severe when intracranial pressure rises due to venous obstruction.
  • Griesinger’s sign - this is due to thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein. Edema appears over the posterior part of the mastoid.
  • Papilloedema - its presence depends on obstruction to venous return.
  • Tenderness along the jugular vein - This is seen when thrombophlebitis extends along the jugular vein. There may be associated enlargement and inflammation of the jugular chain of lymph nodes and torticollis.

Investigations:

  • Blood culture
  • CSF analysis - normal except for increased CSF pressure that helps in ruling out meningitis.
  • CECT shows a typical delta sign.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment:

  • Intravenous antibacterial therapy
  • Mastoidectomy and exposure of sinus to remove the infected clot
  • Ligation of internal jugular vein
question: A patient with a history of foul-smelling ear discharge, for which he did not complete treatment now presents with complaints of fever with chills and swelling over the mastoid. On examination, there is tenderness along the jugular vein. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Otosclerosis affects the otic capsule.

The inner ear is divided into:

  • The membranous labyrinth/otic labyrinth. It is filled with endolymph.
  • The bony labyrinth/otic capsule.
  • The periotic labyrinth, which is the space between the bony and membranous labyrinth and is filled with perilymph.

The otic capsule has three layers: endosteal, enchondral and periosteal. It is the enchondral layer with islands of unossified cartilage rests, sometimes, that later give rise to otosclerosis. One or more foci of irregularly laid spongy bone replace part of the normally dense enchondral layer of otic capsule.
question: Which of the following structures does otosclerosis affect?

explanationHtml:
The most common site of origin of otosclerosis is the fissula ante fenestram lying in front of the oval window. It leads to stapedial type of otosclerosis.

Types of otosclerosis :

  • Stapedial-lesion starts in fissula ante fenestram
  • Cochlear-involves round window
  • Histological-asymptomatic type

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis.
question: What is the most common site of origin of otosclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The otosclerotic focus is biscuit type when the disease process involves the entire footplate except for the annular ligament.

The stapes has a head, neck, anterior and posterior crura, and a footplate. The footplate is held in the oval window by the annular ligament.

The otosclerotic foci in the stapedial type of otosclerosis can be of various types:

  • Anterior focus - involving only the fissula ante fenestrum- most common
  • Posterior focus - involving only the fissula post fenestrum
  • Circumferential - affects the margin of the footplate only (annular ligament alone)
  • Biscuit type - affects the entire footplate except for the annular ligament
  • Obliterative - affects the entire footplate & its annular ligament.

[[figure-1]]
question: What is the type of otosclerotic focus when the disease process involves the entire footplate except for the annular ligament?

explanationHtml:
Otosclerosis has an autosomal dominant type of inheritance.

About 50% of the cases of otosclerosis have a positive family history while the rest are sporadic. Genetic studies reveal that it is an autosomal dominant trait with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.
question: You are an OBGYN resident, and your patient is a primigravida who has just been diagnosed with otosclerosis and wants to know its inheritance pattern. Which of the following is the inheritance pattern for otosclerosis?

correctAnswer: C. HRCT shows double ring sign in stapedial otosclerosis.
explanationHtml:
HRCT shows the double-ring sign in cochlear otosclerosis, not in the stapedial type.

Other options:

Option A: Otosclerosis affects females twice as often as males. But in India, otosclerosis seems to predominate in males. The most common age group when the hearing loss in otosclerosis usually manifests is 20-30 years of age. It is rare before 10 and after 40 years.

Option B: Stapedotomy is contraindicated in children because recurrent eustachian tube dysfunction is common in them. This can displace the prosthesis or cause acute otitis media.

Option D: Measles RNA has been found in otosclerotic foci implicating its possible role in pathogenesis.

Note: Otosclerosis may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta. The triad of symptoms of osteogenesis imperfecta, otosclerosis, and blue sclera is called van der Hoeve syndrome.

options.text: Females are affected twice as often as males.
Stapedotomy should be avoided in children.
HRCT shows double ring sign in stapedial otosclerosis.
It may be associated with measles.

question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding otosclerosis?

explanationHtml:
Presbycusis is not seen in otosclerosis. It is the hearing loss associated with the physiological aging process and is unrelated to otosclerosis.

The following hearing defects are seen in otosclerosis:

  • Painless progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss is most commonly seen.
  • Sensorineural hearing loss may be seen in cochlear type of otosclerosis.
  • Paracusis willisii: Patient hears better in noisy surroundings as other people raise their voices to be heard.
question: Which of the following hearing defects is not seen in otosclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The blue mantle sign of Manasse is a histopathological finding seen in otosclerosis.

On histopathological examination of an otosclerotic foci, the osteoblasts and osteoclasts lie in an abundance of cement substance, which stains blue with hematoxylin and eosin stain.

Other options:

Option B: Blue dot sign is seen in the torsion of the testicular appendage.

Options C & D: Blue cement sign and islets in ocean sign do not exist.
question: In a stapedectomy specimen of a patient with otosclerosis, a pathologist noted that a few areas of the otic capsule appeared more basophilic than normal. What is this appearance called?

explanationHtml:
The otoscopic picture of both the tympanic membranes (TM) shows the Schwartze sign. This finding along with the history of bilateral conductive deafness is seen in active otosclerosis.

A reddish hue may be seen on the promontory through the tympanic membrane (Schwartze sign). This is indicative of an active focus with increased vascularity. It is also known as the Flamingo pink/flush sign.

In contrast, the normal TM appearance is indicative of a matured or inactive focus of otosclerosis. This is the most common finding in otosclerosis.

Other options:

Option A: Brown sign is seen in a glomus tumor.

Option C: Setting sun sign is an eye sign seen in hydrocephalus.

Option D: Cartwheel appearance of TM is seen in acute suppurative otitis media.
question: A 20-year-old female patient presents with features of bilateral conductive hearing loss. The following image shows the otoscopic findings of her tympanic membranes. What is this sign called?

explanationHtml:
Gelle’s test was a tuning fork test done to clinically confirm otosclerosis in the past. It is not popular these days.

It is based on the fact that in a normal ear if pressure is increased in the external ear canal with the means of Siegel's speculum, the stapes footplate will get medialized and will stop conducting sound. But, in an ear with otosclerosis of the footplate, there will be no movements and the patient will continue to hear the sound. Thus, Gelle’s test is considered positive in normal people and in those with sensorineural hearing loss. It is negative when the ossicular chain is fixed or disconnected.

Other options:

Option B: Stenger’s test is done to rule out malingering.

Option C: Schwabach's test is a tuning fork test that compares the bone conduction of the patient with that of the examiner.

Option D: Rinne’s test is a tuning fork test that compares bone conduction with air conduction.
question: An ENT senior resident posted in a remote village comes across a patient in whom he suspects otosclerosis. Which of the following tests can be used if he wants to clinically confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of otosclerosis and the single best investigation to diagnose otosclerosis is impedance audiometry.

Other options:

Option B: In pure tone audiometry (PTA), Carhart's notch with an air-bone gap indicates otosclerosis. The Carhart's notch is not specific for otosclerosis and may be seen in other middle ear diseases like otitis media with effusion.

Option C: MRI is usually not done. HRCT is the preferred imaging modality for otosclerosis.

Option D: Schwabach’s test is a tuning fork test that shows conductive hearing loss.
question: A 25-year-old woman with a family history of hearing loss in her mother developed a hearing problem during pregnancy. Hearing loss is bilateral and progressive. Which of the following is the single best investigation to establish the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Carhart's notch typically dips at 2000 Hz in bone conduction.

Otosclerosis mainly causes conductive hearing loss. Pure tone audiometry in otosclerosis reveals following findings:

  • Air conduction is poor & worse for lower frequencies.
  • Bone conduction is normal.
  • There is a large air-bone gap
  • In some cases, there is a dip in the bone conduction curve. It is different at different frequencies but the maximum dip is at 2000 Hz and is called Carhart’s notch. The presence of this notch is not specific to otosclerosis.

[[figure-1]]

Note: Boiler’s notch is a similar dip in BC and AC curve but at 4000 Hz, seen in noise-induced hearing loss.

options.text: 4000 Hz in both BC and AC

question: Carhart’s notch typically dips at which of the following frequencies?

correctAnswer: C. As graph with loss of stapedial reflex
explanationHtml:
The above case is suggestive of a long-standing case of otosclerosis and impedance audiometry will show As graph and loss of stapedial reflex as a result of fixation of ossicles.

Impedance audiometer measures 2 parameters in the middle ear:

  • Tympanogram - Type As is seen in otosclerosis due to decreased compliance at or near ambient air pressure
  • Stapedial reflex - Stapedial reflex is lost due to immobile ossicles.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Ad graph with increased stapedial reflex
As graph with loss of stapedial reflex
As graph with increased stapedial reflex

question: An elderly woman with a history of otosclerosis has now come with worsening deafness. She attained menopause 1 year ago. What would be the most likely report if impedance audiometry was done for her?

explanationHtml:
Sodium fluoride is used in the medical management of otosclerosis. This is an active case of otosclerosis evidenced by Schwartze’s sign.

In an active case of otosclerosis, medical management with sodium fluoride (NaF) is preferred because NaF hastens the maturity of active focus in otosclerosis. It acts by inhibiting the osteoclasts and decreasing the proteolytic enzymes. Surgery is contraindicated if Schwartze’s sign is positive.

Note: Bisphosphonates may also be useful in the medical management of active otosclerosis.
question: A patient was diagnosed with otosclerosis and Schwartze’s sign was positive on otoscopy. How will you manage this patient?

explanationHtml:
The treatment of choice for otosclerosis with normal tympanic membranes, signifying mature otosclerosis, is stapedotomy.

Stapedotomy is the excision of the superstructure of stapes and drilling a hole in the footplate & placing a piston in the hole. This is the treatment of choice. The piston replaces the stapes superstructure and takes over the function of conducting sound. It is shown in the illustration below:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Sodium fluoride (NaF) is used in an active case of otosclerosis to hasten maturation.

Option B: Type V tympanoplasty (fenestration operation) was done earlier for otoclerosis. It is not the preferred treatment for otosclerosis.

Option C: Stapedectomy is the excision of the entire stapes (superstructure + footplate) and placing a piston in its place. It is outdated. It is not preferred as it leads to an increased risk of fistula formation.

Note: Stapedotomy is performed under local anesthesia.

Special considerations for stapedotomy:

  • In a case of active otosclerosis, surgery is not performed until it matures. Medical management with sodium fluoride is used to hasten the maturation.
  • During pregnancy, the procedure is not performed. It is performed only after delivery.
  • In a patient with co-morbid Meniere's disease, the surgery is performed after managing Meniere's disease or is performed with caution.
  • For divers and frequent air travellers (or pilots), a scheduled break from these activities is required after the procedure.
  • The procedure is contraindicated if otosclerosis involves the only hearing ear.

Post-op complications:

  • Conductive hearing loss (due to prosthesis displacement, incus erosion, or recurrence of otosclerosis)
  • Sensorineural hearing loss with possible dead ear
  • Facial nerve injury
  • Vertigo
  • Perilymphatic fistula
  • Discomfort from loud noise
  • Alteration in taste
  • Cholesteatoma
  • Meningitis
question: What is the treatment of choice for otosclerosis in a patient with normal tympanic membranes on examination?

explanationHtml:
Perilymphatic hydrops is not the other name or a variant of Ménière’s disease. Instead, Ménière’s disease is also called endolymphatic hydrops.

Ménière’s disease is a disorder of the inner ear where the endolymphatic system is distended with endolymph. This occurs due either due to excessive production or faulty absorption of endolymph.

Vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus are the characteristic clinical features of Ménière’s disease, but it has different variants:

  • Cochlear hydrops: Here, the main feature is hearing loss. Vertigo is absent.
  • Vestibular hydrops: Here, repeated episodes of vertigo are seen, without loss of hearing.
question: Which of the following is not the other name or a variant of Ménière’s disease?

explanationHtml:
Otalgia is least likely to be present in a patient diagnosed with Ménière’s disease.

Ménière’s disease is commonly seen in the second to sixth decade of life. It involves males and females equally. Usually, it is unilateral, but the other ear may be affected after a few years. The characteristic triad of Ménière’s disease includes:

  1. Episodic vertigo- Each episode of vertigo lasts anywhere from 20 minutes to 24 hours. Attacks come in clusters, with periods of spontaneous remission lasting for weeks, months, or years.
  2. Fluctuating hearing loss- hearing is affected during episodes of vertigo, improves after the attack, and may be normal during remissions. Hearing loss is added with each attack and therefore there is gradually progressive loss. The hearing loss is sensorineural type.
  3. Tinnitus- low-pitched whistling or roaring type

Warning symptoms preceding an attack of vertigo in Ménière’s:

  • Sense of fullness in the ear
  • Change in pitch or increasing intensity of tinnitus
  • Decrease in hearing

Note: Differentials of Ménière’s disease:

  • Vestibular neuronitis
  • BPPV
  • Cervical spondylosis
  • Acoustic tumours
  • Vertebrobasilar insufficiency
  • Labyrinthitis
  • Perilymph fistula
  • Migraine-induced vertigo
question: Which of these symptoms is least likely to be present in a patient diagnosed with Ménière’s disease?

explanationHtml:
Intolerance to loud sounds in this patient is due to the recruitment phenomenon (sound is amplified to be heard better). It is a feature of all cochlear pathologies.

Ménière’s disease is a cochlear pathology, hence showing the recruitment phenomenon.

Other options:

Option B: The rollover phenomenon is a feature of retro-cochlear pathologies like an acoustic neuroma.

Option C: Diplacusis is the perception of a single auditory stimulus as sounds of a different pitch in two ears. This is also seen in Ménière’s disease.

Option D: Tullio phenomenon is a condition where loud sounds precipitate a vertiginous attack.
question: A 35-year-old patient diagnosed with Ménière’s disease complains of intolerance to loud sounds. What is the probable cause of intolerance to loud sounds in this patient?

correctAnswer: D. ASOM with a perforated tympanic membrane
explanationHtml:
The phenomenon described above is the Tullio phenomenon and is not seen in ASOM with a perforated tympanic membrane.

The Tullio phenomenon refers to sound-induced vertigo. People with this condition experience unsteadiness, vertigo, nausea, and rapid involuntary eye movements (nystagmus) when exposed to loud sounds or noise. Some cases of Ménière’s disease show the Tullio phenomenon due to the distended saccule lying against the stapes footplate.

It is also seen whenever there is a third mobile window lesion, such as otic syphilis, perilymph fistula, and dehiscence of semicircular canals.

question: A middle-aged man presented with a history of vertigo, tinnitus, and intolerance to loud sounds. He constantly gets vertiginous episodes when exposed to loud sounds or noise. This phenomenon is not seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Early Ménière’s disease affects lower frequencies. As the disease progresses, all the frequencies become affected.

There is no classical audiogram pattern that can be used to identify Ménière’s disease. However, there are certain features that have been commonly observed. These include:

  • A varying degree of sensorineural hearing loss.
  • This hearing loss is usually low frequency.
