question: A second-year resident performs the tuning fork tests on a patient with hearing loss. The Rinne test is positive in both ears and Weber is lateralized towards the right. What is the interpretation?

explanationHtml:
Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) damages the outer hair cells, starting in the basal turn of the cochlea. Outer hair cells are affected before the inner hair cells.

NIHL occurs after chronic exposure to less intense sounds. The damage caused by noise trauma depends on the frequency of noise (frequency of 2000 to 3000 Hz causes more damage) intensity, duration of the noise, and preexisting ear disease.

The audiogram in noise-induced hearing loss shows a typical notch at 4000Hz both for air and bone conduction known as acoustic dip/boiler's notch. Patients at this stage complain of high-pitched tinnitus and difficulty hearing in noisy surroundings. Pre-employment and annual audiograms for persons working at places where noise is above 85 dB (A) help in the early detection of NIHL.

The human ear can hear frequencies from about 20 to 20,000 Hz. Below 20 Hz, the vibrations are infra-audible, and above 20,000 Hz, they are ultra-sonic. Pure tone audiometry can detect only up to 8000 Hz.

Extended high-frequency audiometry is recommended for early detection of hearing loss, as it can identify hearing impairments before the frequencies necessary for speech comprehension are affected. Distortion product otoacoustic emissions is a more sensitive tool than conventional audiometry, particularly in children under 5 years old for early detection of hearing loss.

A noise of 90 dB(A) SPL (acceptable noise levels, sound pressure level), 8 hours a day for 5 days per week is the maximum safe limit as recommended by the Ministry of Labour. As per WHO, 85 dB(A) is considered the highest safe exposure level up to a maximum of 8 hours.

The silence zone extends to a distance of 100 meters around the premises of hospitals, nursing homes, educational institutions, and courts.

Permissible limits of noise as per the noise pollution (Regulation and Control) rules:

Zone/Area Day (6 am to 10 pm) limits in dB(A) Night (10 pm to 6 am) limits in dB(A)
Industrial 75 70
Commercial 65 55
Residential 55 45
Silence 50 40

Noise levels are measured in dB(A), which prioritizes middle-range frequencies for assessing noise-induced hearing loss while giving less weightage to low and high frequencies.

The image below shows an acoustic dip at 4000Hz:

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Crista ampullaris is a thickened ridge of neuroepithelium in the ampullated end of semicircular ducts.

Option B: Macula is the sensory epithelium of the utricle

Option C: Cupula is a gelatinous mass extending from the surface of the crista (peripheral receptor located in the ampullated end of semicircular ducts) to the ceiling of the ampulla, into which project the cilia of sensory hair cells.

question: The audiogram of a patient with difficulty in hearing is given below. What is your interpretation?

explanationHtml:

Interpretation of the result:

  • Red indicates the right ear.

question: The audiogram of a patient who presented with a gradually progressive hearing loss is given below. Which among the following would be the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario describes a patient with post-pregnancy hearing loss. The audiogram shows conductive deafness along with Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz). These findings are highly suggestive of otosclerosis.

[[figure-1]]

Otosclerosis is caused by bony overgrowth involving the enchondral layer of the bony otic capsule. It presents with bilateral progressive conductive hearing loss and tinnitus. It has an autosomal dominant inheritance and can worsen with stress and hormonal changes like during pregnancy and menopause.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fistula ante fenestrae.

The presence of a reddish hue on the promontory through the tympanic membrane, known as the Schwartze sigbn, suggests an active focus. PTA shows loss of air conduction with air-bone gap, more for lower frequencies and Carhart's notch may be seen. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage. Definitive treatment is stapedectomy/stapedotomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Carhart notch usually disappears after a successful stapedectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Ototoxicity causes SNHL and shows a high-frequency hearing loss in the SNHL curve.

Option B: In Meniere's disease, pure tone audiometry shows an SNHL pattern with a rising curve in the early stages (as lower frequencies are involved first) and as the disease progresses higher frequencies are involved, the curve becomes flat or a falling type.

Option D: Noise-induced hearing loss is SNHL and PTA shows a characteristic acoustic dip at 4000 Hz both for air and bone conduction.

question: A 25-year-old woman presented with hearing loss that developed shortly after her first pregnancy. Her audiometry report is given below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Impedance audiometry can be used to test malingering. It is an objective test and consists of tympanometry and acoustic reflex measurements.

A person who feigns total deafness and does not give any response on pure tone audiometry but shows a positive acoustic reflex is a malingerer.

Tests for malingering or nonorganic hearing loss:

  • Stenger test
  • Lombard test
  • Stapedial reflex (a part of impedance audiometry)
  • Inconsistent results on repeat pure tone and speech audiometry tests
  • BERA

Objective tests are preferred to detect malingering and the following tests are the best ones available currently:

  • Acoustic reflex threshold
  • Brain stem evoked response audiometry (BERA)

Other options:

Options A & B: Inconsistent results on repeat pure tone and speech audiometry tests can also be used to detect malingering, but the acoustic reflex is a better test since it is objective.

Option D: The tone decay test measures auditory nerve fatigue and is primarily used to detect retrocochlear lesions. It is not a tool for identifying malingering.

explanationHtml:
The given symptom is indicative of a recruitment phenomenon and is seen in cochlear hearing loss (e.g., Ménière’s disease and presbycusis). It refers to abnormal growth of loudness.

Recruitment is tested by ABLB (Alternate Binaural Loudness Balance) test. Lesser intensity sounds are heard louder in the normal ear. However, a greater intensity sound is heard equally, or even better in the abnormal ear. This is referred to as abnormal growth of loudness.

In contrast, in the conductive and retrocochlear hearing loss, a constant difference of intensity is maintained throughout, i.e., the recruitment phenomenon is not seen.

question: A woman is brought by her son to the ENT OPD due to hearing problems. He says that she always requests him to speak loud and whenever he speaks slightly louder, she tells him to stop shouting. Which of the following is the likely cause for this patient's condition?

explanationHtml:

In a patient with retrocochlear hearing loss, with an increase in speech intensity above a particular level, the speech discrimination score falls rather than maintaining a plateau as seen in the cochlear type of sensorineural hearing loss. The rollover phenomenon is caused by nerve fatigue and desynchronized firing in the auditory nerve at high intensities, which is a feature of retrocochlear pathologies.

question: Patient with hearing loss undergoes speech audiometry whose report is given below. What is it suggestive of?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the MRI are suggestive of vestibular schwannoma which is a retrocochlear disease. The presence of otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) is a feature consistent with the diagnosis.

Since OAEs are generated by the outer hair cells within the cochlea, and a retrocochlear lesion is located beyond this structure, the mechanism for producing OAEs remains completely intact, as opposed to cochlear pathologies, where OAEs are absent.

Vestibular schwannoma typically presents at 40-60 years of age. Progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, often accompanied by tinnitus, is the presenting symptom in the majority of cases. The MRI shows left cerebellopontine angle mass causing widening of the porous acousticus. The mass is seen extending into intracanalicular portion of the internal acoustic meatus which is suggestive of vestibular schwannoma.

Other options:

Option A: In the threshold tone decay test, >25 dB decay, and not <25 dB decay is diagnostic of retrocochlear lesions.

Option B: SISI score 0-20 %, and not 70-100 %, is a feature of retrocochlear lesions.

Option D: The recruitment phenomenon is seen in cochlear lesions and not retrocochlear lesions.

question: A middle-aged woman presents to you with a progressive hearing loss accompanied by tinnitus. An MRI of the patient with gadolinium contrast is given below. Which of the following results is consistent with the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Electrical activity of hair cells
explanationHtml:
Summating potential in electrocochleography indicates the sum of electrical activity in hair cells within the organ of Corti.

Electrocochleography (ECoG) is an objective test which records the electrical activity of the cochlea and 8th nerve in response to auditory stimuli. The recording electrode is passed through the tympanic membrane to rest over the promontory.

The three parameters measured in ECoG are:

  1. Cochlear microphonics – measures the electrical activity that follows the stimulus and reflects the instantaneous displacement of the basilar membrane.
  2. Summating potential (SP) – measures the electrical activity of the hair cells within the organ of Corti.
  3. Action potential (AP) – electrical activity in the distal part of the auditory nerve.

Normal SP: AP ratio is <30% but it is increased in Meniere’s disease.

question: A preterm neonate with an Apgar score of 4 at 5 minutes of birth undergoes otoacoustic emission study.  Which of the following is false about this test?

explanationHtml:
Wave V in BERA is produced by the lateral lemniscus.

The generators of ABEPs (Auditory nerve and brainstem evoked potentials) have been the subject of much research and controversy, and are still not entirely agreed upon.

The literature available to us states the following:

  • Scott Brown's Otorhinolaryngology- wave V arises from the lateral lemniscus and possibly the inferior colliculus. The negative potential following wave V is thought to arise from the inferior colliculus. So lateral lemniscus is the better option.
  • Current Diagnosis and Treatment in Otorhinolaryngology- auditory brainstem response waves 2, 3, 4, and 5 represent the sequential activation of neurons as the signal is passed up the brainstem from the proximal part of the cochlear nerve, cochlear nucleus, superior olivary complex, and lateral lemniscus.
  • NIH Journals- generation of wave V reflects the activity of multiple anatomic auditory structures. A sharp positive peak of wave V arises mainly from the lateral lemniscus, following a slow negative wave represents dendritic potential in the inferior colliculus.

Considering the sources above, we believe that it is better to mark the lateral leminiscus if both options are present.

question: Wave V in brainstem evoked response audiometry is produced by which of the following structures?

explanationHtml:
In CERA or cortical evoked response audiometry, a tone stimulus is used instead of a click stimulus.

It is an objective hearing test, that records the signals from the auditory cortex (part of the brain that recognizes sound) that have been generated in response to sounds introduced to the ears.

The test gives information about the level of sound needed to produce a signal and confirms the status of the auditory cortex. This is valuable information that we can not obtain from a normal hearing test.

Differences between BERA and CERA:

BERA CERA
The recording is made from brain stem potentials The recording is made from cortical potentials
Click stimulus is used Tone stimulus is used
Responses are not frequency specific Responses are frequency specific
Can be performed in awake and restless patients The patient must lie still throughout the process
Responses begin after 1 -10 milliseconds after stimuli Responses begin after 50 – 300 milliseconds after stimulation
Suitable for even younger children Unsuitable for children

question: As a medical officer in an occupational health program, you encounter an employee with hearing loss. You are suspicious that he is faking it to claim compensation. Which of the following tests is least useful in this scenario?

correctAnswer: C. Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side
explanationHtml:
In caloric testing, cold water irrigation produces horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side of irrigation. The direction of nystagmus can be remembered by the mnemonic, COWS (cold–opposite, warm–same).

The mechanism for the nystagmus is the creation of a temperature gradient by the cold water, which pulls the cupula away from the utricle, causing nystagmus towards the opposite side. As the horizontal semicircular canal is closer to the outer ear canal, most of the response comes from it and the nystagmus is horizontal.

The Fitzgerald–Hallpike test (bithermal caloric test) is done to assess this phenomenon. The patient lies in a supine position with head tilted forward at a 30° angle, ensuring the horizontal canal becomes vertical. Alternatingly, water at temperatures of 30°C and 44°C (7° below and above normal body temperature, respectively) is irrigated into the ears for a duration of 40 seconds each. The examiner closely observes the patient's eyes for the emergence of nystagmus until its endpoint is reached. The time taken from the start of irrigation to the endpoint of nystagmus is recorded and plotted on a calorigram.

If no nystagmus is evoked from either ear, the test is repeated with water at a temperature of 20°C for a duration of 4 minutes before labeling the labyrinth dead. A 5-minute interval should be allowed between testing each ear to ensure accurate results.

question: Which of the following is correct about the framework of the external nose?

explanationHtml:
The external nose is made up of 3 paired and 1 unpaired cartilages.

Paired cartilages:

  • Upper lateral cartilage - From nasal bone above to alar cartilage below.
  • Lower lateral (alar) cartilage - U-shaped. Lateral crus forms the ala and medial crus runs in the columella. Limen nasi or limen vestibuli is the junction of the upper and lower lateral cartilages.
  • Lesser alar (sesamoid) cartilage - multiple, above, and lateral to the alar cartilage.

Unpaired cartilage:

  • The septal cartilage (quadrangular or quadrilateral cartilage) is the only unpaired cartilage. It forms the midline of the lower 2/3rd of the dorsum of nose and supports lower 2/3rd of the dorsum of external nose.

In Water's view, the patient’s head is positioned such that the nose and the chin touch the film while the X-rays are projected from backward. The mouth is usually kept open, which allows visualizing the sphenoid sinus.

question: During inspiration, through which part of the nasal cavity does the main current of airflow take place?

explanationHtml:
The movement of the mucus blanket of the nose is by ciliary action.

The nasal mucosa is rich in goblet cells and both mucous and serous secretory glands. Their combined secretions form a continuous layer known as the mucous blanket spread over the normal mucosa.

The mucous blanket consists of a superficial mucus layer and a deeper serous layer, floating on top of cilia that are constantly beating to carry it, like a conveyor belt, towards the nasopharynx.

The mucous blanket moves at a speed of 5–10 mm/min, and the complete sheet of mucus is cleared into the pharynx every 10–20 min. In mammals, cilia beat 10–20 times per second at room temperature.

  • Drugs (adrenaline)
  • Excessive heat or cold
  • Smoking
  • Infections
  • Noxious fumes like sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide

question: Which of the following factors does not directly impair mucociliary clearance in the nasal cavity?

explanationHtml:
The mucociliary clearance, a key component of the innate defense system of the lower airways, is the primary protective function compromised in this patient.

The clinical triad of chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus (dextrocardia, as seen in the chest X-ray) is characteristic of Kartagener syndrome, also known as Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia/Immotile Cilia Syndrome. Mucociliary clearance is compromised in this case due to the presence of immotile cilia.

The lower airway is protected by the following mechanisms:

  • Mucociliary mechanism - The inspired pathogens and dust are trapped on the viscous mucus blanket. By beating the cilia, the mucus is carried to the nasopharynx to be swallowed.
  • Chemical mechanisms - Immunoglobulins such as IgA, IgE, and Lactoferrin, lysozyme, provide innate immunity.
  • Sneezing - It is a protective reflex due to irritation of the nasal mucosa.

Temperature regulation and humidification are due to the large surface area of the mucosa and highly vascular cavernous spaces. This is achieved by an increase or decrease in blood flow, which in turn increases or decreases the size of the turbinates.

explanationHtml:
Anosmia refers to the complete loss of the sense of smell. Allergic rhinitis is more commonly associated with hyposmia (a partial reduction in smell) due to nasal mucosal inflammation and congestion. Anosmia in allergic rhinitis is uncommon and occurs only when it leads to nasal polyposis.

Causes of anosmia:

  • Nasal obstruction due to nasal polyps, enlarged turbinates, or mucosal edema due to infections.
  • Atrophic rhinitis, a degenerative disorder of the nasal mucosa.
  • Peripheral neuritis (toxic or influenzal).
  • Injury to the olfactory nerves or the olfactory bulb in fractures of the anterior cranial fossa.
  • Intracranial lesions like abscesses, tumors, or meningitis, which cause pressure on the olfactory tracts.
  • COVID-19 is associated with a complete lack of taste and smell, and is a common presenting symptom.

Note:

Merciful anosmia: In primary atrophic rhinitis, there is a foul smell from the nose, making the patient a social outcast, though the patient himself is unaware of the smell due to marked anosmia.

Parosmia is the perversion of smell due to misdirected regeneration of nerve fibers.

Phantosmia is the sensation of olfaction in the absence of a stimulus.

Olfactory agnosia is the inability to recognize an odour sensation.

question: A 17-year-old girl was evaluated for delay in the onset of puberty. On further enquiry, she revealed that she has always had a very poor sense of smell. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Paranasal sinuses are filled with air during expiration
explanationHtml:
Paranasal sinuses are ventilated during expiration.

Ventilation of the sinuses is paradoxical, as they are emptied of air during inspiration and filled with air during expiration.

During inspiration, negative pressure is created in the nose by the air current, whereas during expiration, positive pressure is created in the nose, and this sets up eddy currents, which ventilate the sinuses.

Little’s area, situated at the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, is the most common site of epistaxis in children and young adults.

Factors that increase the risk of epistaxis in children when compared to adults include the habit of nose picking and increased friability of mucosa due to frequent upper respiratory tract infections.

question: A 15-year-old boy was brought to the ER with a nose bleed secondary to trauma. The bleeding started an hour ago and has not stopped. Where is the bleed most likely to be from?

question: Where is Little’s area situated?

explanationHtml:
The posterior ethmoidal artery does not contribute to the formation of Kiesselbach’s plexus.

Kiesselbach’s plexus is a rich vascular anastomotic network located in Little’s area, which is situated in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum.

The contributing arteries are as follows:

  • Sphenopalatine and greater palatine branches of the maxillary artery, which in turn is a branch of the external carotid artery.
  • Septal branch of the superior labial artery which in turn is a branch of the facial artery. The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery.
  • Anterior ethmoidal branch of the ophthalmic division of internal carotid artery.

[[figure-1]]
question: A worried mother brought her 4-year-old son to the ER with complaints of a nose bleed. On examination, the bleed was found to be from the Kiesselbach’s plexus. Which of the following arteries does not contribute to its formation?

explanationHtml:

It is called the artery of epistaxis because the majority of the blood supply to the nasal cavity is derived from it. It is also the most commonly involved artery in epistaxis.

1 - Anterior ethmoidal artery

2 - Posterior ethmoidal artery

4 - Greater palatine artery

explanationHtml:

2 – Sphenopalatine artery

question: Which of the following marked structures is a branch of the internal carotid artery?

correctAnswer: C. Posterior end of middle turbinate
explanationHtml:
The most common cause of posterior epistaxis is arterial, and the vessel involved is the sphenopalatine artery. It is located at the posterior end of the middle turbinate.

Woodruff's plexus is a venous plexus located at the posterior end of the inferior turbinate and is also sometimes implicated in epistaxis associated with systemic conditions such as hypertension and coagulopathy. However, it only accounts for about 5-10% of all nose bleeds.

Note: The most common vessel involved in both anterior and posterior epistaxis is the sphenopalatine artery and not Woodruff's plexus.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of refractory posterior epistaxis. The artery most commonly ligated in cases of refractory posterior epistaxis is the sphenopalatine artery.

Posterior epistaxis is most commonly seen in older age groups. The bleeding is spontaneous, often due to hypertension, and is severe, requiring hospitalization.

Refractory epistaxis is defined as recurrent or persistent bleeding after appropriate packing or multiple episodes of epistaxis during a short period, each requiring medical attention.

Sphenopalatine artery ligation yields high success in controlling refractory posterior bleeds. Therefore, transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL) is the preferred method.It is ligated at the sphenopalatine foramen situated 1 cm behind the posterior end of the middle turbinate.

The table below shows the differences between the anterior and posterior epistaxis:

Anterior epistaxis Posterior epistaxis
Age Children & young adults >40 years
Incidence Most common Less common
Cause Trauma Spontaneous, often due to Hypertension or arteriosclerosis
Site Little’s area - anteroinferior part of the nasal septum Posterosuperior part of the nasal cavity; difficult to localize
Bleeding Mild- can be controlled by local pressure or nasal packing. Severe-often requires hospitalization and posterior nasal packing.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 65-year-old hypertensive patient presented with a history of recurrent episodes of spontaneous nose bleeds over the past two weeks, each episode requiring medical attention. After evaluating the patient, the ENT surgeon recommended endoscopic artery ligation to prevent further episodes of bleeding. Which of the following arteries is most commonly ligated in this procedure?

explanationHtml:
The maxillary artery is ligated at the pterygopalatine fossa (sphenopalatine fossa) situated behind the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus.

  • The internal maxillary artery can be accessed via a transantral approach using the Caldwell-Luc procedure(anterior antrostomy).
  • After creating an opening in the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus, the posterior wall of the sinus is removed to expose the pterygopalatine fossa, where the internal maxillary artery and its terminal branches can be identified and clipped.
  • The posterior sinus wall is then packed with Gelfoam, and the gingivobuccal incision is closed.
  • In recent years, transoral and transnasal endoscopic approaches have also been developed as less invasive alternatives.

Note: This step is considered when transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL) fails to control bleeding.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: As a first-year resident, you have scrubbed in to assist with a maxillary artery ligation procedure on a patient with intractable epistaxis. After opening the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, the surgeon asks you to ligate the maxillary artery. Where would you ligate the artery?

explanationHtml:
The ethmoidal artery can be a source of epistaxis that is not controlled by ligation of the external carotid artery. This is because the ethmoidal arteries (anterior and posterior) are branches of the ophthalmic artery, which arises from the internal carotid artery.

In contrast, the sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and facial arteries are branches of the external carotid artery. Therefore, if bleeding persists after ligating external carotid artery branches, the next step is to consider ligation or cauterization of the ethmoidal artery.

[[figure-1]]

The stepwise management of epistaxis:

  1. Pinching the nose
  2. Hippocratic or Trotter’s method
  3. Cauterisation
  4. Anterior nasal packing
  5. Posterior nasal packing
  6. Endoscopic Cauterisation
  7. Ligation
  8. Embolization

Ligation should be performed as close as possible to the likely bleeding point. The recommended hierarchy of ligation to be followed is Sphenopalatine artery → Internal maxillary artery → External carotid artery → Anterior /posterior ethmoidal artery.

Ethmoidal vessels are exposed in the medial wall of the orbit by an external ethmoid (Lynch) incision.

[[figure-2]]
question: A 58-year-old male presents with profuse nasal bleeding that persists despite nasal packing and ligation of branches of the external carotid artery. Which of the following arteries is the most likely source of ongoing bleeding in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Internal carotid artery is not ligated for controlling epistaxis due to the high percentage of cerebral complications and mortality.

Ligation of the following arteries is done in epistaxis control :

  • Trans nasal Endoscopic Sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL)
  • If not controlled, maxillary artery ligation
  • If still not controlled, external carotid artery ligation
  • In case, bleeding site is superior to the level of middle turbinate, then anterior and posterior ethmoidal vessels should be ligated.

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario showing an isolated mass arising from the root of the nose should raise the index of suspicion of meningoencephalocele. It is the herniation of brain tissue along with its meninges through a congenital bony defect. They typically appear as cystic, bluish, compressible, and translucent masses.

When intranasal, they often present as a smooth, polyp-like mass in the upper nasal cavity between the septum and middle turbinate, usually in infants and young children. The mass enlarges with crying or straining due to increased intracranial pressure.Transillumination is positive in meningoencephaloceles.

These can be mistaken for simple nasal polyps. If avulsed or biopsied without prior imaging, there is a high risk of cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea or meningitis. Therefore, biopsy is contraindicated until intracranial communication has been definitively ruled out.

Imaging:

  • CT scan – for bony defect visualization
  • MRI – to assess soft tissue and brain herniation
  • Endoscopy: Reveals a grape-like, polypoidal mass within the nasal cavity.

Treatment: Transnasal endoscopic excision with the closure of the defect using bone or cartilage graft, along with temporalis fascia and fat.

[[figure-1]]

Other options :

  • Nasal glioma is a nipped-off portion of an encephalocele without intracranial communication. It typically presents as a firm, non-compressible subcutaneous swelling causing nasal obstruction. Furstenberg’s test is negative. Location: 60% extranasal, 30% intranasal, 10% both.
  • Lacrimal sac cyst (dacryocystocele) occurs near the medial canthus, not the nasal root.
  • An ethmoid cyst is intranasal, not visible as an external swelling.

question: A patient presented with atrophic dry nasal mucosa, extensive crustations, and a woody hard external nose. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Surgical excision is the primary treatment modality
explanationHtml:
Biopsy findings of Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies are characteristic of rhinoscleroma. Medical management is the mainstay of treatment for rhinoscleroma. Streptomycin (1 g/day) and tetracycline (2 g/day) are administered for a minimum of 4-6 weeks and continued until 2 consecutive biopsies are negative. Surgery is reserved to establish the airway or to correct deformity.

Biopsy in the case of rhinoscleroma shows infiltration of the submucosa with plasma cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils, Mikulicz cells, and Russell bodies.

  • Mikulicz cells are large foam cells with a central nucleus and vacuolated cytoplasm containing causative bacilli.
  • Russell bodies are homogenous, eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in the plasma cells. They occur due to the accumulation of immunoglobulins secreted by the plasma cells.

The image below displays foamy Mikulicz cells with intracellular organisms, characteristic of rhinoscleroma.

[[figure-1]]

H&E showing a mixture of plasma cells (arrow), lymphocytes (short arrow), Mikulicz cells, which are vacuolated macrophages containing causative bacilli (double arrow).

Other options:

Option A: Rhinoscleroma is endemic in several parts of the world. In India, it is seen more often in the northern than in the southern parts.

explanationHtml:

question: Which of the following statements is false about nasal T-cell lymphoma?

explanationHtml:
The mulberry appearance of the turbinate is seen in patients with hypertrophic rhinitis.

Hypertrophic rhinitis is characterized by thickening of the mucosa, submucosa, seromucinous glands, periosteum, and underlying bone, with the changes being most pronounced in the turbinates.

The inferior turbinate may be hypertrophied completely or partially—at the anterior end, posterior end, or along the inferior border—resulting in a characteristic mulberry appearance.

Other options :

Option A: Atrophic rhinitis shows roomy nasal cavities, crusting, foul odor, and thinned turbinates, not a mulberry appearance.
Option B: Coryza is acute viral rhinitis, presenting with congestion and discharge, but not turbinate hypertrophy or mulberry appearance.
Option D: Vasomotor rhinitis is a non-allergic rhinitis marked by nasal congestion and watery discharge, but again, no mulberry-like turbinate changes.

[[figure-1]]
question: You are an intern examining a patient with nasal obstruction and nasal discharge. The anterior rhinoscopy shows mulberry appearance of the inferior turbinate. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common organism causing primary atrophic rhinitis is Klebsiella ozaena[also known as Perez bacillus]

Various organisms have been cultured from cases of atrophic rhinitis, such as Coccobacillus foetidus ozaenae, Proteus vulgaris, Escherichia coli, staphylococci, diphtheroids, and streptococci, but they are all considered to be secondary invaders responsible for foul smell rather than the primary causative organisms of the disease.

Etiology of atrophic rhinitis:

Primary atrophic rhinitis:

  • Hereditary- Involves more than one member of a family
  • Endocrinal- More common in females, starts at puberty and regresses after menopause
  • Racial- More common in mongoloid and caucasian races
  • Nutritional deficiency- Vitamin A, D, and iron deficiencies
  • Autoimmune- Antigens of the nasal mucosa
  • Organism- Klebsiella ozaenae.

Secondary atrophic rhinitis:

  • Specific infections like syphilis, lupus, leprosy, and rhinoscleroma
  • Long-standing purulent sinusitis
  • Radiotherapy to the nose
  • Excessive surgical removal of turbinates-Empty nose syndrome
  • Diphtheroids, Proteus vulgaris, Escherichia coli, staphylococci, and streptococci.
question: A middle-aged woman with nasal discharge and crusting is diagnosed to have primary atrophic rhinitis. Which of the following organisms is most commonly associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Atrophic rhinitis is almost always bilateral.

It shows a higher prevalence in females, and often begins around puberty.

Merciful anosmia - Refers to the loss of smell that spares the patient from the foul odor of their nasal discharge.
question: Which of the following is false about atrophic rhinitis?

explanationHtml: The clinical scenario is suggestive of bilateral atrophic rhinitis. While primary atrophic rhinitis is characteristically bilateral, deviated nasal septum typically causes unilateral atrophic changes. Other causes like syphilis, rhinoscleroma, and Wegener’s granulomatosis can lead to bilateral atrophic features.
question: A 25-year-old woman presented to the OPD with foul-smelling nasal discharge and obstruction. On examination, crusts are present bilaterally and on the removal of the crust, bleeding is present. Which of the following is least likely to cause this?

explanationHtml:
Nasal obstruction in a patient with atrophic rhinitis is due to excessive crust formation.

Note:

Sensory nerve degeneration contributes to paradoxical obstruction (feeling of blockage without true blockage). Patients may feel obstructed due to a loss of airflow sensation. But actual physical obstruction is mainly due to crust formation.
question: In a patient with atrophic rhinitis, what is the main reason for nasal obstruction?

explanationHtml:
Potassium chloride is not a part of the alkaline nasal solution used in the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

The composition of the alkaline solution is:

  • Sodium chloride - 2 parts
  • Sodium bicarbonate - 1 part
  • Sodium biborate - 1 part

It is dissolved in 280 mL of water, and the nasal cavities are irrigated to loosen the crusts and ease their removal.

Other treatment options:

  • Glucose in glycerine – 25% glucose in glycerine is applied after crust removal to reduce bacterial growth and odor.
  • Antibiotics – Short-course fluoroquinolones with metronidazole help control secondary infection.
  • Hormonal therapy – Oestradiol spray and placental extract have limited proven benefit.
  • Mucolytics – Potassium iodide drops help liquefy nasal secretions.
  • Diet – A balanced diet rich in vitamin A, D, folic acid, iron, and protein supports mucosal health.
question: You are an intern in the ENT department preparing the alkaline nasal solution for a patient with atrophic rhinitis. Which of the following will you not use for the preparation?

explanationHtml:
Sodium bicarbonate is not a component of the kemicetine antiozaena solution. It is used in an alkaline nasal solution to soften crusts and aid in nasal hygiene

The components of the kemicetine antiozaena solution are:

  • Chloramphenicol
  • Oestradiol
  • Vitamin D

It is used in the medical management of atrophic rhinitis.
question: An adolescent girl with atrophic rhinitis is using kemicetine antiozaena solution. Which of the following is not a component of this solution?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of atrophic rhinitis. Young’s and modified Young’s operations are surgical treatments used for atrophic rhinitis.

In Young’s operation, both nostrils are closed completely just within the nasal vestibule by raising flaps. They are opened after 6 months or later, where the mucosa may revert to normal, and crusting will be reduced.

Modified Young’s operation aims at partially closing the nostrils.

Options A and C: Submucous resection and septoplasty are done for a deviated nasal septum.

Option D: Vidian neurectomy is done for vasomotor rhinitis.
question: A housewife presents with complaints of a blocked nose, loss of smell, and dry, greenish, crusty nasal discharge. On examination, the nasal cavities appear roomy, and the turbinates are atrophied. Which of the following surgeries can be done on this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Mainly affects posterior 2/3rd of nose
explanationHtml:
Rhinitis sicca affects the anterior 1/3rd of the nose since this part is exposed to the effects of the dry, dusty air.

It is a crust-forming condition seen in patients working in hot, dry, and dusty surroundings, e.g., bakers, ironworkers, and goldsmiths. It is usually confined to the anterior third of the nasal cavity, especially the nasal septum.

Histologically, the normal ciliated columnar epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia, accompanied by atrophy of the seromucinous glands.

Treatment involves improving the occupational environment and applying bland ointments containing a combination of antibiotics and steroids to the affected area.

Note:

Rhinitis Caseosa is a unilateral condition that mostly affects males, characterized by the nose being filled with foul-smelling, purulent discharge and cheesy material, often arising from chronic sinusitis. The sinus mucosa becomes granulomatous, and bony walls may be destroyed, mimicking malignancy. Treatment involves the removal of debris, granulation tissue, and ensuring free drainage of the affected sinus.

options.text: More common in people working in hot, dry, dusty surroundings
Antibiotic &amp; steroid ointment is used for treatment

question: A 40-year-old ironsmith came to the ENT clinic with complaints of a dry nose, nasal crusting, and bleeding on removal of the crusts. A diagnosis of rhinitis sicca was made. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated immunologic response of the nasal mucosa to airborne allergens.

Patients typically present with recurrent bouts of sneezing, nasal obstruction, watery nasal discharge, and itching, and clinical signs include allergic shiners (dark circles around the eyes) and allergic salute (black transverse nasal crease on the dorsum of the nose due to repeated upward rubbing).

Treatment options include:

  • Avoidance of the allergen
  • Treatment with drugs like oral antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, and intranasal cromolyn sodium
  • Immunotherapy is through the delivery of allergen in gradually increasing doses till the maintenance dose is reached. It suppresses the development of IgE. It has to be given for a year to see a significant improvement in symptoms

Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) remain the preferred monotherapy for persistent allergic rhinitis (AR). However, additional studies support the additive benefit of combination treatment with INCS and intranasal antihistamines in AR. For patients receiving INCS, an intranasal decongestant may be added to the treatment for up to 4 weeks.
question: Allergic rhinitis is mediated by which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of a child with watery nasal discharge, frequent sneezing, itching of the nose, and seasonal variation is suggestive of allergic rhinitis; hypertrophy of turbinates is seen, not atrophy. Atrophy of turbinates is not a feature of allergic rhinitis; it occurs in atrophic rhinitis.

Other features of allergic rhinitis:

Option A: Dennie-Morgan lines - transverse skin creases in the infraorbital area.

[[figure-1]]

Option B: Allergic salute - is a transverse nasal crease that appears as a black line across the middle of the dorsum of the nose due to constant upward rubbing of the nose, simulating a salute.

[[figure-2]]

Option D: Serous otitis media occurs as a result of eustachian tube blockage.
question: A mother brought her a 6-year-old child with watery nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, frequent sneezing and itching in the nose. She also adds that the symptoms occur during the winter season and there is a history of asthma in the family. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
A patient with perennial allergic rhinitis will have a pale and edematous nasal mucosa with swollen turbinates.

Option B & C: Crusts that bleed on removal & atrophied turbinates are features seen in atrophic rhinitis.

Option D: Congested and edematous mucosa is more commonly seen in vasomotor rhinitis, where the mucosa over the turbinates is red and hypertrophied.

Note: Typical allergic mucosa appears pale and swollen, while the mucosa is reddened in acute infections and after the overuse of topical medications.
question: An ENT resident is evaluating a patient with suspected allergic rhinitis. On anterior rhinoscopy, which of the following is most likely to be seen?

correctAnswer: C. Vidian neurectomy is a treatment option.
explanationHtml:
Vidian neurectomy is a treatment option in vasomotor rhinitis.

Vasomotor rhinitis is a non-allergic condition that occurs due to parasympathetic overactivity, causing vasodilatation and congestion of the nasal mucosa. The vidian nerve carries the parasympathetic supply to the nose.

The usual presentation is excessive rhinorrhea, sneezing, and nasal obstruction, which is similar to allergic rhinitis. But the turbinates appear congested and edematous.

Treatment includes antihistamines, oral and nasal decongestants, and topical intranasal steroids, short-term systemic steroids [for severe cases], and anticholinergic therapy [Ipratropium bromide nasal spray].

In case of failed medical treatment, vidian neurectomy is done.

Vidian neurectomy is a treatment option.
Pale and atrophied turbinates are seen.

question: A 30-year-old man came with complaints of excessive nasal discharge, sneezing, and nasal obstruction. There is no history of allergen exposure or asthma in the family. You are suspecting vasomotor rhinitis. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Rhinitis medicamentosa is caused by the prolonged use of nasal decongestants.

The treatment includes the withdrawal of nasal decongestant drops, a short course of systemic steroid therapy, and, in some cases, surgical reduction of turbinates if they have become hypertrophied.
question: Prolonged use of which of the following drugs can cause rhinitis medicamentosa?

explanationHtml:
Complete closure of the nostrils (Young's operation) or partial closure of the nostrils (Modified Young's operation) is done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

In Young's operation, both nostrils are closed completely by raising flaps within the nasal vestibule. They are opened after 6 months. During this time, the mucosa becomes normal, and the crusting is reduced.

In Modified Young's operation, the procedure has been modified to avoid discomfort from the complete closure of the nostrils. Here, the nostrils are only partially closed. The results are the same when compared to Young's operation.

Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) is a chronic inflammation of the nose with atrophy of the nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. Roomy nasal cavities with foul-smelling crusts are seen. The patient presents with a foul smell from the nose, marked anosmia (merciful anosmia), and paradoxical nasal obstruction (nasal obstruction despite wide nasal passages). Paradoxical nasal obstruction occurs due to degenerative changes in the sensory nerves of the nasal mucosa, leading to an inability to sense airflow.

Medical management includes nasal irrigation and removal of crusts. 25% glucose in glycerine, antibiotics (quinolones or metronidazole), estradiol nasal spray, and mucolytics can be used.
question: Surgery where nostrils are partially or completely occluded is done for which condition?

correctAnswer: D. Chronic nasal allergy with mucosal hypertrophy
explanationHtml:
Chronic nasal allergy with mucosal hypertrophy does not cause deviated nasal septum (DNS).

Etiology of DNS:

  • Trauma - during passage through the birth canal or trauma after birth, leading to fracture of the nasal septum
  • Developmental error - may be associated with cleft lip, cleft palate
  • Racial factor - more common in Caucasians
  • Hereditary - affects more than one member of the same family

question: Which of the following is least likely to cause a deviated nasal septum?

explanationHtml:
Nasal polyps are not typically visible in patients with a deviated nasal septum.

Clinical features of DNS:

  • Nasal obstruction - unilateral in C-shaped deviation and bilateral in S-shaped deviation
  • Headache - may be due to associated sinusitis or due to a spur pressing on the lateral wall of the nose
  • Sinusitis - due to obstruction of the ostia and poor ventilation of the sinuses
  • Epistaxis - from vessels over spur or due to crusting of the nasal mucosa
  • Anosmia - especially in bilateral nasal obstruction
  • Compensatory hypertrophy of turbinates on the roomier side
  • Frequent middle ear infections
  • Association with external deformities

question: A 3rd-year MBBS student is examining a case of deviated nasal septum. Which of the following findings is unlikely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The clinical test depicted in the image is Cottle’s test, where the cheek is drawn laterally while the patient breathes quietly.

This test is used to assess the patency of the nasal valve in patients with a deviated nasal septum. If the nasal airway improves on the test side, the test is positive and indicates an abnormality of the vestibular component of the nasal valve on that side.

Option A: Epley’s maneuver is used in the treatment of BPPV.

[[figure-1]]

Option B: Heimlich manoeuvre is used in the treatment of accidental inhalation of a foreign body.

Procedure: Stand behind the person and place your arms around his lower chest, and give four abdominal thrusts. The residual air in the lungs can dislodge the foreign body, thereby providing some airway clearance.

[[figure-2]]

Option D: Trotter’s method is used in the treatment of epistaxis. In Trotter’s method, the patient is made to sit, leaning a little forward over a basin to spit any blood. He should pinch the nose firmly for 5 to 10 mins and breathe quietly from the mouth.

[[figure-3]]

question: What clinical test is depicted in the image?

correctAnswer: D. Chronic nasal discharge without anatomical obstruction or sinus disease
explanationHtml:
Nasal discharge is not an indication for surgery in a patient with deviated nasal septum (DNS).

Indications for surgery in DNS:

  • Symptoms of nasal obstruction and recurrent headaches
  • Recurrent sinusitis and otitis media
  • Recurrent epistaxis from the septal spur
  • Septal deviation causing sleep apnea or hypopnoea syndrome

Other indications for SMR (submucous resection) and septoplasty:

  • As a part of septorhinoplasty for cosmetic correction of external nasal deformities
  • As a preliminary step in hypophysectomy (trans-septal trans-sphenoidal approach) or vidian neurectomy (transseptal approach)
  • For the approach to the middle meatus or frontal recess in endoscopic sinus surgery when a deviated septum obstructs the view and access to these areas
  • To gain access for endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy

question: An ENT surgeon is performing septoplasty in a patient with a deviated nasal septum. Which of the following is least likely to be a valid indication for performing septoplasty?

explanationHtml:
Killian’s incision is used in submucosal resection. It is a slightly curvilinear incision, placed about 1 cm cephalad from the caudal end of the septum. At this point, the perichondrium is less adherent to the underlying cartilage, and the flap can be raised more easily.

Other options:

Option B: Shobinger incision is used in modified radical neck dissection.

Option C: Freer’s hemitransfixation incision is used in septoplasty. It is a septocolumellar incision taken between the caudal end of the septal cartilage and the columella.

Option D: Weber Ferguson incision is used in maxillectomy.

[[figure-1]]

question: A patient diagnosed with deviated nasal septum is undergoing submucous resection. What is the key incision is used in this procedure?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is a case of deviated nasal septum, and septoplasty is the treatment of choice.

Both submucous resection and septoplasty can be done for DNS. Septoplasty is a conservative approach and is more commonly done nowadays. Septoplasty is also the preferred surgery for DNS in less than 17 years, if DNS is bilateral and severe.

question: A 20-year-old college student presented with complaints of facial pain, nasal discharge, headache, and nasal bleeding. He has a history of recurrent sinusitis in the past. On anterior rhinoscopy examination, the nasal septum is deviated. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?

correctAnswer: B. Can result in hump nose deformity
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with bilateral septal swelling following trauma is suggestive of a septal hematoma and can result in saddle nose deformity, not hump nose deformity.

Septal hematoma is a collection of blood under the perichondrium or periosteum of the nasal septum. It is caused by trauma, septal surgery, and bleeding disorders. Clinical features include pain, swelling, and bilateral nasal obstruction (the most common presenting feature), as well as frontal headache.

Complications include septal abscess, depression of the dorsum (saddle nose), and a permanently thickened septum.

Treatment:

  • Aspiration of small hematomas
  • Incision and drainage of large hematomas via a small anteroposterior septal incision, placed parallel to the nasal floor, followed by nasal packing done post-drainage to prevent reaccumulation.
  • Systemic antibiotics to prevent abscess formation

question: A mother brought her 5-year-old child with complaints of pain and swelling in the nose and difficulty in breathing after an alleged history of fall while playing. On examination, there is bilateral swelling of the nasal septum which is tender and erythematous. Which of the following is false about the given condition?

explanationHtml:
Trauma is the most common cause of septal perforation.

Causes of septal perforation:

  • Trauma - nasal surgery, nose picking, septal cauterization, nasal packing, septal hematoma, foreign bodies
  • Surface irritants - cocaine, heroin, decongestant nasal sprays
  • Infections - syphilis, typhoid, tuberculosis, lepromatous leprosy, rhinosporidiosis, rhinoscleroma, aspergillosis
  • Neoplastic - melanoma, SCC, adenocarcinoma, lymphoma
  • Inflammatory - sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease, RA, Granulomatosis with polyangitis

Small anterior perforations may present with a whistling sound during respiration. Large perforations may obstruct the nose or even bleed due to the formation of crusts.

Treatment:

Small asymptomatic perforations can be closed by plastic flaps.

In larger perforations, treatment is aimed at keeping the nose crust-free using nasal douches and bland ointments.

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of septal perforation?

explanationHtml:
The patient has a nasal septal perforation caused by syphilis. In syphilis, the bony part of the nasal septum is most commonly affected.

Other chronic granulomatous conditions like lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy can cause perforation in the cartilaginous part.

Wegener’s granulomatosis causes perforation of both bony and cartilaginous parts.

question: A middle-aged man with tertiary syphilis presented with complaints of epistaxis, nasal crusting, and nasal twang on speaking. On examination, nasal septal perforation was noted. What is the most likely site for the perforation?

explanationHtml:
Myiasis (maggots in the nasal cavity) is a complication of atrophic rhinitis. It is treated with chloroform diluted with water.

The maggots are larval forms of flies, especially the genus Chrysomia. The flies are attracted by the foul-smelling nasal discharge in conditions like atrophic rhinitis, syphilis, leprosy, and lay eggs in the nasal cavity. These eggs hatch into larvae within 24 hrs and cause intense irritation, lacrimation, sneezing, and blood-tinged nasal discharge.

Treatment:

  • All visible maggots should be picked up with forceps
  • Instillation of chloroform water and oil kills them
  • Nasal douche with warm saline is used to remove slough, crusts, and dead maggots.

question: A 30-year-old woman from a rural area presented with foul-smelling nasal discharge, nasal crusts, and epistaxis. She was diagnosed with atrophic rhinitis. On examination, maggots were seen in the nasal cavity. Which of the following is used in the treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Bernoulli’s phenomenon explains the pathogenesis of nasal polyp formation.

Bernoulli’s principle states that when the velocity of air increases, the lateral pressure will decrease.

When air passes through the nasal valve area, which is the narrowest region of the nasal cavity, velocity increases. This creates a negative pressure that sucks mucosa of sinuses into the nasal cavity leading to polyp formation.

question: A middle-aged man with recurrent diffuse ethmoidal polyps is scheduled for a laser-assisted FESS procedure. Which of the following lasers is ideal in this scenario?

explanationHtml:
The first step in the primary care of a patient with a maxillofacial injury is control of hemorrhage in line with the xABCDE trauma assessment protocol.

The xABCDE approach includes:

  • x - External hemorrhage: Immediately control massive, active, compressible bleeding to prevent exsanguination.
  • A & B - Airway & Breathing: Ensure an adequate airway, which may require intubation or tracheostomy due to the risk of airway compromise from facial trauma.
  • C - Circulation: Continue to control haemorrhage by pressure or ligation of bleeding vessels.
  • D - Disability: Rule out head and spinal injuries with neurological evaluation.
  • E - Exposure: Examine the patient thoroughly for injuries to other body parts.

Additional care includes wound management, documentation for medico-legal purposes, and detailed examination of the facial skeleton for fractures involving the mandible, maxilla, zygoma, and orbit.

Note:

Controlling hemorrhage does not diminish the importance of airway management, especially in maxillofacial injuries where airway obstruction is common. However, in the presence of heavy, ongoing external bleeding, hemorrhage control takes priority to prevent life-threatening blood loss.

Airway management remains essential and may proceed simultaneously, but bleeding control must not be delayed.

In this scenario, with heavy facial bleeding, control of hemorrhage is the first step in primary care.
question: A biker met with an accident and sustained a maxillofacial injury with heavy bleeding from the face. Which of the following is the first step in the primary care of this patient?

explanationHtml:
The most commonly fractured bone of the face is the nasal bone because of the projection of the nose on the face.

Types of nasal bone fractures:

  1. Frontal Blow leads to depressed fracture (both nasal bones pushed inward) or open-book fracture (nasal bones splayed outward)
  2. Lateral Blow leads to: angulated fracture (deviation of nasal bridge to opposite side of impact or unilateral depression of one nasal bone)

Note: After the nasal bones, the zygoma is the second most frequently fractured bone.
question: Which of the following facial bones is most commonly fractured?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of a nasal bleed following trauma and the image showing a horizontal fracture line is suggestive of a Jarjaway fracture.

It is a fracture of the nasal septum that results from direct blows from the front. The fracture line runs horizontally from just above the anterior nasal spine to just above the junction of the septal cartilage with the vomer.

Other options:

Option B: Le Fort I fracture (fracture of maxilla) runs above and parallel to the palate. It crosses the lower part of the nasal septum, maxillary antra, and the pterygoid plates.

Option C: Chevallet fracture results from blows from below. The fracture line runs vertically from the anterior nasal spine upwards to the junction of the bony and cartilaginous dorsum of the nose.

Option D: Tripod fracture is another name for zygoma fracture.

question: A 30-year-old man presented with a nasal bleed after sustaining a blow to the nose in a fistfight. On evaluation, a nasal septal fracture similar to the one in the image below was identified. What is your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The ideal time for the reduction of fracture of the nasal bone is 5-7 days following injury, once the edema has subsided.

The presence of edema interferes with the accurate reduction of the fracture. In most cases, the deformity is due to edema. So, ice packs and head elevation are advised initially after injury. After 3-5 days, the edema would subside, and the underlying deformity would be apparent on clinical assessment.

After 2 weeks, it is difficult to reduce since the process of callus formation and the bony and fibrous union would have started.
question: A young adult presents with a deformed nose after falling from a ladder. The CT scan shows a displaced nasal fracture. What is the ideal time to reduce the fracture in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Walsham forceps (Image 2) is used to reduce a nasal bone fracture.

Asch forceps is mainly used to reduce nasal septum fracture.

[[figure-2]]

Option A: Luc’s forceps is used in Caldwell Luc operation, submucous resection, and polypectomy.

[[figure-3]]

Option C: Tilley’s forceps is used in nasal packing in the epistaxis.

[[figure-4]]

question: As an ENT resident, you are assisting in the reduction of a nasal bone fracture. Which of the following instruments would you use?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of diplopia, flat malar prominence, trismus, and step deformity in the infraorbital margin is suggestive of fracture of the zygoma or tripod fracture.

Zygoma is the second most frequently fractured bone in the face. The zygoma fracture is separated at its three processes - the zygomaticofrontal suture, infraorbital margin, and the zygomaticotemporal suture. It has the following clinical features:

  • Flattening of malar prominence.
  • Trismus, due to depression of the zygoma on the underlying coronoid process.
  • Anesthesia in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve.
  • Step deformity of the infraorbital margin.
  • Oblique palpebral fissure, due to the displacement of the lateral palpebral ligament.
  • Restricted ocular movements due to entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle. It may cause diplopia.
  • Periorbital emphysema, due to escape of air from the maxillary sinus on nose blowing.

The following x-ray shows a right-sided zygoma fracture:

question: A boxer is wheeled into the ER with complaints of seeing double after having suffered a severe blow to his face during a match. On examination, there is a flattening of malar prominence, trismus and a step deformity of the infraorbital margin. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml: Infraorbital nerve injury in a tripod (zygomatic) fracture can cause loss of sensation over the cheek. It is commonly injured in tripod fractures involving the orbital floor/rim.
question: A patient with a tripod fracture is having decreased sensation over the cheek. Which of the following nerve injuries can result in this?

correctAnswer: A. Fracture of floor of orbit
explanationHtml:
Fracture of the floor of the orbit is called a blow-out fracture.

Zygomatic and Le Fort II maxillary fractures are always accompanied by fractures of the orbital floor.

It occurs when a large, blunt object strikes the globe. Orbital contents may herniate into the antrum.

options.text: Fracture of lateral wall of orbit
Fracture of medial wall of orbit

question: Which of the following is called blow-out fractures?

explanationHtml:
The given X-ray shows the tear-drop sign. It is seen in orbital floor or blow-out fractures when the orbital contents herniate into the maxillary antrum. Waters’ view shows a convex opacity bulging into the antrum from above (tear-drop opacity).

Other options:

Option B: Phelps’ sign is seen in a CT scan of a glomus jugulare tumor. It is the erosion of the normal crest of bone between the carotid canal and the jugular foramen.

Options C and D: Antral and Holman Miller signs are the same. It is the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus and is pathognomonic of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

[[figure-1]]
question: A teenage boy suffered trauma to his left eye while playing cricket. He is rushed to the ER in severe pain. His X-ray appears as below. What is the characteristic sign noted?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with diplopia, periorbital emphysema, and a step deformity can be seen in both orbital floor fracture and tripod fracture. In both conditions, diplopia is due to:

  • Entrapment of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles
  • Displacement of the eyeball.

The common features seen in both orbital floor fracture and tripod fracture are:

  • Periorbital emphysema
  • Step deformity of the infraorbital margin
  • Diplopia
  • Enophthalmos.
question: A 19-year-old college student presented with complaints of seeing double after sustaining a blow to his face in a scuffle with his seniors. On examination, there is a step deformity and periorbital emphysema. Entrapment of which of the following muscles is likely to be responsible for his double vision?

question: The CT scan of a patient who met with a motorcycle accident shows a fracture of the maxilla. The fracture line passes through the floor of the nose separating the palate from the rest of the face. How will you classify the fracture?

explanationHtml:
The most common site of fracture of the mandible in children is the condyle. It is because the condylar head is connected to the vertical ramus of the bone by a thin neck, which gives away easily to an impact. They are followed, in frequency, by fractures of the angle, body, and symphysis (mnemonic CABS).

Mandibular fractures:

Children:

  • Due to falls and sports injuries.
  • Most common site - condyle.

Adults > 50 years:

  • Most commonly due to falls.
  • Most common site - body (the molar area is the weakest area in an edentulous mandible).

Young Adults:

  • Due to falls, assaults, and accidents.
  • The site of fracture depends on the nature of the impact and the direction of the force applied.
question: Which of the following is the most common site for fracture of the mandible in children?

correctAnswer: A. Lamina cribrosa of the ethmoid
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of CSF rhinorrhea and fracture of the cribriform plate ( also known as lamina cribrosa) of the ethmoid is the most common cause for this.

Causes of CSF rhinorrhea:

  • Trauma (accidental or surgical) - most cases follow trauma. Surgical trauma includes endoscopic sinus surgery, transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, nasal polypectomy, or skull base surgery.
  • Inflammations - mucoceles of sinuses, sinonasal polyposis, the fungal infection of sinuses, and osteomyelitis, can all erode the bone and dura.
  • Neoplasms - tumours, both benign and malignant, invading the skull base.
  • Congenital lesions - meningocele, meningoencephaloceles, and gliomas can have associated skull base defects.
  • Idiopathic - where the cause is unknown and the patient has a spontaneous leak.
question: Following trauma, a patient presented with clear watery nasal discharge that cannot be sniffed back. Fractures of which of the following bones is the most likely cause for this?

explanationHtml: Le-Fort I fracture is not associated with CSF rhinorrhea. It does not involve the cranial base, so CSF rhinorrhea is not expected. In contrast, fractures such as Le Fort II, III, and naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures are associated with CSF rhinorrhea.
question: Which of the following fractures is not associated with CSF rhinorrhea?

correctAnswer: D. Discharge can be sniffed back
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of CSF rhinorrhea secondary to surgery. CSF flows continuously and cannot be sniffed back. This is a key distinguishing feature from normal nasal discharge.

Identifying features of CSF Rhinorrhea:
1. The CSF discharge is thin, watery, and clear in appearance.
2. It cannot be sniffed back.
3. It does not stiffen a handkerchief.
4. It shows positional variation: The watery CSF discharge occurs suddenly and gushes in drops only on bending the head forward/straining.
5. The Halo sign is a marker of CSF rhinorrhea post-head trauma. It is considered positive when a clear ring surrounds a central bloody spot after the discharge is dropped on a handkerchief/paper towel.
6. Reservoir sign: The discharge is seen on rising in the morning and bending the head, as fluid accumulated in the sinuses empties into the nose.

options.text: The reservoir sign is commonly observed
The fluid forms a halo sign when placed on filter paper

question: A middle-aged woman, who had undergone a polypectomy complains of watery nasal discharge on bending forward. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
The presence of β2 transferrin protein in the nasal discharge confirms the presence of CSF in the specimen.

  • It is produced by the choroid plexus and meninges, and is found almost exclusively in CSF, perilymph, and aqueous humor, but is absent in nasal and mucosal secretions, making it an excellent biochemical marker for detecting CSF leaks.
  • CSF glucose is 60% of blood glucose. In contrast, nasal secretions usually have glucose levels <10 mg/dL.
  • False negatives can occur in meningitis, where CSF glucose may be low or absent, or when CSF is mixed with blood, which can interfere with the accuracy of the test.
  • Intrathecal fluorescein study is used to detect the site of leak of CSF.
question: In a patient with suspected CSF rhinorrhea, the presence of which of the following in the nasal discharge will confirm the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Head elevation and activity restriction
explanationHtml:
Patients with CSF rhinorrhea who are stable are managed conservatively.

The conservative measures are:

  • Bed rest
  • Elevation of the head end
  • Stool softeners
  • Avoidance of nose-blowing, sneezing, and straining.

Prophylactic antibiotics can be used to prevent meningitis, and acetazolamide to decrease CSF formation. Surgery is done if the conservative management fails or only if the leak persists or is severe.
question: What is the preferred line of management in a patient with CSF rhinorrhea who is otherwise stable?

explanationHtml:
Inverted papilloma most commonly occurs in middle-aged men (typically between 40–70 years).

Note: Inverted papilloma is characterized by inward growth into the underlying stroma — hence the name "inverted."

Presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis

question: Which of the following statements about inverted papilloma is false?

correctAnswer: B. Postoperative radiotherapy is usually given
explanationHtml:
Radiotherapy is not advised in inverted papilloma since it may induce malignancy.

Other options:

Option A: The Endoscopic approach is preferred over surgical resection.

Option C: There is a high rate of recurrence of inverted papillomas.

Option D: MRI is the first imaging modality to perform during follow-up.

question: A 46-year-old man presented with left-sided nasal blockage and discharge for 3 years. On anterior rhinoscopy, a pale, red polypoidal mass is seen in the left nostril. explanationHtml: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the nasal cavity, seen in about 80% of cases. It is also referred to as nose-pickers’ cancer.
question: Which of the following is the most common malignant tumor of the nasal cavity?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of esthesioneuroblastoma. It arises from the olfactory epithelium of the upper third of the nose.

Note:

It is a vascular tumor, and biopsy should not be attempted immediately unless imaging studies have been performed.
question: A 15-year-old presented with a cherry red, polypoidal mass detected on anterior rhinoscopy. Biopsy of the mass suggested that it originated from the olfactory neural epithelium. Which of the following is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Osteomas are most commonly seen in the frontal sinus, followed by the ethmoid and maxillary sinuses.

They remain asymptomatic and are incidentally found on X-rays. Treatment is required only when they cause obstructive symptoms or pressure effects.

The image shown is an X-ray of an osteoma in the frontal sinus.

question: Which of the following is the most common site for osteomas?

explanationHtml:
The maxilla is the most common site for fibrous dysplasia.

Fibrous dysplasias and ossifying fibromas are both skeletal lesions where normal architecture is replaced by vascularized fibrous tissue.

However, the difference between the two is as follows -

Fibrous dysplasia Ossifying fibroma
Site More common in the maxilla. More common in the mandible
Radiology No well-defined edge, lesion merges with surroundings Well-demarcated lesion
Pathology Strongly reactive for osteocalcin Weakly reactive for osteocalcin
question: The most common site of occurrence of fibrous dysplasia is

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis is fibrous dysplasia. A ground-glass appearance in CT or X-ray is characteristic of fibrous dysplasia.

It can present with disfigurement of the face, nasal obstruction, and displacement of the eye.

The X-ray image below shows a ground-glass appearance present in the left maxillary sinus due to fibrous dysplasia. The lesion is not well demarcated and merges with the surrounding area. There is orbital displacement on the left side.
