question: A patient is referred to the ENT OPD with left-sided nasal obstruction, disfigurement of the face, and displacement of his left eye. Imaging of paranasal sinuses shows an ill-defined expanding lesion with ground glass appearance in the maxillary sinus. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histologic type of paranasal sinus carcinoma.It occurs most frequently in the maxillary sinus, followed by the ethmoid, frontal, and sphenoid sinuses.
question:
A 60-year-old man presents with left-sided facial swelling, nasal obstruction, and intermittent blood-tinged nasal discharge. CT scan reveals an expansile mass involving the left maxillary sinus with erosion of the posterior wall. Biopsy confirms malignancy.
Which of the following is the most likely histological diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Adenocarcinoma is the most likely tumor type in patients with occupational exposure to wood dust, such as furniture industry workers and carpenters.

It is most commonly found in the ethmoid sinuses and upper nasal cavity.

Workers engaged in nickel refining may develop squamous cell carcinoma and anaplastic carcinoma.

Note: While squamous cell carcinoma is the most common overall type of paranasal sinus carcinoma, Adenocarcinoma is specifically associated with occupational wood dust exposure.
question: A carpenter was diagnosed with sinonasal carcinoma and planned for surgical resection. which of the following tumor types is most likely?

explanationHtml:
Blood-tinged nasal discharge is an early feature of maxillary carcinoma.

Other early features include:

  • Nasal stuffiness
  • Facial paraesthesias
  • Pain
  • Epiphora

These symptoms may be missed or simply treated as sinusitis.

Other options:

Option B: Lymphatic spread occurs in the late stages of the disease. Among the cervical lymph nodes, the submandibular and upper jugular lymph nodes are enlarged.

Option C: Proptosis is a late feature that occurs after the invasion of the orbit.

Option D: Dental pain is a late feature that occurs due to the expansion of the alveolus after the tumor spreads inferiorly.
question: Which of the following is an early feature of maxillary carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Ohngren’s classification is used for maxillary carcinoma.

The image below illustrates Ohngren’s line: An imaginary plane is drawn, extending between the medial canthus of the eye and the angle of the mandible.

[[figure-1]]

Growths situated above this plane (suprastructural) have a poorer prognosis than those below it (infrastructural).
question: Which of the following conditions is classified using Ohngren’s classification?

explanationHtml:
Ledermann’s classification is used to classify maxillary carcinoma in this case.

It uses two horizontal lines of Sebileau; one passes through the floors of the orbits and the other through the floors of the antra, dividing the area into:

  • Suprastructure: Ethmoid, sphenoid, and frontal sinuses and the olfactory area of the nose.
  • Mesostructure: Maxillary sinus and the respiratory part of the nose.
  • Infrastructure: Alveolar process.

Note: The suprastructure and infrastructure of Lederman’s classification are not the same as in Ohngren’s classification.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 43-year-old factory worker presents to you with nasal obstruction, cheek swelling, and diplopia. The ENT resident suspects maxillary carcinoma and uses the following image to classify the same. Which one of the following classification systems are used?

explanationHtml:
Radiotherapy is preferred here, as in this case, surgery has already been performed. The tumor staging is T4 by the AJCC classification.

T3 and T4 lesions are treated by combined modalities of radiation and surgery. Radiation in such cases may be given preoperatively or postoperatively.

T1 and T2 lesions without nodal or distant metastasis are treated with surgery or radiation with equal results.

Stage Description
T1 Tumour restricted to the maxillary sinus mucosa
T2 Bony erosion - extension into the hard palate or the middle meatus, except the posterior wall and the pterygoid plates
T3 Invasion into suprastructures such as:
  • Posterior wall of the maxillary sinus
  • Subcutaneous tissues
  • Floor or medial wall of the orbit
  • Pterygoid fossa
  • Ethmoid sinus
T4a Tumour invades any of the following:
  • Anterior orbital contents
  • The skin of the nose or cheek
  • Infratemporal fossa
  • Pterygoid plates
  • Cribriform plate
  • Sphenoid or frontal sinuses
T4b Tumour invades any of the following:
  • Orbital apex
  • Brain/dura
  • Middle cranial fossa
  • Nasopharynx
question: In a known case of maxillary carcinoma, histopathology of the surgically resected region shows that the tumor has eroded into the floor and medial wall of the orbit and the frontal sinus. Which of the following is the best management strategy?

explanationHtml:
Nasal infections are the most common cause of sinusitis since the sinus mucosa is a continuation of the nasal mucosa, and infections from the nose can travel directly by continuity or by way of submucosal lymphatics.


The most common cause of acute sinusitis is viral rhinitis, followed by bacterial invasion.

Other causes:

  • Dental infections cause maxillary sinus infections.
  • Trauma
  • Swimming and diving.
question: Which of the following is the most common cause of sinusitis?

explanationHtml:
The structure marked 4 is the maxillary sinus and is the most common sinus involved in acute sinusitis in adults.

The order of frequency of sinuses involved in acute sinusitis in adults is maxillary > ethmoid > frontal > sphenoid.

[[figure-1]]
question: Identify the most common sinus involved in sinusitis in adults.

explanationHtml:
Diplopia is least likely to be seen in sinusitis.

Patients with sinusitis typically present with a dull throbbing headache which worsens on moving the head or bending forward, nasal discharge and blockage, & constitutional symptoms like fever, general malaise, and bodyache.

Other options:

Option A: Occipital headache can be seen in sphenoid sinusitis.

Option B: Eyelid edema can be seen in frontal and ethmoidal sinusitis.

Option D: Post-nasal drip and nasal discharge are common clinical features of sinusitis.
question: A patient with sinusitis is least likely to present with which of the following symptoms?

explanationHtml: Headache in frontal sinusitis shows characteristic periodicity, i.e. comes upon waking, gradually increases, reaches its peak by about midday, and then starts subsiding. It is also called office headache because of its presence only during office hours.
question: A 28-year-old IT professional with a recent history of upper respiratory tract infection has a headache that worsens during office hours. The headache comes upon waking, tends to be at its worst by about midday and improves as the day progresses. This characteristic periodicity is seen in?

explanationHtml:
The ethmoid sinus is the most common sinus involved in pediatric sinusitis.

Infections frequently spread through the lamina papyracea, a thin bony wall separating the ethmoid sinus from the orbit, increasing the risk of orbital complications such as orbital cellulitis or subperiosteal abscess.
question: Which of the following is the most common sinusitis in children?

explanationHtml:
Headache in sphenoid sinusitis is localized to the occiput or vertex. Pain may also be referred to the mastoid region.

Note: Frontal headache is commonly associated with maxillary and frontal sinusitis. Headaches related to frontal sinusitis exhibit a characteristic periodicity.
question: A 12-year-old child diagnosed with sphenoid sinusitis was brought to the hospital with complaints of a fever and headache. The headache would most likely be localised to?

explanationHtml:
The clinical history strongly suggests chronic maxillary sinusitis. Mucoid or mucopurulent discharge in the middle meatus seen on anterior rhinoscopy is a pathognomonic finding in chronic maxillary sinusitis. This is because the middle meatus is the drainage pathway for the maxillary sinus.

Other findings may include mucosal edema, particularly in the middle meatus, and the presence of nasal polyps.

Clinically, patients present with nasal blockage, congestion, postnasal drip, reduced olfaction, and facial pain or pressure.

CT imaging often reveals mucosal changes within the osteomeatal complex and affected sinuses, which are characteristic of chronic rhinosinusitis.
question: A middle-aged man with a history of recurrent episodes of sinusitis for two years presented with complaints of a dull aching pain over his cheek, persistent nasal obstruction which worsens at night and an urge to constantly clear his throat. Which of the following anterior rhinoscopy findings is pathognomonic of the condition?

explanationHtml:
The lateral view shows all the paranasal sinuses in a single film.

The lateral side of the skull lies against the film, and an X-ray beam is projected perpendicular to the other side.

Structures seen are:

  • Anterior and posterior extent of the sphenoid, frontal sinus
  • Maxillary sinuses
  • Ethmoid sinuses
  • Sella turcica
  • Alveolar process
  • Condyle and neck of the mandible.

Note: Though all the abnormalities and diagnoses of paranasal sinuses cannot be concluded through the lateral view alone, the lateral view radiographically covers all the sinuses in the same view.

  • The maxillary sinus is best visualized on the Waters’ (occipitomental) view.
  • The frontal sinus is best seen on the Caldwell’s (occipitofrontal) view.
  • The sphenoid sinus is best visualized on the submentovertical (SMV) view.
  • The ethmoid sinuses are best seen on the Caldwell’s(especially anterior cells) and SMV view (for posterior cells)

[[figure-1]]
question: A 21-year-old female patient presented with fever, headache and, hawking sensation. Suspecting severe sinusitis, you order an X-ray of the PNS. Which view would be best in capturing all the paranasal sinuses in a single film?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of frontal sinusitis. The best view for evaluating the frontal sinus is Caldwell's view.

It is also known as the occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position.

Structures seen are:

  • Frontal sinuses
  • Ethmoid sinuses
  • Maxillary sinuses
  • Frontal process of the zygoma and the zygomatic process of the frontal bone
  • Superior margin of orbit and lamina papyracea
  • Superior orbital fissure
  • Foramen rotundum (inferolateral to superior orbital fissure)

Note: CT scan is the preferred modality these days.

[[figure-1]]
question: A patient with deviated nasal septum presents with a headache that starts upon waking and reaches its peak by about midday. On examination, she has upper eyelid oedema and tenderness on pressing just above the medial canthus. Which of the following X-ray views is preferred to best evaluate the sinus involved?

explanationHtml:
Diagnostic nasal endoscopy findings are used to confirm the diagnosis of sinusitis.

Indications of diagnostic nasal endoscopy:

  • To diagnose any disease of the nose and the PNS
  • To find the source of bleeding in epistaxis
  • To assess the response to medical or surgical treatment of the nose and PNS disease
  • To take a precise biopsy from the nose and nasopharynx

Other options :

  • Option A: X-ray PNS may show sinus opacity, air-fluid levels, or mucosal thickening, but is less sensitive and specific.
  • Option C: Proof puncture (antral lavage) is rarely used today and is considered invasive and outdated as a diagnostic tool.
  • Option D: The transillumination test is non-specific and unreliable, especially in the presence of thick facial tissues or anatomical variation.
question: A 28-year-old patient presents with nasal congestion, facial pain, and postnasal drip persisting for over 4 weeks despite medical therapy. An X-ray PNS shows mucosal thickening in the maxillary sinus. Which of the following is the most useful next step to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Soft palate paralysis is not a known complication of sinusitis.

Complications of paranasal sinus infection:

  • Local
    • Mucocele/Mucopyocele
    • Mucous retention cyst
    • Osteomyelitis - Frontal bone (more common), maxilla
  • Orbital
    • Preseptal inflammatory oedema of the lids
    • Subperiosteal abscess
    • Orbital cellulitis
    • Orbital abscess
    • Superior orbital fissure syndrome
    • Orbital apex syndrome
  • Intracranial
    • Meningitis
    • Extradural abscess
    • Subdural abscess
    • Brain abscess
    • Cavernous sinus thrombosis
  • Descending infections
  • Focal infections
question: Which of the following complications would you not expect to see in a patient diagnosed with sinusitis?

explanationHtml:
Orbital cellulitis is the most common complication following acute rhinosinusitis. Ethmoid sinusitis is most commonly implicated due to its anatomical proximity and the thin lamina papyracea, which allows for the easy spread of infection.

Complications of acute rhinosinusitis are typically classified as orbital (60–75 percent), intracranial (15–20 percent), and osseous (5–10 percent), as well as local and descending infections.
question: Which of the following is the most common complication following acute rhinosinusitis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical history and findings are suggestive of a mucocele secondary to frontal sinusitis. The frontal sinus is most commonly involved in mucocele formation. It presents as a cystic and nontender swelling in the superomedial quadrant of the orbit (≈90% of cases). Expansion of the mucocoele may produce ophthalmological symptoms such as periorbital swelling, headache, pain and exophthalmos. It also leads to displacement of the eyeball forward (proptosis), downward, and laterally, further resulting in visual disturbances, diplopia, limited ocular mobility and, rarely, optic neuropathy.

  • Radiological findings: clouding of the frontal sinus and loss of the scalloped outline that is normally seen in healthy frontal sinuses.
  • Treatment is frontoethmoidectomy with free drainage of the frontal sinus into the middle meatus.

Note: The sinuses commonly affected by mucocele in order of frequency are the frontal>ethmoidal>maxillary>sphenoid

The image given below shows a coronal MRI demonstrating a frontal mucocele and an orbital cystic mass.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 60-year-old lady presents with pain and swelling around the left upper eyelid region, diplopia and a headache. She gives a history of recurrent episodes of rhinosinusitis in the past. On examination, there is a downward, and outward deviation of the eyeball & the most prominent part of the swelling has a punctum with a mucopurulent discharge, just above the upper eyelid. Which of the following sinuses is most commonly involved in this complication?

correctAnswer: C. Maxillary division of trigeminal nerve
explanationHtml:
The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve does not pass through the superior orbital fissure and thus is the least likely nerve to be involved in this condition.

Superior orbital fissure syndrome is characterized by the compression of cranial nerves III, IV, VI, and the ophthalmic division of V.

The superior orbital fissure lies between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid. The structures passing through include cranial nerves III, IV, VI, the ophthalmic branch of V, and the superior ophthalmic vein.

[[figure-1]]

Note: Orbital apex syndrome is superior orbital fissure syndrome with additional involvement of the optic nerve and the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve.
question: A young man was referred to the maxillofacial surgeon with complaints of pain and tenderness over the left cheek, inability to move the left eye, and numbness over the left forehead. He gave a history of chronic sinusitis for two years. Superior orbital fissure syndrome was suspected. Which of the following nerves is least likely to be involved in this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Pott’s puffy tumor is related to osteomyelitis of maxilla
explanationHtml:
Pott's puffy tumor refers to osteomyelitis of the frontal bone with the development of a subperiosteal abscess, manifesting as a puffy swelling on the forehead or scalp.

  • It usually occurs as a complication of frontal sinusitis. It can also happen after an injury or surgery to the frontal sinus, especially if there is an infection.
  • Pus may collect under the skin, causing a soft, swollen lump called Pott’s puffy tumor, or it may form inside the skull as an extradural abscess.

Other options:

Option A: Osteomyelitis of the maxilla is more often seen in infants and children than in adults because of the presence of spongy bone in the anterior wall of the maxilla.

Option B: Osteomyelitis of the frontal bone is more often seen in adults as the frontal sinus is not developed in infants and children.

Option C: Ethmoidal sinusitis spreads through the lamina papyracea,a thin bone separating the ethmoid sinus from the orbit.

options.text: Osteomyelitis of maxilla is more common in children
Osteomyelitis of frontal bone is more common in adults
Ethmoidal sinusitis spreads through lamina papyracea
Pott’s puffy tumor is related to osteomyelitis of maxilla

question: Which of the following statements is not true?

explanationHtml: The given clinical vignette is suggestive of orbital complications secondary to sinusitis. The orbit and its contents are closely related to the ethmoid, frontal, and maxillary sinuses, but most of the complications, however, follow infection of ethmoids as they are separated from the orbit only by a thin lamina of bone called the lamina papyracea.
question: A middle-aged patient with a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections presents with diplopia and protrusion of the left eyeball. Inflammation of which of the following paranasal sinuses would most likely lead to this complication?

explanationHtml:
The procedure referred to is antral lavage or proof puncture, which involves puncturing the medial wall of the maxillary sinus in the region of the inferior meatus to allow for irrigation and drainage of the sinus. It is called proof puncture, as the presence of an infection can be proven during the procedure.

Indications: Antral lavage is usually done therapeutically to remove pus and diagnostically for confirmation of chronic maxillary sinusitis. It can also be done to collect the specimen of the antral contents for culture and sensitivity, or cytological examination to exclude early malignancy.

Contraindications: In acute maxillary sinusitis, antral lavage is contraindicated due to the risk of osteomyelitis

question: Which of the following conditions is not an indication for functional endoscopic sinus surgery?

correctAnswer: C. Acute rhinosinusitis with epidural abscess
explanationHtml:
Acute rhinosinusitis with an epidural abscess is a contraindication for functional endoscopic sinus surgery.

It involves intracranial complications requiring neurosurgical intervention. FESS alone is not adequate and may pose serious risks.

The endoscopic approach is contraindicated in the presence of an intracranial complication of acute infection, such as:

  • Meningitis
  • Subperiosteal abscess
  • Epidural abscess
  • Cavernous sinus thrombosis
  • Any visual loss

Note: FESS can access the pituitary gland, optic nerve, and lacrimal sac. However, it cannot reach posterior brain structures like the cerebellum, highlighting why intracranial abscesses may require alternate surgical approaches.

question: A 45-year-old-man with a history of chronic sinusitis unresponsive to medications is planned for functional endoscopic sinus surgery. Which of the following is the first step in the procedure?

explanationHtml:
During functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) for chronic maxillary sinusitis, the medial wall of the infundibulum is punctured near the maxillary sinus ostium to gain access to the middle meatus.

The middle meatus is the anatomical space beneath the middle turbinate where the natural openings of the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain.

Purpose: Opening the medial wall of the infundibulum creates a pathway into the middle meatus, allowing drainage and ventilation of the maxillary sinus, which is essential for resolving chronic infection and inflammation.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma originating from the site is hard to detect unless carefully inspected during endoscopy, as it also spreads submucosally and infiltrates the palatal muscles and obstructs the Eustachian tube.

The descending pharyngeal artery does not pass through the sinus of Morgagni and is hence least likely to be affected. All the other options are contents of the sinus of Morgagni.

The sinus of Morgagni is a space between the base of the skull and the upper free border of the superior constrictor muscle.

The structures passing through the space are:

  • Eustachian tube
  • Levator veli palatini
  • Tensor veli palatini
  • Ascending palatine artery - a branch of the facial artery

Trotter's triad or sinus of Morgagni syndrome is seen in nasopharyngeal carcinoma which spreads laterally to involve the sinus of Morgagni. It is characterized by:

  • Ipsilateral immobility of the palate

Pyriform sinus lies on either side of the larynx and extends from the pharyngoepiglottic fold to the upper end of the esophagus. It forms the lateral channel for food. The rich lymphatic network of pyriform fossa explains the high frequency of nodal metastasis seen in carcinoma of this region.

The given x-ray shows enlarged adenoids and suggests the diagnosis of adenoid hypertrophy. Patients show an absent nasolabial fold, which occurs due to nasal obstruction, causing disuse atrophy of the nose.

The following includes the features of adenoid facies, which occur due to chronic nasal obstruction and mouth breathing:

  • Elongated face with a dull expression
  • Open mouth
  • High-arched palate
  • crowding of teeth anteriorly
  • Absent nasolabial crease
  • Pinched nose
  • Absent alar prominence

Other clinical features include:

  • Nasal obstruction is the most common symptom that leads to mouth breathing. Nasal obstruction also interferes with feeding or suckling in a child. As respiration and feeding cannot take place simultaneously, a child with adenoid enlargement fails to thrive.
  • Nasal discharge, sinusitis, and epistaxis.
  • Bilateral conductive hearing loss and serous otitis media due to eustachian tube obstruction.
  • Rhinolalia clausa - hyponasal voice.
  • Sleep apnoea - chronic cases lead to hypoxemia and pulmonary vasoconstriction. This consequently leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
  • Aprosexia - lack of concentration.

It is also seen in other conditions such as:

  • Common cold
  • Nasal allergy
  • Nasal polyp
  • Nasal growth

Option A - Hot potato voice is a muffled and thick speech which is often seen in a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy).

Option C - Rhinolalia aperta causes a hypernasal voice, which is seen in conditions such as velopharyngeal insufficiency, congenital short soft palate, submucous palate, large nasopharynx, Cleft or paralysis of soft palate, Oronasal fistula, and postadenoidectomy.

question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to you by her mother with complaints of mouth breathing. She has a flat, expressionless long face with an open mouth. On examination, a high arched palate and crowded upper teeth are noted. What is the voice abnormality that can be noted in this child?

explanationHtml:
Beta-2 agonists have no role in conditions of upper airway obstruction like adenoid hypertrophy. They are bronchodilators used in lower airway obstructive diseases.

When symptoms of adenoid hypertrophy are not marked, breathing exercises, decongestant nasal drops, and antihistamines for any coexisting nasal allergy can cure the condition without resorting to surgery.

Marked adenoid hypertrophy with associated complications can be treated with adenoidectomy and grommet insertion. The question doesn't ask for immediate management, hence adenoidectomy can be done once the acute infection is resolved.
question: A 5-year-old child is brought by his mother to the ENT OPD with frequent upper respiratory tract infections. His mother gives a history of loud snoring at night and posterior rhinoscopy examination shows enlarged adenoids. Which of the following will you not advise in the management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Multiple adenoids are not an indication for adenoidectomy.

Indications of adenoidectomy:

  • Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnoea syndrome, or speech abnormalities, i.e., rhinolalia clausa
  • Recurrent rhinosinusitis
  • Chronic otitis media with effusion associated with adenoid hyperplasia
  • Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis/adenoid hyperplasia
  • Dental malocclusion. Adenoidectomy does not correct dental abnormalities but will prevent its recurrence after orthodontic treatment.

Contraindications include:

  • Cleft palate or submucous palate, removal could lead to velopharyngeal insufficiency
  • Bleeding diathesis
  • Acute infections

question: Which of the following is not an indication for an adenoidectomy procedure?

explanationHtml:
Cleft palate is a contraindication to perform adenoidectomy as removal of adenoids causes velopharyngeal insufficiency.

Velopharyngeal insufficiency is a condition where the soft palate does not close tightly against the back of the throat. This leads to air coming out of the nose (characterized by hypernasality) during speech.

Contraindications for adenoidectomy:

  • Cleft palate or submucous palate.
  • Hemorrhagic diathesis.
  • Acute infection of the upper respiratory tract.

Indications of adenoidectomy:

  • Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnoea syndrome, or speech abnormalities, i.e., rhinolalia clausa
  • Recurrent rhinosinusitis
  • Chronic otitis media with effusion associated with adenoid hyperplasia
  • Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis/adenoid hyperplasia
  • Dental malocclusion. Adenoidectomy does not correct dental abnormalities but will prevent its recurrence after orthodontic treatment.
question: A 6-year-old child has been posted for an adenoidectomy procedure. Which of the following conditions if present in this child will be a contraindication to performing the surgery?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of adenoid hypertrophy. The best line of management is adenoidectomy with grommet insertion.

The adenoid hypertrophy can cause chronic eustachian tube dysfunction, which is responsible for the impaired hearing in the clinical picture. To treat it, adenoidectomy with grommet insertion is done to restore the eustachian tube function until recovery. The grommet helps provide continued aeration of the middle ear and is used in cases where fluid collection recurs.

Indications of adenoidectomy:

  • Adenoid hypertrophy causing snoring, mouth breathing, sleep apnoea syndrome, or speech abnormalities, i.e., rhinolalia clausa
  • Recurrent rhinosinusitis
  • Chronic otitis media with effusion associated with adenoid hyperplasia
  • Recurrent ear discharge in benign CSOM associated with adenoiditis/adenoid hyperplasia
  • Dental malocclusion. Adenoidectomy does not correct dental abnormalities but will prevent its recurrence after orthodontic treatment.

question: A school-going child presents with a history of recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, mouth breathing, and impaired hearing. On examination, a high arched palate is noted. What is the management of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Grisel's syndrome is a postoperative complication of adenoidectomy which involves paraspinal muscle spasm.

Grisel syndrome refers to non-traumatic atlantoaxial joint subluxation, which is a rare risk associated with adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy. The patient complains of neck pain and develops torticollis. Early recognition is crucial and might require a cervical collar. It can be avoided by ensuring minimum power settings and preventing overuse of diathermy with special care for the child's neck during surgery and recovery.

Pathophysiology of Grisel's Syndrome:

  • Post-surgical inflammatory edema leading to paraspinal muscle spasm, which leads to non-traumatic atlantoaxial subluxation

Management of Grisel's Syndrome:

  • Anti-inflammatory drugs to reduce the edema and spasm
  • Immobilization of the neck
  • Neurosurgical intervention, if required

Other complications of adenoidectomy include:

  • Hemorrhage; coroner's clot, leading to fatal laryngeal aspiration
  • Injury to the Eustachian tube opening
  • Injury to the pharyngeal muscles and vertebrae
  • Unmasking of velopharyngeal insufficiency
  • Nasopharyngeal stenosis
  • Recurrence due to the regrowth of adenoid tissue.

Thornwaldt's cyst is located in the midline of the posterior wall of the Nasopharynx.

Thornwaldt's Bursa is an epithelial-lined median recess found within the adenoid mass and extends from the pharyngeal mucosa to the periosteum of the basiocciput in the midline. It is a remnant of the embryonic communication between the primitive pharynx and notochord.

When infected repeatedly, it may present with occipital headache, persistent postnasal discharge, and might lead to the formation of Thornwaldt's cyst. Diagnosis can be confirmed with endoscopy; CT and MRI can be done to screen for adhesions to the cervical vertebrae. Treatment can be conservative with antibiotics or excision in severe cases, and marsupialization of the cyst if surgery is not recommended.

question: Where is Thornwaldt cyst located?

explanationHtml:
Incision & drainage is not used in the treatment of Thornwaldt’s abscess.

Thornwaldt’s abscess is formed due to the infection of Thornwaldt's cyst. Treatment includes administration of antibiotics to treat the infection, excision in severe cases, and marsupialization of the cyst, where the edges of the cyst are everted to drain the secretions persistently if surgery is not recommended, with adequate removal of its lining membrane.

explanationHtml:
The medial surface of the tonsil is covered by non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium.

Tonsils are ovoid masses of lymphoid tissue situated in the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the anterior and posterior pillars.

The medial surface of the tonsil is covered in 12-15 crypts. Crypta magna or intra-tonsillar cleft is the largest & deepest of the crypts. It is situated near the upper part of the tonsil and represents the ventral part of the second pharyngeal pouch.

The lateral surface of the tonsil presents a well-defined fibrous capsule.

The bed of the tonsils is formed by the structures that are lateral to the tonsils and on which the tonsils rest. It is formed by:

  • Loose areolar tissue
  • External palatine vein (paratonsillar vein)
  • Palatopharyngeus
  • Superior constrictor
  • Buccopharyngeal fascia
  • Styloglossus
  • Glossopharyngeal nerve

options.text: Bed of the tonsil is formed by the superior constrictor and styloglossus muscles.

Crypta magna is a remnant of the ventral part of second pharyngeal pouch.
A capsule covers the lateral surface of the tonsils.

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about tonsils?

The growth of tonsils is rapid around the age of 5-6 years of age and usually reaches their maximum size by 12 years of age.

Tonsillar involution begins at puberty when the reactive lymphoid tissue begins to atrophy, and by old age, only a little tonsillar lymphoid tissue remains.

  2. Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery
  3. Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery

The bed of the tonsil is formed by the superior constrictor and styloglossus muscles.

question: You are the second-year ENT resident performing tonsillectomy in a patient with chronic tonsillitis. question: A 7-year-old child was brought to the hospital by his mother with complaints of a sore throat, earache, and pain on swallowing for three days. On examination, the tonsils were enlarged and hyperaemic. Which of the following is the most common organism implicated in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The image shows purulent inflammation of the tonsils suggestive of acute tonsillitis. Jugulo-digastric (tonsillar) lymph nodes will primarily enlarge in this condition.

The lymphatics from the palatine tonsils pierce the superior constrictor muscle and primarily drain into the upper deep cervical nodes (level II), particularly the jugulo-digastric (tonsillar) node situated below the angle of the mandible. So, it is the most likely group of lymph nodes to enlarge in case of acute tonsillitis.
question: A young lady presents to the ENT OPD with the finding shown below. Which of the following group of lymph nodes will primarily enlarge in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical vignette is suggestive of acute tonsillitis. Excessive bleeding is not a known complication of this condition.

Complications of acute tonsillitis:

  • Chronic tonsillitis - chronic infection may persist in lymphoid follicles of the tonsil in the form of microabscesses
  • Peritonsillar abscess
  • Parapharyngeal abscess
  • Cervical abscess due to suppuration of jugulodigastric lymph nodes
  • Acute otitis media
  • Rheumatic fever - often seen in association with tonsillitis due to group A β-hemolytic streptococci
  • Acute glomerulonephritis
  • Subacute bacterial endocarditis - acute tonsillitis in a patient with valvular heart disease may be complicated by endocarditis. It is usually due to Streptococcus viridans infection
question: An anxious mother brought her 4-year-old-child to the hospital with complaints of sudden onset fever and refusal to eat. On examination, the given finding was noted and he was started on analgesics and antibiotics. Which among the following is not a known complication of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis.

The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal nerve and the styloid process lie in relation to the lower part of the tonsillar fossa. Therefore, any irritation or pain can be referred to the ear along the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal (Jacobson's) nerve.

Causes of referred otalgia via the glossopharyngeal nerve include acute pharyngitis, tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, post-tonsillectomy, foreign bodies embedded in the base of the tongue or tonsillar area, and an elongated styloid process (Eagle's syndrome).

The ear receives extensive sensory innervation via four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) and two spinal segments (C2 and C3).

The image below shows a pictorial representation of referred otalgia with the nerves involved:

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following nerves is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical presentation is suggestive of obstructive sleep apnea syndrome(OSAS) secondary to chronic parenchymatous tonsillitis.

In parenchymatous tonsillitis, the tonsils grow very large following repeated attacks of acute tonsillitis and lead to obstructive symptoms, including OSAS.

Types of chronic tonsillitis:

  • Chronic follicular tonsillitis- tonsillar crypts are full of infected cheesy material, which shows on the surface as yellowish spots.
  • Chronic parenchymatous tonsillitis- there is hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue. Tonsils are very much enlarged and may interfere with speech, deglutition, and respiration. Attacks of sleep apnoea may occur. Long-standing cases develop features of cor pulmonale.
  • Chronic fibroid tonsillitis- tonsils are tiny but infected, with a history of repeated sore throats.

The following image shows chronic parenchymatous tonsillitis:

[[figure-1]]

Note: Acute tonsillitis can be classified as:

  • Acute catarrhal or superficial tonsillitis.
  • Acute follicular tonsillitis.
  • Acute parenchymatous tonsillitis.
  • Acute membranous tonsillitis.
question: A 15-year-old girl presented to the ENT surgeon with a history of loud snoring, restless sleep leading to daytime somnolence, and poor academic performance. Her medical history was unremarkable, except for recurrent episodes of acute tonsillitis. Which of the following types of tonsillitis may be implicated in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Müller's sign is the pulsation of uvula during systole seen in aortic regurgitation. It is not seen in patients with chronic tonsillitis.

The classical signs of chronic tonsillitis are:

  • Irwin-Moore sign- tonsils are tiny, but pressure on the anterior pillar expresses frank pus or cheesy material.
  • Enlargement of jugulo-digastric lymph nodes even in the absence of acute infection is a reliable sign of chronic tonsillitis. During acute attacks, the nodes enlarge further and become tender.
  • Congestion of anterior pillars compared to the rest of the pharyngeal mucosa is a vital sign of chronic tonsillar infection.
question: You are an intern posted in the ENT department working up a case of chronic follicular tonsillitis. Which of the following clinical signs would you not expect to see in this patient on examination?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a tonsillar cyst. It is a condition due to the blockage of a tonsillar crypt and appears as a yellowish swelling over the tonsil. Very often, it is asymptomatic and can be easily drained.

Other options:

Option A: Intratonsillar abscess is an accumulation of pus within the substance of the tonsil. It usually follows a blockage of the opening of the crypt in acute follicular tonsillitis. There is marked local pain and dysphagia. The tonsil appears swollen and red.

Option B: Tonsilloliths (calculus of the tonsil) are seen in chronic tonsillitis when its crypt is blocked with retention of debris. Inorganic salts of calcium and magnesium are then deposited, leading to the formation of a stone. It may gradually enlarge and then ulcerate through the tonsil. It generally causes local discomfort or a foreign body sensation.

Option D: Follicular tonsillitis presents with purulent material at the opening of the crypts as yellow dots. It presents with fever, dysphagia, and soreness of the throat.
question: A 25-year-old man presented to the OPD with a complaint of persistent soreness of the throat. There is no history of recurrent tonsillitis. On examination, a smooth yellowish swelling is noted on the right tonsil. The lesion is non-tender, non-erythematous, and does not discharge on applying pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Ludwig’s angina is not associated with the formation of a grey-white membrane over the tonsils. It is a rapidly progressing cellulitis of the floor of the mouth involving all three primary mandibular spaces bilaterally, which are the sublingual, submandibular, and submental spaces.

Differential diagnosis for the membrane over the tonsil:

  • Streptococcus & other pyogenic organisms
  • Diphtheria - dirty-grey pseudomembrane
  • Infectious mononucleosis - membrane over the tonsils with petechiae over the soft palate, swelling over the upper eyelid, also known as the Hoagland sign.
  • Vincent’s angina - dirty grey membrane
  • Leukemia
  • Candidal infection of the tonsils - creamy white membrane-like coating
  • Agranulocytosis
  • Malignancy
  • Aphthous ulcer
  • Traumatic ulcer

The clinical image below shows a patient with Ludwig's Angina:

[[figure-1]]
question: On examining the oral cavity of a patient who presented with fever and a sore throat, you notice a greyish-white membrane over the tonsils. Which of the following conditions would you not consider as a differential diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Vincent’s angina, also known as acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis or trench mouth, is caused by fusiform bacilli and spirochaetes, namely Bacillus fusiformis and Borrelia vincenti.

The condition presents with low-grade fever, sore throat, and a membrane over the tonsil. The membrane is easily removed to reveal irregular ulcers over the tonsil. A throat swab will show both the organisms typical of the disease.

The condition can be seen in the following image:

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following organisms is implicated in Vincent’s angina?

correctAnswer: B. Firmly adherent and bleeds on removal
explanationHtml:
The given clinical history with immunisation history and bull-neck appearance (image) point to the diagnosis of diphtheria. The diphtheritic membrane is firmly adherent and bleeds on removal.

The bacteria produce exotoxin, which leads to local mucosal destruction.

It forms a greyish-white membrane which spreads to the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall. The membrane in diphtheria extends beyond the tonsils onto the soft palate and could cause airway obstruction in the larynx.

Cervical lymph nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric, become enlarged and tender, sometimes presenting a bull-neck appearance. The patient is ill and toxaemic, but fever seldom rises above 38°C.

The following image shows diphtheria pseudomembrane in a patient:

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Firmly adherent and bleeds on removal

question: A worried mother brought her 6-year-old unimmunized child to the ER with complaints of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. On examination, a pseudomembrane was noted in the oral cavity along with the neck finding as shown in the image. Which of the following statements is true regarding the membrane observed?

explanationHtml:
Hard palate paralysis is not seen in diphtheria. Diphtheria can cause neurological complications that usually appear a few weeks after infection and include paralysis of the soft palate, diaphragm, and ocular muscles.

Other complications include:

  • Myocarditis, cardiac arrhythmias, and acute circulatory failure due to the effects of exotoxin on the heart
  • Airway obstruction due to sloughing off of the pseudomembrane.
question: Which of the following complications would you not expect to see in a patient diagnosed with diphtheria?

correctAnswer: D. Sensitivity to antitoxin should be tested prior to therapy
explanationHtml:
The pseudomembrane on oral examination and bull neck appearance is characteristic of diphtheria. Sensitivity to diphtheria antitoxin is common and should be tested prior to the initiation of therapy.

Treatment is started on clinical suspicion without waiting for the culture report. The aim is to neutralize the free exotoxin still circulating in the blood and to kill the organisms producing this exotoxin.

Antitoxins:

  • Dose- based on the site involved, duration, and severity of the disease
    • If < 48 hours or just confined to tonsils: 20,000–40,000 units
    • If > 48 hours or extensive membrane: 80,000–120,000 units
  • Given by I.v. infusion in saline in about 60 min
  • Sensitivity tested by a conjunctival or intracutaneous test with diluted antitoxin
  • If a hypersensitivity reaction occurs, desensitization should be done

Antibiotics:

  • Benzyl penicillin 600 mg 6 hourly for 7 days or
  • Erythromycin is used in penicillin-sensitive individuals (500 mg 6 hourly orally)

options.text: Treatment is started after the culture comes positive
Treatment is with penicillin or macrolide alone
Sensitivity to antitoxin should be tested prior to therapy

question: A patient with diphtheria presents to the OPD. Which of the following statements is true regarding the treatment of this patient?

correctAnswer: A. A 7-year-old child with acute tonsillitis
explanationHtml:
Acute tonsillitis is a contraindication for tonsillectomy and hence, cannot be posted for surgery.

Acute tonsillitis or any upper respiratory tract infection is a contraindication for tonsillectomy since there is an increased chance of hemorrhage and sepsis.

Other contraindications include:

  • Bleeding diathesis.
  • Cleft palate, as the tonsils support the palate and mask the symptoms of velopharyngeal insufficiency, repair of the cleft initially has to be done before tonsillectomy.
  • During the polio epidemic, the virus could enter the bloodstream and nerves, causing paralytic polio.

Indications for tonsillectomy are:

Absolute -

  • Recurrent episodes of acute tonsillitis – the most common indication

Paradise criteria -

Seven or more episodes in 1 year, or
Five episodes per year for 2 consecutive years, or
Three episodes per year for 3 consecutive years

  • Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) - recurrent episodes in adults and a single episode in children.
  • Chronic tonsillitis.
  • Tonsillitis causing sleep apnea
  • Asymmetrical unilateral enlargement of the tonsil with suspicion of malignancy.

Relative -

  • Carriers of Streptococcus and Diphtheria.
  • To approach structures in the bed of the tonsil for glossopharyngeal neuralgia, or an enlarged styloid process.
  • Tonsillolith.

options.text: A young adult with chronic tonsillitis refractory to treatment
A patient with unilateral enlargement of tonsil with suspected malignancy
A middle-aged man with recurrent quinsy

question: Which of the following cases cannot be posted for tonsillectomy?

explanationHtml:
Bleeding from the surgical site within a period of 24 hours is categorised as a reactionary haemorrhage.

Haemorrhage is the most common complication following tonsillectomy. It can be of the following types:

Hemorrhage Timing Common causes
Primary during the surgery external palatine/paratonsillar vein injury
Reactionary within 1 day of surgery dislocated clot, slipped ligature, high BP
Secondary Usually postop days 5-6 infection


Other complications include:

  • Injury to teeth, tonsillar pillars, uvula, soft palate, and tongue.
  • Aspiration of blood.
  • Facial oedema.
  • Surgical emphysema, atelectasis.
  • Infection leading to pharyngeal abscess or otitis media.
  • Hypertrophy of lingual tonsils.
  • Tonsillar remnants or tags that may get infected.
question: A patient develops bleeding from the surgical site five hours after an elective tonsillectomy. Which among the following would best describe the condition?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows Rose's position, and it is not the suitable position to perform direct laryngoscopy. The barking-dog position is used for direct laryngoscopy.

Rose’s position: The patient lies supine with head extended by placing a pillow under the shoulders. It is followed in procedures such as adenoidectomy, tonsillectomy, and tracheostomy.

[[figure-1]]

Barking-dog position: Patient lies supine. The head is elevated by 10–15 cm by placing a pillow under the occiput or raising the operation table’s head flap. The neck is flexed on the thorax, and the head is extended on the atlanto-occipital joint.

The following image shows the barking-dog position used for direct laryngoscopy:

[[figure-2]]
question: While preparing for a procedure, the patient was kept in a specific position as depicted in the image. In which of the following procedures is this position not adopted?

explanationHtml:
Option A is the space of Gillette, which lies behind the pharynx between the buccopharyngeal fascia covering the pharyngeal constrictor muscles and the prevertebral fascia. It extends from the base of the skull to the bifurcation of the trachea. It houses the lymph node of Rouviere, into which the internal Waldeyer's ring drains.

Other options:

Option B: Danger space, it is the space that lies between the alar fascia anteriorly and the prevertebral fascia posteriorly, and can get infected by the rupture of a retropharyngeal abscess that could lead to the spread of infection into the mediastinum.

Option C: Prevertebral space, it lies between the vertebrae on one side and the prevertebral muscles with the prevertebral fascia on the other, can get infected by tuberculosis of the spine or penetrating trauma, causing an abscess which is diffuse and in the midline.

Option D: Anterior cervical space, it is a small infrahyoid compartment containing fat present above the submandibular space.
question: Which of the following marked structures is the space of Gillette?

explanationHtml:
Rouviere node is the most superior node of the lateral group of retropharyngeal lymph nodes, which can suppurate to form a retropharyngeal abscess. Suppuration of these lymph nodes is the most common cause of retropharyngeal space abscess in children.

Other options:

Option B: Delphian nodes are the pre-laryngeal lymph nodes. It drains the subglottic region of the larynx and the pyriform sinuses, and it can present as a midline swelling of the neck

Option C: Virchow's node is an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node infiltrated with metastatic cancer from a gastrointestinal primary.

Option D: Cloquet’s nodes are the deep inguinal lymph nodes present within the femoral canal.
question: An ENT surgeon is performing an incision and drainage for a retropharyngeal abscess due to suppurative lymphadenitis. Which among the following groups of lymph nodes is most likely to be involved?

correctAnswer: B. Caries of the cervical spine is the most common cause
explanationHtml:
The above clinical condition is suggestive of acute retropharyngeal abscess, whereas caries of the cervical spine results in a chronic retropharyngeal abscess.

Acute retropharyngeal abscess is commonly seen in children below 3 years. It is the result of suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes secondary to infection in the adenoids, nasopharynx, posterior nasal sinuses, or nasal cavity.

In adults, it may result from penetrating injury of the posterior pharyngeal wall or cervical esophagus.

Clinical features of a retropharyngeal abscess include:

  • Dysphagia and difficulty in breathing, as the abscess obstructs the air and food passages.
  • Stridor and croupy cough
  • Torticollis: the neck becomes stiff, and the head is kept extended.
  • A bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall is usually seen on one side of the midline.

Chronic retropharyngeal abscess is the result of:

  • Caries of the cervical spine.
  • Tuberculous infection of retropharyngeal lymph nodes secondary to tuberculosis of deep cervical nodes.

options.text: Suppuration of nodes of Rouvier can cause the above condition
Caries of the cervical spine is the most common cause
In adults similar condition may result from penetrating injury of the cervical esophagus
Torticollis is one of the symptoms

question: A concerned mother brought her toddler to the ER with complaints of noisy breathing and the child refusing to feed. On examination, the child has adenoid facies, and there is a bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall lateral to the midline. Which of the following is a false statement regarding the disease described above?

correctAnswer: B. Between alar fascia and prevertebral fascia
explanationHtml:
The likely route of spread of infection is between the alar fascia anteriorly and the prevertebral fascia posteriorly. It is known as the alar space or danger space.

Lying posterior to the retropharyngeal space, the alar space extends from the base of skull to the diaphragm. Infections from this space can spread to the mediastinum, and hence it is named the danger space.

options.text: Between buccopharyngeal fascia and alar fascia
Between alar fascia and prevertebral fascia
Between the capsule of tonsil and superior constrictor muscle

question: A 42-year-old HIV positive man presents with an acute onset high-grade fever with chills and shortness of breath. On evaluation, he's diagnosed to have a necrotising mediastinitis secondary to rupture of a retropharyngeal abscess. What is the likely route of spread of infection to the mediastinum?

explanationHtml:
The given image is suggestive of a retropharyngeal abscess. It can be diagnosed on a lateral x-ray of the soft tissues of the neck. The features include :

  • Widening of the prevertebral soft tissue shadow
  • Loss of cervical lordosis
  • In an acute abscess, air-fluid levels can be seen.

A contrast-enhanced CT shows the extent of the abscess and if it extends below the hyoid bone or into the mediastinum.
question: Given below is an X-ray of a child who presented with stridor. What is your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of a parapharyngeal abscess. It is synonymous with pharyngomaxillary or lateral pharyngeal abscess.

Parapharyngeal abscess presents with:

  • Trismus due to the spasm of the medial pterygoid
  • Tonsils pushed medially
  • Swelling in the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid (space limited to the level of the hyoid bone).

Other options:

Option A: Retropharyngeal abscess presents as a bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall on one side of the midline.

Option C: Although Ludwig's angina presents with fever and trismus, the infection is seated in the primary spaces around the mandible.

Option D: Peritonsillar abscess doesn’t produce swelling in the upper 1/3rd of the sternocleidomastoid.

The image attached below shows the components of the parapharyngeal space:

[[figure-1]]
question: A middle-aged diabetic man who had undergone a tooth extraction presents with fever and trismus. On examination, his posterior pillar is pushed medially and there is a swelling in the neck at the upper 1/3rd of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Trismus is not a feature of infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space. Trismus is seen in pre-styloid abscess due to the involvement of the medial pterygoid muscle.

The parapharyngeal space is divided into two compartments by the styloid process and its attachments. Clinical features depend on the compartment involved.

In post-styloid abscess, there is a bulge of the pharynx behind the posterior pillar, accompanied by paralysis of cranial nerves IX, X (resulting in vocal cord paralysis), XI, XII, and the sympathetic chain, which can manifest as Horner's syndrome. Torticollis might be present due to the involvement of prevertebral muscles. Swelling in the parotid region may also be present. Notably, trismus, the inability to fully open the mouth, is usually absent in this type of abscess.

The pre-styloid abscess exhibits distinct features, including the prolapse of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa, along with trismus caused by the spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle. Marked odynophagia is also common. Additionally, an external swelling can be observed behind the angle of the jaw.

Diagnosis can be established using a contrast-enhanced CT scan (CECT). If there is suspicion of thrombosis of the internal jugular vein or an aneurysm of the internal carotid artery, magnetic resonance arteriography (MRA) can be useful.

Patients require intravenous antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, carbapenem antibiotics, plus drugs that target anaerobic organisms, such as clindamycin or metronidazole. A parapharyngeal abscess is drained by an external horizontal incision made on the skin a few centimeters below the angle of the mandible.

The image attached below shows the components of both spaces:

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following features will not be manifested in an infection of the post-styloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space?

correctAnswer: B. A 50-year-old diabetic man with fever, neck swelling over upper ⅓ rd of the left sternocleidomastoid and the tonsils on the same side pushed medially
explanationHtml:
An intraoral incision is not sufficient in the case of option B, which is a case of parapharyngeal abscess, as the swelling is in the upper 1/3rd of the neck, and the tonsil of the same side is pushed medially. An external neck incision must always be made to ensure complete drainage of the abscess.

Other options:

Option A: This is a case of quinsy as the child has odynophagia and a hot potato voice. Intraoral incision is given at the site of maximal bulge or the intersection between an imaginary line drawn from the anterior pillar and a horizontal line from the base of the uvula.

Option C: This is a case of retropharyngeal abscess since there is fever and swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall lateral to the midline.

Option D: This is a case of Sublingual abscess involving the sublingual space, which is caused by penetrating injuries of the oral mucosa due to a fishbone or wood splinters.

Indications for Incision and Drainage:

  • Sublingual abscess: Always an intraoral incision.
  • Parapharyngeal abscess: Always an external neck incision.
  • Peritonsillar abscess: Always intraoral.
  • Retropharyngeal abscess:
    • Intraoral - in rose position.
    • External - Dean approach or posterolateral cervicotomy.
  • Ludwig’s angina:
    • Intraoral—if the infection is still localized to the sublingual space.
    • External—if the infection involves the submaxillary space.

options.text: A 21-year-old woman with fever, hot potato voice and bulging of soft palate and anterior pillar above the tonsil on the right side.
A 50-year-old diabetic man with fever, neck swelling over upper ⅓ rd of the left sternocleidomastoid and the tonsils on the same side pushed medially
A 3-year-old child with fever and swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall lateral to the midline
A 50-year-old man with fever due to penetrating injury of oral mucosa by wood splinters

question: In which of the following clinical scenarios will you not perform an intraoral incision?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario describes a child with fever, otalgia, trismus, and odynophagia with a normal external facial examination. The oral cavity shows congested and edematous tonsil and tonsillar pillars with edematous uvula pushed to the opposite side. These findings are highly suggestive of quinsy (peritonsillar abscess).

It is the collection of pus in the peritonsillar space between the fibrous capsule of the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscles of the pharynx. Both aerobic and anaerobic organisms are seen.

Patient presents with fever, unilateral throat pain, odynophagia, hot potato voice, torticollis, foul breath, referred otalgia through glossopharyngeal nerve and trismus due to spasm of pterygoid muscles.

Oral cavity examination may show congested and edematous tonsils, pillars, and soft palate on the involved side. Edematous uvula pushed to the opposite side. Pus may be seen on the tonsillar region. Jugulodigastric lymph nodes may be enlarged.

The management of quinsy is by antibiotics and incision and drainage to drain the abscess followed by interval tonsillectomy 4 to 6 weeks later.

Rare complications seen are parapharyngeal abscess, edema of the larynx, septicemia, lung abscess, or jugular vein thrombosis.

Other options:

Option A: Pharyngitis presents with fever, throat pain, enlarged tonsils, and lymphoid follicles on the posterior pharyngeal wall.

Option B: Parotid abscess occurs due to the suppuration of parotid space. It presents with swelling, redness, firmness, and tenderness in the parotid area and at the angle of the mandible. It is usually unilateral, but bilateral abscesses can occur. Due to the thick capsule, fluctuation is often difficult to elicit.

Option C: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.
question: A 9-year-old boy comes with complaints of right ear pain, difficulty in opening the mouth, painful swallowing, and fever. The oral cavity examination reveals the following. The external facial examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is likely?

explanationHtml:
Peritonsillar abscess or quinsy is usually unilateral.

It is an abscess forming in the space between the tonsilar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle (peritonsillar space).

It presents with the following features:

  • Marked odynophagia - the patient cannot even swallow his saliva which dribbles from the angle of his mouth
  • Muffled and thick speech (hot potato voice)
  • Foul breath - due to sepsis of the oral cavity
  • Referred pain to the ipsilateral ear via CN IX
  • Trismus - because of spasm of the pterygoid muscles which are located close to the superior constrictor

options.text: It does not present with an external bulge
Presents with odynophagia and drooling of saliva

question: Which of the following statements about quinsy is false?

correctAnswer: C. Incision & drainage along with antibiotics
explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of peritonsillar abscess or quinsy, and management involves incision and drainage with antibiotics.

Management of quinsy:

  • Hospitalization
  • Intravenous fluids to combat dehydration
  • Antibiotics - Suitable antibiotics in large IV doses to cover aerobes and anaerobes
  • Analgesics
  • Drainage by needle aspiration or incision and drainage
  • Tonsillectomy is performed when there is airway obstruction or recurrence in adults.

Incision and drainage of the abscess: A peritonsillar abscess is opened at the point of the maximum bulge above the upper pole of the tonsil or just lateral to the point of junction of the anterior pillar with a line drawn through the base of the uvula.
question: A 19-year-old woman presented with complaints of fever, right-sided throat pain, and difficulty in swallowing. On examination, she had hot potato speech and halitosis. The right tonsil was not visualised due to oedematous pillars and the uvula was pushed to the left. How will you manage this patient?

explanationHtml:
In a patient with recurrent peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), ideally, an interval tonsillectomy is done 4-6 weeks after the infection settles down.

Hot tonsillectomy: Earlier, tonsillectomy was done during incision and drainage. But this is not followed now as it is dangerous and can lead to aspiration, bleeding & spread of infection.
question: In a patient with recurrent peritonsillar abscess, when is the ideal time to perform a tonsillectomy?

correctAnswer: D. H.influenza is the most common organism implicated
explanationHtml:
Mixed infection with aerobes and anaerobes is seen in Ludwig’s angina. Among these, alpha-hemolytic streptococci, staphylococci, and the Bacteroides group are common.

Ludwig’s angina is an infection of the three primary spaces of the mandible bilaterally, which includes:

  • Sublingual space,
  • Submandibular space and
  • Submental space.

The most common cause of Ludwig's angina is dental infections (accounts for 80% of cases).

Other causes include submandibular sialadenitis, injury to the oral mucosa, and mandibular fractures.

Note: The secondary spaces of the mandible are collectively called the masticator space, which can be involved due to the posterior spread of infection from the primary spaces.

options.text: It involves both sublingual and submandibular space
Dental infections are the most common cause
H.influenza is the most common organism implicated

question: Which of the following is a false statement about Ludwig’s angina?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of a parotid abscess and excessive gland stimulation is not a cause for its formation.

Etiology of Parotid Abscess:

  • Dehydration, particularly in postsurgical cases (5-7 post-op days) and debilitated patients, with stasis of salivary flow is the predisposing cause.
  • Infection from the oral cavity travels via the Stenson’s duct to invade the parotid gland (retrograde spread of infection). The most common organism is Staphylococcus aureus but Streptococci, anaerobic organisms, and rarely the gram negative organisms have also been cultured.
question: A 50-year-old man with multiple comorbidities, post-op day 5 of major abdominal surgery has developed high-grade fever and swelling over the parotid area. On examination, there is tenderness, induration and pus exuding from the Stenson’s duct on applying pressure over the parotids. Which of the following options is not a likely cause for the above condition?

correctAnswer: D. Wait for the swelling to become fluctuant before performing I & D
explanationHtml:
In a case of a parotid abscess, one must never wait for fluctuation or pus point to occur. This is because the superficial layer of parotidomasseteric fascia is tense, and the fluctuation will be apparent only in later stages.

A parotid abscess refers to an infection and pus formation in the parotid space. It is caused most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. Post-surgical cases and debilitated patients with stasis of salivary flow are at risk of developing parotid abscesses.

Patients typically present with unilateral swelling, redness, induration, and tenderness over the parotid gland and angle of the mandible. Dehydration and fever are also present. Diagnosis is by ultrasonography or a CT scan. Multiple small loculi of pus are seen in the parenchyma. Aspiration of abscess can be done to determine the culture and sensitivity of the infective agent.

Correction of dehydration, improving oral hygiene, and promoting salivary flow are required. Intravenous antibiotics are also used in treatment.

Surgical drainage under local or general anesthesia is carried out by a preauricular incision as employed for parotidectomy. A skin flap is raised to expose the surface of the gland, and the abscess or abscesses are bluntly opened, working parallel to the branches of the CN VII. The skin incision is loosely approximated over a drain and allowed to heal by secondary intention.

options.text: Put an incision that is similar to parotidectomy
Blunt dissection of the pus pockets
Dissection parallel to the facial nerve branches
Wait for the swelling to become fluctuant before performing I &amp; D

question: A patient with a parotid abscess is planned for incision and drainage (I & D). Which of the following practices will you avoid in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The above patient with odynophagia, trismus, swelling in the floor of the mouth with a woody-hard feel, and the tongue is pushed up and back is likely to have Ludwig's angina.

Ludwig's angina is the infection of the submandibular space present on the floor of the mouth. The mylohyoid muscle divides this space into the sublingual space (above the mylohyoid) and the submaxillary and submental compartment (below the mylohyoid). Dental infections are the most common cause.

The infections are usually polymicrobial. Alpha-hemolytic streptococci, staphylococci, and Bacteroides groups are commonly associated.

Patients present with difficulty in swallowing (odynophagia) and trismus. Examination of the oral cavity will reveal that the floor of the mouth is swollen and the tongue is pushed up and back. The submental and submandibular spaces become swollen, tender, and have a woody-hard feel.

It is treated by systemic antibiotics, incision and drainage of the abscess, and tracheostomy if the airway is threatened.

Ludwig's angina can cause a range of complications like:

  • Spread of infection to the -
    • Parapharyngeal space
    • Retropharyngeal space
    • Mediastinum
  • Obstruction of airway due to laryngeal edema
  • Sepsis
  • Aspiration pneumonia.

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Parapharyngeal abscess can occur from acute and chronic infections of the tonsils, dental infections, and infections of the parotid, retropharyngeal and submaxillary spaces. Patients with anterior compartment involvement present with prolapse of the tonsil and tonsillar pillar, trismus, and external swelling behind the angle of the jaw, and patients with posterior compartment involvement present with bulges of the pharynx behind the posterior pillar, paralysis of cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII and sympathetic chain, and swelling of the parotid region. Symptoms common to both compartments are fever, odynophagia, sore throat, torticollis, and signs of toxemia.

Option B: An acute retropharyngeal abscess usually occurs in children below 3 years of age due to infections of adenoids or tonsils causing suppuration in the retropharyngeal lymph nodes which leads to the formation of an abscess. The clinical features of a retropharyngeal abscess include dysphagia, dyspnea, stridor, croupy cough, torticollis (extended stiff neck), and swelling on one side of the midline. (Posterior pharyngeal wall)

The image given below shows the X-ray of the retropharyngeal abscess.

[[figure-2]]

Option D: Vincent's angina presents with low-grade fever, sore throat, and a membrane over the tonsil. The membrane is easily removed to reveal irregular ulcers over the tonsil. A throat swab will show both the organisms typical of the disease, namely fusiform bacilli and spirochaetes, specifically Borrelia vincentii.
question: A 50-year-old male with poor dental hygiene complaints of painful swallowing, difficulty in opening his mouth, and a neck swelling which has been increasing over the past 3 days. On examination, there is a woody hard swelling of the floor of the mouth. What is the possible diagnosis?

Angiofibroma is a histologically benign tumor but locally aggressive. It is a rare tumor, though it is the commonest of all benign tumors of the nasopharynx.

Angiofibroma arises from the sphenopalatine foramen. Recurrent spontaneous epistaxis is the most common presentation of angiofibroma.

The investigation of choice is a CECT scan. There is anterior bowing of the maxillary sinus's posterior wall, which is referred to as the Holman-Miller sign/ antral sign.

Surgery is the treatment of choice. Radiotherapy is used for tumors with intracranial extension. Chemotherapy is used in combination with surgery or as monotherapy when surgery is contraindicated.
question: What type of lesion is angiofibroma?

explanationHtml:
The image shows a nasopharyngeal mass suggestive of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), which is causing difficulty in breathing and swallowing. It is more common in males.

The tumor is predominantly seen in adolescent males in the second decade of life. It is thought to be testosterone dependent. Patients have a hamartomatous nidus of vascular tissue in the nasopharynx which is activated to form angiofibroma when male sex hormones appear.

A biopsy is contraindicated due to the risk of severe bleeding. The vessels lack contractile components and hence bleeding cannot be controlled with adrenaline.

question: A 16-year-old boy presents to you with complaints of nasal obstruction and frequent nose bleeds. CT scan shows Holman-Miller sign. You suspect a benign tumour of the nasopharynx. What is its most common site of origin?

explanationHtml:
Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma presents with rhinolalia clausa (hyponasal speech), not rhinolalia aperta (hypernasal speech).

The patients present with progressive nasal obstruction and hyponasal speech due to a mass in the postnasal space. Profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous epistaxis is the most common presentation. The patients may be markedly anemic due to repeated blood loss.

Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion occur due to obstruction of the eustachian tube.

It can spread to the orbit, giving rise to proptosis and broadening of the nasal bridge, giving rise to frog face deformity. Other features include swelling of the cheek and cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, and VI) due to orbital involvement.
question: Which of the following features will not be seen in a patient with nasopharyngeal angiofibroma?

explanationHtml:
Angiofibroma is made of vascular tissue, which consists of endothelium-lined spaces without muscular or elastic fibres or an incomplete muscular coat and stromal cells. The lack of elastic tissue is responsible for the inability to contract.

This accounts for severe bleeding as the vessels lose the ability to contract. Hence, the bleeding cannot be controlled by the application of adrenaline. Therefore, biopsy is contraindicated.
question: A mother brought her 16-year-old boy with a unilateral profuse nosebleed. After successful control of bleeding, a CT scan confirmed the diagnosis of juvenile angiofibroma. What is the reason for it to cause excessive bleeding?

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, when it spreads to the orbit, leads to proptosis and broadening of the nasal bridge, giving rise to frog-face deformity.

Other options:

Option A: Gorilla-like facies are seen in acromegaly.

Option C: Chipmunk facies is seen in thalassemia.

Option D: Lion-like facies are seen in Paget's disease of bone when craniofacial bones are involved.

Carotid angiography shows the extent of the tumor, its vascularity, and feeding vessels which mostly come from the external carotid system. Embolization of vessels can be done at this time to decrease bleeding at operation.

A biopsy is contraindicated in this condition as it can lead to massive hemorrhage.

question: Imaging of a patient with recurrent epistaxis shows the following finding. Which of the following statements is false about his condition?

explanationHtml:
The mass has spread into the sphenoid sinus with no lateral extension, so it's stage 1B according to the Radkowski classification.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Multiple classification systems exist for the staging of juvenile nasal angiofibroma, of which the most commonly used ones are the Fisch and Radkowski classification systems:

Staging of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Radkowski et al):

Stage Spread
IA Limited to the nose and/or nasopharyngeal vault
IB Extension into ≥ 1 sinus
IIA Minimal extension into the pterygopalatine fossa
IIB Full occupation of the pterygopalatine fossa with or without erosion of orbital bones
IIC Infratemporal fossa with or without cheek or posterior to the pterygoid plates
IIIA Erosion of the skull base-minimal intracranial
IIIB Erosion of skull base-extensive intracranial with or without cavernous sinus

Fisch staging system of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma:

Type Details
1 Tumour limited to the nasopharyngeal cavity; bone destruction negligible or limited to the sphenopalatine foramen
2 Tumour invading the pterygopalatine fossa or the maxillary, ethmoid, or sphenoid sinus with bone destruction
3 A: Tumour invading the infratemporal fossa or orbital region without intracranial involvement
B: Tumour invading the infratemporal fossa or orbital region with intracranial extradural (parasellar) involvement
4 A: Intracranial intradural tumor without infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm
B: Intracranial intradural tumor with infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm

Note: The Fisch system is considered to be the more robust and practical of the two.
question: A teenager has a mass in his nasopharynx that has minimally spread into the sphenoid sinus with no lateral extension. Which stage of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma could this be?

explanationHtml:
The clinical picture suggests that of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Based on Radkowski classification, it is stage IIB as the mass occupies the pterygopalatine fossa. Surgery is the mainstay of treatment for angiofibroma for stage I and stage II tumors.

Other options:

Option B: Hormonal therapy was used in the past, but not anymore.

Option C: Radiotherapy is indicated in stage III where there is an intracranial extension or when the tumor is unresectable. Recurrent angiofibroma can be treated by Intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) - a newer mode of treatment.

Option D: Chemotherapy can be used for very aggressive recurrent tumors and residual lesions.

Stages of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma:

Stage Spread
IA Limited to the nose and/or nasopharyngeal vault
IB Extension into ≥ 1 sinus
IIA Minimal extension into the pterygopalatine fossa
IIB Full occupation of the pterygopalatine fossa with or without erosion of orbital bones
IIC Infratemporal fossa with or without cheek or posterior to the pterygoid plates
IIIA Erosion of the skull base-minimal intracranial
IIIB Erosion of skull base-extensive intracranial with or without cavernous sinus

question: Which of the following viruses is related to etiology of nasopharyngeal carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is also known as Guangdong tumor. This is because the Southern Chinese province of Guangdong has the highest prevalence of the tumor.

Chinese, especially from southeastern China (Canton), have a higher genetic susceptibility to nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC). Chinese emigrants are also genetically more susceptible; however, the susceptibility falls in subsequent generations.

Other South-East Asian countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, and people of Mongoloid origin are also more susceptible.
question: What is nasopharyngeal carcinoma also known as?

explanationHtml:
Human papillomavirus is not associated with a high incidence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma in high-risk populations of China. EBV (Epstein Barr virus) causes nasopharyngeal carcinoma. HPV(Human papillomavirus) causes inverted papilloma of the nose.

High-risk populations such as the Chinese have a very high incidence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. The following factors have been implicated in the pathogenesis:

  • Burning of incense or wood (polycyclic hydrocarbons)
  • Consumption of preserved salted fish (nitrosamines)
  • Vitamin C deficient diet (vitamin C blocks nitrosification of amines and is thus protective)
